Here, using simultaneous recordings of heartbeat and behavior in tethered Drosophila, we show that mechanical threat triggers locomotion together with rapid cardiac deceleration. We identify two pairs of dopaminergic neurons, termed DA-WED neurons, that mediate this cardiac response. Silencing these neurons markedly attenuates threat-induced cardiac deceleration, whereas optogenetic activation induces cardiac deceleration in the absence of threat. Two-photon calcium imaging further shows that DA-WED neurons are activated by mechanical threat, and manipulating their activity bidirectionally modulates threat-induced locomotion. Linking cardiac dynamics to behavior, direct optogenetic manipulation of cardiomyocytes that quantitatively reproduces threat-evoked cardiac deceleration is accompanied by increased locomotion. Together, these results identify a dopaminergic descending pathway that links threat processing to cardiac modulation and suggest that cardiac dynamics may contribute to shaping defensive behavior.

articles.title: Gcn5 and mTORC1 mediated regulation of autophagy controls Drosophila blood cell homeostasis
articles.abstract: Blood progenitors are regulated by a variety of systemic and nutritional cues from their environment. In the Drosophila lymph gland (LG), the Posterior Signaling Center acts as a stem cell niche striking a balance between progenitors and differentiated blood cells. Autophagy is a vital cellular process that maintains homeostasis by removing unnecessary or dysfunctional cell components through autophagic degradation and recycling. Here, using genetic perturbation analysis, we show that autophagy plays a critical role in regulating LG blood cell homeostasis. General control non-derepressible 5 (Gcn5), a histone acetyltransferase, is expressed in the primary LG lobe, and modulation of Gcn5 levels perturbs LG homeostasis. Our results show that hemocyte-specific Gcn5 modulation controls autophagic flux in the hemocytes. Furthermore, we show that modulation of mTORC1 activity can perturb hematopoiesis. Our results indicate that organismal Gcn5 levels respond to dietary shifts and are modulated by mTORC1 signaling. Chemical intervention shows that mTORC1 overrides the effect exerted by Gcn5 in regulating LG hematopoiesis. Taken together, our findings demonstrate that Gcn5 and mTORC1 regulate autophagy to maintain blood cell homeostasis in Drosophila.

articles.title: Spectraplakin is required for dendritic microtubule organization via a tip-based mechanism in Drosophila
articles.abstract: The differential microtubule organization in axons and dendrites underlies neuronal polarity and developmental processes, like neurite pruning. How neurons achieve their specific microtubule organization during development is an area of active research, and it has been especially hard to explain how dendritic microtubules are oriented with their plus ends toward the soma. Transient microtubule nucleation from tips of early growing dendrites has been proposed as a mechanism that would explain how this orientation is set up. In a survey for cytoskeletal regulators involved in dendrite pruning and microtubule organization in Drosophila, we found the spectraplakin Short stop (Shot), an actin/microtubule crosslinker. Loss of Shot causes microtubule orientation defects already during early dendrite development, when Shot is transiently recruited to tips of growing dendrites via its actin-binding domain. Genetic and functional evidence suggests that Shot’s primary function in this process is to locally stabilize microtubules. We also provide evidence for an independent, developmentally transient microtubule nucleation mechanism. Our data highlight the importance of transient and localized microtubule regulation for dendritic microtubule organization.

articles.title: A multi-center retrospective chart analysis identifying clinical, biochemical, and radiographic signatures of short-chain enoyl-CoA hydratase (ECHS1) deficiency
articles.abstract: Short-chain enoyl-CoA hydratase (ECHS1) catalyzes the hydration of C4-C6 acyl-CoA molecules to produce ATP in fatty acid {beta}-oxidation. Deficiency of the ECHS1 enzyme, ECHS1D, is a rare autosomal recessive disorder that presents with a large and pleomorphic clinical spectrum. We present the largest comprehensive study of known diagnosed ECHS1D patients to date, reporting 26 new patients and 8 novel variants in conjunction with a literature review of 87 previously reported patients. All patients were categorized into neonatal, infantile, and late-onset groups based on age of onset and clinical course. Neonatal-onset cases were characterized by early and severe multisystem disease, often with lactic acidosis, hypotonia, cardiomyopathy, and high early mortality (62.5%). The infantile-onset group was heterogeneous, but many exhibited hallmark features such as dystonia, developmental delay, and basal ganglia involvement on neuroimaging. Mortality was significantly lower than the neonatal cohort (24.4%). Late-onset patients had more localized neurologic symptoms, particularly dystonia, and significantly lower mortality overall (0%). Moreover, we report a 37.5% survival rate in newly reported neonatal onset patients compared with 18.2% in prior reports, possibly reflective of earlier recognition of ECHS1D and greater utilization of therapies including N-acetylcysteine, sodium dichloroacetate, and valine-restricted diet.

articles.title: Anticholinergic Medications and Health in Adults with Autism or Intellectual Disability
articles.abstract: Objective: Contributors to autistic adults' elevated risk for negative aging-related outcomes, including Alzheimer's disease and related dementias (ADRD), falls, and mortality remain underexplored. One candidate factor is exposure to medications with anticholinergic (AC) effects. Thus, this study assessed prevalence of medications with AC effects, and their associations with ADRD, falls, and mortality across four groups: autism-only, autism+intellectual disability (ID), ID-only, and controls. Methods: We conducted a retrospective cohort study of 2017-2019 US linked Medicare and Medicaid claims data for 40+ year-olds. Autism, ID, ADRD, and falls were identified using validated algorithms, and mortality was based on Medicare/Medicaid death indicators. Medications were coded using a comprehensive AC potency scale. AC medication exposure effects and interactions between AC potency and group were examined using modified Poisson regressions. Sensitivity analyses to address indication bias excluded persons prescribed antidepressant and/or antipsychotic medication(s). Results: All three clinical groups experienced significantly greater AC medication exposure (autism+ID: 92.5%>ID-only: 88.6%>autism-only: 80.0%) than non-autistic/non-ID controls (61.3%). Additionally, AC medications were more frequently associated with ADRD, falls, and mortality in all of these groups. Stepwise associations between AC potency levels and ADRD, falls, and mortality were found, and these effects were more prominent for persons with autism and/or ID relative to the control sample. Interpretation: This study provides a foundational examination of exposure to AC medication effects and their associations with aging-related outcomes in middle-age and older autistic adults and adults with ID. AC medication exposure represents one potential modifiable risk factor for negative aging-related outcomes in these groups.

articles.title: Application of Machine Learning and Deep Learning in diagnosis Covid19
articles.abstract: Predicting the progression of COVID-19 in hospitalised patients was an important challenge during the pandemic, particularly when healthcare resources were limited. This study investigates the use of machine learning (ML) and deep learning (DL) models to predict three clinical outcomes: death, admission to the intensive care unit (ICU), and clinical status (improvement or worsening). The study uses two patient datasets: an Algerian cohort of 80 patients from the Internal Medicine Department of the University Hospital Centre of Constantine, collected between July and August 2020, and a French cohort of 99 patients collected between March and May 2020. Five ML classifiers were evaluated: logistic regression (LR), k-nearest neighbours (KNN), classification and regression trees (CART), Naive Bayes (NB), and support vector machines (SVM). Their performance was examined in combination with three feature-selection methods: analysis of variance (ANOVA), mutual information (MI), and recursive feature elimination (RFE). The results were also compared with multilayer perceptron (MLP) models using one to five hidden layers. Model evaluation included 30 repetitions of five-fold cross-validation on the training data, followed by evaluation on a separate hold-out test set. The results showed that selecting 20 features generally provided better cross-validated accuracy than selecting 30 features or using the full feature set. The best-performing classifier-feature-selection combination varied across the six dataset-outcome tasks. LR combined with RFE was selected for three tasks, LR combined with ANOVA for one task, and CART combined with ANOVA for two tasks. The selected ML models achieved test-set accuracies ranging from 0.47 to 0.95 and higher accuracy than the average MLP results in five of the six tasks. These findings suggest that ML methods can be useful for exploring clinical outcomes in hospitalised COVID-19 patients. However, the small sample sizes and limitations of the available data mean that the results should be interpreted with caution. Further evaluation using larger and independent patient datasets is needed before these models can be considered for clinical use.

articles.title: Associations of Pathogenic Sequence Variants and Copy Number Variants with Cardiovascular and Major Clinical Outcomes in Adults with Congenital Heart Disease
articles.abstract: Background: Genetic abnormalities contribute to the phenotypic heterogeneity of congenital heart disease, yet their prognostic significance in adults with congenital heart disease remains incompletely understood. We examined the associations of pathogenic sequence variants and copy number variants (CNVs) with cardiovascular and major clinical outcomes in ACHD. Methods: In this prospective observational cohort study, 1,000 adults with structurally confirmed CHD were recruited from a tertiary care center in Noida, India, between January 2022 and January 2026 and followed through August 2026. Participants underwent exome sequencing and chromosomal microarray analysis and were classified into four mutually exclusive groups: reference, sequence-variant-only, CNV-only, and dual-positive. The primary outcome was time to first occurrence of a composite of cardiovascular death, unplanned heart failure hospitalization, resuscitated cardiac arrest, sustained ventricular tachyarrhythmia, heart transplantation, or durable mechanical circulatory support. Associations were evaluated using multivariable Cox regression. Results: Of 1,000 participants, 800 comprised the reference group, 120 had sequence variants only, 60 had CNVs only, and 20 had both sequence variants and CNVs. Over a median follow-up of 4.2 years, the primary outcome occurred in 12.0%, 20.0%, 25.0%, and 30.0% of participants, respectively. In fully adjusted analyses, the sequence-variant-only group had a higher risk of the primary outcome versus the reference group (hazard ratio [HR], 1.65; 95% confidence interval [CI], 1.01?2.69; p=0.0455). The CNV-only group had an HR of 1.92 (95% CI, 1.04?3.52; p=0.0360). Neither association remained significant after Holm adjustment (adjusted p=0.072 for both). The dual-positive group had an HR of 2.12 (95% CI, 0.83?5.42; p=0.1182). Extracardiac congenital anomalies and neurological disorders were more prevalent among individuals with genetic variants, while secondary outcomes showed no significant associations. Conclusions: Pathogenic sequence variants and CNVs were associated with numerically higher risks of adverse cardiovascular outcomes in ACHD, but independent prognostic significance was not established after adjustment for multiple testing.

articles.title: Baseline Severity and Early Multiorgan Failure to Predict In-Hospital Mortality in Critically Ill COVID-19 Patients: A Retrospective Cohort Study
articles.abstract: Background: Intensive Care Unit (ICU) mortality remains high among patients with severe coronavirus disease. Static admission severity scores may fail to capture the dynamic clinical trajectory of critically ill patients. We hypothesized that early multiorgan failure (MOF) at 24 hours would improve mortality discrimination beyond admission severity alone. Methods: Retrospective, single-center cohort study of 345 adults with severe COVID-19 pneumonia admitted to a Spanish ICU (March 2020-December 2022). The primary outcome was all-cause in-hospital mortality. Univariate comparisons between survivors and non-survivors were performed, followed by multivariable logistic regression to identify independent predictors of mortality. Three sequential models were constructed and compared by Area Under the Receiver Operating Characteristic Curve (AUC-ROC) discrimination. Results: Overall, in-hospital mortality was 20.6%. Non-survivors were older and had higher Simplified Acute Physiology Score (SAPS) II and Acute Physiology and Chronic Health Evaluation (APACHE) II scores (p<0.001). MOF at 24 hours was more frequent among non-survivors than survivors (88.4% vs. 61.7%, p<0.001). The baseline model (age, sex, Chronic Obstructive Pulmonary Disease (COPD), hypertension, and SAPS II) achieved an AUC of 0.798 (95% CI 0.742-0.852). The final model incorporating MOF at 24 hours achieved an AUC of 0.812 (95% CI 0.754-0.860); early MOF nearly tripled the odds of death (OR 2.78, 95% CI 1.22-6.33, p=0.015). Conclusions: Combining baseline severity with early multiorgan dysfunction provides a simple, interpretable approach to mortality risk stratification in critically ill COVID-19 patients; however, external validation is needed before it can inform escalation-of-care or treatment-limitation decisions in clinical practice.

articles.title: Beyond Haploinsufficiency: Protein Domain and Variant Class Shape Language Outcomes in SYNGAP1-DEE
articles.abstract: Background SYNGAP1-related developmental and epileptic encephalopathy (SYNGAP1-DEE) is generally considered a haploinsufficiency disorder, yet language development varies considerably between affected individuals. With targeted therapies, including antisense oligonucleotides (ASOs), approaching clinical evaluation, understanding genotype-specific differences is increasingly important. We investigated whether expressive language and functional communication are associated with SynGAP protein domains and variant class. Methods We analyzed cross-sectional caregiver-reported data linked to genetic reports from the international PATRE SYNGAP1 registry. Of 440 participants, 334 had variants that could be assigned to a protein domain and classified as missense (n=79) or truncating/splicing (n=255). Variants were mapped to seven predefined SynGAP protein regions. The primary outcome was a five-level current expressive language score. Secondary outcomes included acquisition of two-word phrases and CFCS-derived functional communication. Each domain was compared with all other regions within the same variant class using nonparametric tests and age-adjusted ordinal or logistic regression. Benjamini-Hochberg false discovery rate correction was applied. Results Missense variants in the C2 domain (aa248-392; n=28) were associated with markedly poorer expressive language (median score 1 vs. 2; age-adjusted OR 0.16, 95% CI 0.06-0.46; q=0.0025). Only 7.1% had acquired two-word phrases compared with 52.0% of individuals with missense variants outside C2 (OR 0.07; q=0.0023). Functional communication was also significantly impaired (OR 0.23, 95% CI 0.09-0.56; q=0.0052). Conversely, truncating/splicing variants in the PH domain (aa103-247; n=50) were associated with better expressive language (median 3 vs. 2; OR 3.52, 95% CI 1.99-6.24; q<0.001) and more frequent acquisition of two-word phrases (62.0% vs. 31.5%). No corresponding language association was observed for C2 truncating/splicing variants or for variants in the RasGAP domain. Conclusions Language outcomes in SYNGAP1-DEE are associated with both variant class and protein location. The marked impairment associated with C2 missense variants contrasts with the relatively preserved language abilities observed in PH truncating/splicing variants, suggesting that SYNGAP1-related disease cannot be fully explained by a uniform haploinsufficiency model alone. These findings support considering protein domain and variant class in future ASO trials, particularly for patient stratification, endpoint selection, and interpretation of treatment outcomes.

articles.title: Clinician Counseling and Patient Storage and Disposal Practices for Opioids Prescribed for Acute Pain: A Multicenter Prospective Cohort Study
articles.abstract: BACKGROUND: Opioids prescribed for acute pain frequently remain unused, creating opportunities for unintended use, accidental ingestion, or diversion. Little is known about counseling patients receive from prescribers or pharmacists on storage and disposal of opioids. OBJECTIVE: To characterize clinician counseling on opioid disposal and patient-reported storage, use, and disposal practices among opioid-naive patients prescribed opioids for acute pain. DESIGN: Multicenter prospective cohort study with participant recruitment between September 2020 and March 2023. PARTICIPANTS: Opioid-naive patients prescribed opioids for acute pain in emergency departments, primary care or urgent care clinics, inpatient settings, and dental practices. MAIN MEASURES: Patient-reported receipt of counseling on the importance of opioid disposal and appropriate disposal methods; opioid storage practices; use and disposition of prescribed opioids; disposal methods; and reasons for keeping or disposing of leftover opioids. KEY RESULTS: Among 1708 participants, the median age was 38 years (IQR, 28-52); most were recruited from emergency departments (n=915; 53.6%) and primary care or urgent care clinics (n=307; 18.0%). Among 1233 participants who answered the question on counseling about the importance of opioid disposal, 811 (65.8%) reported receiving no counseling. Among 1220 participants who answered the question on counseling about appropriate disposal methods, 832 (68.2%) reported receiving no counseling. Among 812 participants who answered the question about storing opioids in a locked location, 610 (75.1%) reported never doing so. Among 929 participants providing information on opioid leftovers and disposition, 618 (66.5%) did not use all prescribed opioids. Among these 618 participants, 258 (42.8%) kept leftover opioids and 345 (57.2%) disposed of them. Among 256 participants who reported reasons for keeping leftover opioids, 159 (62.1%) wanted medication available for the same condition, 70 (27.3%) wanted medication available for a different condition, and 36 (14.1%) did not know how to properly dispose of the medication. CONCLUSIONS: Among opioid-naive patients prescribed opioids for acute pain, counseling about opioid disposal was uncommon, secure storage was infrequent, and leftover opioids were frequent, with many patients keeping leftover opioids for possible future use. These findings suggest opportunities to improve counseling on opioid storage and disposal and encourage safe disposal of unused opioids after acute pain treatment.

articles.title: Community health workers experiences with a digital clinical decision support system for longitudinal hypertension and diabetes care in rural Lesotho: a mixed-methods study
articles.abstract: Community health workers (CHWs) are increasingly delivering chronic care in resource-constrained settings but require support to manage complex longitudinal clinical workflows. In the Community-Based chronic Care Lesotho (ComBaCaL) project in rural Lesotho, CHWs provide longitudinal hypertension and diabetes care, supported by the ComBaCaL Community Health Toolkit (CHT) application. The application combines longitudinal participant management and task coordination with clinical decision support for screening, diagnosis, treatment initiation and adjustment, cardiovascular risk management, referral, and follow-up for hypertension and diabetes care. This model of care has demonstrated improved or maintained clinical outcomes compared to facility-based care only. We conducted a mixed-methods study among all 103 participating CHWs to evaluate their experiences with the application. All CHWs completed a 38-item questionnaire, and 22 participated in qualitative interviews or focus group discussions. Overall usability was high, with a mean System Usability Scale score of 75.6 (SD 13.0), and 98 (95%) CHWs were satisfied or very satisfied with the application. General application functions and diagnosis and treatment tasks were rated easy or very easy by 98% of participants. The most frequently reported benefits were task reminders (92%), structured clinical guidance (87%), overview of allocated participants (81%), and retention of participant information (81%). Main challenges were lengthy questionnaires, difficulties charging tablets, and limited internet connectivity. Qualitative findings showed that ease of use increased with experience, supported by training and supervision. Participants described how algorithmic guidance and task reminders supported care delivery, while also identifying tensions between standardized workflows and flexibility in day-to-day care. The ComBaCaL CHT application was highly usable and valued by CHWs. High perceived usability extended from general application functions to complex clinical workflows. CHT demonstrated suitability as a configurable framework for implementing such context-specific workflows for hypertension and diabetes care when accompanied by appropriate workflow design, training, and supervision.

articles.title: Cortical Thinning in Adults with Prader-Willi Syndrome: Distribution Across Functional Networks and Associations with BMI and the GH/IGF-1 Axis
articles.abstract: Prader-Willi syndrome (PWS) is a rare neurogenetic disorder associated with neuropsychiatric, metabolic, endocrine, and physical abnormalities. Although previous neuroimaging studies have identified regional gray matter alterations, cortical thickness (CT) abnormalities and their distribution across large-scale functional brain networks remain poorly characterized in adults with PWS. We investigated cortical morphology in 23 adults with PWS and 22 age- and sex-matched healthy controls who underwent structural MRI. Cortical reconstruction and surface-based morphometric analyses were performed using FreeSurfer. Between-group differences in CT were assessed using age, sex, and intracranial volume as covariates. Associations between CT and clinical, cognitive, anthropometric, and endocrine measures were examined using Spearman correlations. Significant cortical regions were further mapped onto an a priori functional network atlas. Adults with PWS showed reduced CT in a left-hemispheric cluster involving the inferior precentral gyrus, insula, inferior temporal cortex, and orbitofrontal cortex. This cluster overlapped predominantly with the somatomotor, auditory, cingulo-opercular, language, and frontoparietal networks. Within the PWS group, lower CT was associated with higher body mass index and poorer global functioning. CT was positively associated with IGF-1 levels and was greater in participants with a history of growth hormone therapy during childhood. These findings indicate cortical thinning across regions belonging to multiple functional networks involved in sensorimotor, attentional, language, and executive processes, extending previous volumetric findings. The associations with body mass index, functional measures, and the GH/IGF-1 axis suggest that cortical morphology may reflect an interplay between genetic vulnerability and potentially modifiable metabolic and endocrine factors, raising the possibility of a neuroprotective role for GH/IGF-1 signaling.

articles.title: Cost Analysis of Vasopressin Use in Septic Shock and Predictive Performance of GOSSIS in ICU Mortality
articles.abstract: Background: Vasopressin is a commonly used adjunctive therapy in the management of septic shock. While vasopressin may provide clinical benefits, at times its acquisition cost has risen to being substantially more expensive than other second-line vasopressors such as epinephrine, phenylephrine, or dopamine. Additionally, mortality prediction tools such as the Global Open-Source Severity of Illness Score (GOSSIS) have emerged as a valuable resource to guide resource allocation in critical care. This study aimed to evaluate the healthcare costs associated with vasopressin use and assess the predictive performance of GOSSIS in patients with septic shock. Methods: We conducted a multi-center retrospective cohort study of adult ICU patients with septic shock treated throughout the UPMC Health System from January 2021 to January 2022. Patients who received norepinephrine as a first-line vasopressor followed by either vasopressin or an alternative vasopressor were included. Generalized linear models with a log link and gamma distribution were used to compare adjusted total healthcare costs. Recycled predictions were used to estimate marginal cost differences. GOSSIS performance was evaluated by comparing predicted versus observed ICU mortality across risk groups. Results: Among 3,898 eligible patients, 1,060 received vasopressin and 2,838 received alternative second-line vasopressors. Vasopressin use was associated with significantly higher adjusted hospital costs (cost ratio = 1.14, 95% CI: 1.08, 1.20). The estimated marginal cost difference was $5,887 per patient. Drug costs accounted for a greater proportion of total hospitalization costs among vasopressin users (20% vs. 12%). GOSSIS demonstrated strong calibration, with predicted ICU mortality closely aligning with observed rates across all severity strata. Conclusions: Vasopressin use in septic shock was associated with a 14% increase in hospitalization costs compared to alternative second-line vasopressors. The GOSSIS demonstrated strong predictive validity for ICU mortality, supporting its potential use in guiding resource allocation decisions in critically ill populations.

articles.title: Deep learning screening of otoscopic images for ENT referral: development, validation and deployment of NHREF OtoScan
articles.abstract: Background. Middle and external ear disease is common and largely treatable, but accurate otoscopic interpretation requires training that is scarce outside specialist ENT services. Published deep learning models for otoscopy report high accuracy, yet most are optimised for closed set classification rather than the referral decision a non specialist actually makes, report uncalibrated probabilities, and do not report the near duplicate controls that video derived otoscopic datasets demand. We developed, validated and deployed a screening aid framed around referral rather than diagnosis. Methods. We merged 4,763 otoscopic images from 16 folders across three public datasets into 12 clinically meaningful classes. Every image was passed through a single field of view normalisation function (crop to the illuminated field, square, resize to 224 px, mask to one fixed circle) shared identically by training and inference, to remove the framing cue that otherwise identifies the source dataset. Because one source is video derived, images were grouped by cosine similarity of generic ImageNet features (threshold 0.93, joined transitively) and whole groups assigned to a single split, giving 3,326 training, 719 validation and 718 test images. A MobileNetV2 backbone initialised from ImageNet was fine tuned from block9expand. Probabilities were averaged over the eight dihedral transforms of each image and temperature scaled. The referral score was one minus the probability of a normal ear, and its threshold was set on the validation abnormal ears as the highest value still meeting a target sensitivity of 97%, applied with an inclusive comparison. Model selection, calibration and threshold were frozen before the test split was scored once. Results. On the 718 held out test images, referral sensitivity was 97.0% (95% CI 95.1 to 98.2) and specificity 75.6% (95% CI 69.4 to 80.8), with AUROC 0.974 for abnormal versus normal; a cluster bootstrap over the 363 similarity groups in the test split widens those intervals to 93.8 99.6% and 66.0 83.4% respectively. Of 501 abnormal ears, 15 were not referred; 11 of these were myringosclerosis and none was cholesteatoma. Twelve class macro F1 was 0.686, balanced accuracy 68.3%, and accuracy 85.0% (86.2% with chronic subtypes merged). Temperature scaling (T = 1.2) reduced expected calibration error from 0.0498 to 0.0430. A low confidence flag fired on 4.0% of test images, separating 87.2% accuracy on unflagged from 31.0% on flagged cases. Recall was consistently highest on the largest source dataset and fell on the other two, for example acute otitis media 95.5% on source A versus 50.0% on source B. Conclusions. A compact, calibrated model run on ordinary CPU hardware achieved the pre specified 97% referral sensitivity with clinically interpretable failure modes. The source stratified gap, and an earlier perceptual hash split that inflated scores until it was corrected, indicate that headline accuracy in this field is strongly dependent on leakage control and acquisition style. The system is deployed with mandatory specialist review, a daily backtest and approval gated retraining, so that prospective performance on local equipment is measured rather than assumed. It is research software and not a medical device.

articles.title: Development and psychometric evaluation of the Severity of Myalgic Encephalomyelitis Scale (SoMES) and the Myalgic Encephalomyelitis Occupational Status Scale (MEOSS)
articles.abstract: Objective: To develop and psychometrically evaluate two new brief assessments measuring disease severity (the Severity of ME Scale, SoMES) and occupational status (the ME Occupational Status Scale, MEOSS) in myalgic encephalomyelitis/chronic fatigue syndrome (ME/CFS) Methods: Draft SoMES and MEOSS were co-produced from relevant literature and lived experience. An online survey completed by adults with ME/CFS and was repeated two weeks later to assess reliability. The SF-36 (physical function) assessed criterion-related validity (Spearmann correlations) and discriminant validity (Kruskal-Wallis tests). Weighted kappa co-efficients assessed test-retest reliability and measurement error calculated minimal detectable difference (MDD). Results: 995 adults with ME/CFS participated and 579 completed the retest survey. Construct validity was confirmed from feedback. Criterion related validity was moderate-good (SoMES r = 0.663, MEOSS r=0.472, both p<0.001). Discriminant validity was demonstrated by significant differences in SF36-PF scores in different levels of SoMES and MEOSS (p=0.003 - 0.0001). SoMES test-retest reliability was moderate (k =0.53, P<0.001) with a MDD of 1.6, and excellent for the MEOSS (k = 0.76 p<.001) and the MDD was 1.4 Conclusions: The Severity of ME Scale (SoMES) and the ME Occupational Status Scale (MEOSS) are valid, reliable, sensitive assessments of ME/CFS severity and occupational status respectively.

articles.title: Diagnostic Value in Discarded Reads: Re-evaluating Multi-Mapping cfDNA Fragmentomics and GC Bias in Early-Stage Cancer.
articles.abstract: Background. Low-coverage plasma cell-free DNA (cfDNA) sequencing is an inexpensive substrate for cancer detection. Standard pipelines discard fragments with low mapping quality, which originate mostly from repetitive DNA, although pericentromeric satellite repeats are frequently hypomethylated in cancer. We asked whether the fraction of multi-mapping cfDNA fragments differs between early-stage cancer and matched healthy controls, and how it compares with conventional fragmentomic features under strict control of technical factors. Methods. We analysed public plasma cfDNA whole-genome sequencing from 25 patients with stage I to III breast cancer and 25 healthy controls matched 1:1 for age, sex, smoking and alcohol use, each pair processed in the same library and sequencing batch, and from 8 early-stage hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) cases with 8 matched controls. For every sample we computed the fraction of autosomal fragments with MAPQ < 30 and the share of these fragments located in centromeric and heterochromatic cytobands, and related them to stage, grade and copy-number deviation as proxies of tumour burden. Classifiers were evaluated by leave-one-pair-out cross-validation in breast cancer and, trained on breast cancer only, applied unchanged to HCC. Robustness to GC content and sequencing depth was tested by within-fold residualisation and by fragment-level GC weighting. Conventional fragmentomic features (fragment length, end motifs, copy number, DELFI-like profiles and window features at transcription start sites) were evaluated under four GC-handling analyses. Results. The multi-mapping fraction was higher in breast cancer than in matched controls (median 5.38 % vs 5.19 %; higher in 19/25 pairs; paired p = 0.0006; cross-validated AUC 0.81, 95 % CI 0.67 - 0.94), in stage I (9/10 pairs), stage II (7/10) and stage III (3/5) disease and in every sequencing batch. The excess was concentrated in centromeric and heterochromatic bands, whose share of multi-mapping fragments rose from 22.0 % to 23.4 % (19/25 pairs; p = 0.004). Both signals persisted after within-fold adjustment for GC content and/or depth (AUC 0.64 - 0.76 for the multi-mapping fraction, 0.71 - 0.76 for the heterochromatic share) and under fragment-level GC weighting (18/25 pairs; p = 0.003). The multi-mapping difference was largest in stage I and decreased with stage (Spearman {rho} = -0.42, p = 0.04), and neither feature was associated with grade or copy-number deviation. In public tissue methylomes, satellites were hypomethylated in breast tumours to a similar extent as other late-replicating DNA, but the bin-level association between tumour hypomethylation and the cfDNA excess was weak and was explained by GC content. In HCC, the pre-specified endpoint, the breast-trained multi-mapping model, was not met (AUC 0.73; 5/8 pairs; sign test p = 0.36). In an exploratory analysis that was not pre-specified, the heterochromatic share was higher in 7/8 HCC pairs (p = 0.016; locked AUC 0.86, 95 % CI 0.62 - 1.00); across all 33 pairs, including the discovery pairs, it was higher in the cancer case in 26 (post hoc sign test p = 0.0007). In contrast, conventional fragmentomic features reached AUC 0.71 (breast) and 0.77 (HCC) only without fragment-level GC control; they tracked the per-sample coverage GC dependence and fell to chance under each of three GC-controlled analyses, including one that preserves promoter-specific signal. Conclusions. Multi-mapping cfDNA fragments, which are routinely discarded, differed between early-stage breast cancer and batch-matched controls, largely independently of GC content and sequencing depth, with an excess in centromeric and heterochromatic DNA. The signal did not scale with stage, its biological origin is unproven, and a read-quality contribution cannot be excluded from fragment files. It is a candidate marker that requires confirmation in larger cohorts with raw reads and tumour-fraction estimates.

articles.title: Door-to-Valve Time and Clinical Outcomes in Acute Decompensated Severe Aortic Stenosis: Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis
articles.abstract: Background: Acute decompensated aortic stenosis (ADAS) carries high mortality, but the optimal timing of valve intervention is unknown. Objective: To assess the association between time to valve intervention (transcatheter aortic valve replacement [TAVR] or balloon aortic valvuloplasty [BAV]) and clinical outcomes in ADAS. Methods: Embase, Ovid MEDLINE and CENTRAL were searched to May 15, 2026. Hazard ratios (HRs) for delayed versus earlier intervention were pooled using random-effects models with modified Hartung-Knapp inference. Unadjusted short-term mortality risk ratios (RRs) were pooled using the Mantel-Haenszel method. Results: Eight observational cohort studies (n=6,044) met inclusion criteria: six TAVR (n= 5,986) and two BAV (n=58) studies. Patients were approximately 79 years old, and 63% were male. Early-intervention thresholds ranged from <24-48 hours (BAV) to ?22 days (TAVR) from admission. Delayed intervention was not significantly associated with long-term all-cause mortality (HR 1.52, 95% CI 0.46-5.00; p=0.269; I2=58.2%) or mortality per five-day delay (HR 1.09, 95% CI 0.34-3.43; p=0.530; I2=86.7%). Crude short-term mortality was higher with delayed intervention (RR 4.96, 95% CI 1.17-20.92; p=0.029; I2=0.0%), although this association was not robust to sensitivity analyses. Most studies were at serious risk of bias, with substantial heterogeneity in clinical severity, intervention timing, and treatment modality. Conclusion: Point estimates favour earlier intervention, but current observational data do not establish a mortality benefit for an optimal door-to-valve interval, and existing study designs are biased against early treatment. Prospective and randomized-controlled trials on optimal valve intervention timing following ADAS are needed.

articles.title: Dynamic changes in plasma sphingosine-1-phosphate concentrations and mortality in sepsis: a prospective cohort study in the emergency department
articles.abstract: Background Sepsis is a dynamic process with evolving host responses, biomarker changes, and organ dysfunction. Sphingosine-1-phosphate (S1P) is a bioactive lipid involved in endothelial and immune regulation. However, the clinical relevance of dynamic S1P changes in sepsis remains unclear. This study aimed to assess their association with mortality. Methods We conducted a prospective cohort study of adults recruited from the emergency department of Wan Fang Hospital between April 2022 and October 2024. Plasma S1P was measured by ELISA on days 1, 3, and before discharge or death. The primary outcome was 60-day mortality. S1P trajectories were defined by baseline concentrations and longitudinal slopes estimated using linear mixed-effects models. Low-decreasing, low-stable, and high-decreasing trajectories were grouped as descending; the others as ascending. Cox proportional hazards models assessed mortality associations with baseline S1P, trajectory groups, and time-varying S1P. Results Among 278 participants, 156 had sepsis. Baseline S1P concentrations were lower in patients with sepsis (82.2 [IQR, 47.8-141.1] ng/mL) than in those with non-septic infection (129.2 [IQR, 68.1-306.9] ng/mL) and non-infected controls (132.8 [IQR, 74.1-300.2] ng/mL). In the sepsis cohort, 101 patients were classified into the descending S1P trajectory group and 55 into the ascending group. The descending group had a higher hazard of 60-day mortality (adjusted hazard ratio [aHR] 3.43; 95% confidence interval [CI], 1.11-10.58; p = 0.032). Baseline S1P was not significantly associated with 60-day mortality (aHR 1.004 per 10 ng/mL decrease; 95% CI, 0.977-1.032; p = 0.803). Each 10 ng/mL decrease in time-varying S1P was associated with a 3.5% higher mortality hazard (aHR 1.035; 95% CI, 1.002-1.076; p = 0.041). Conclusions Declining plasma S1P over time was associated with higher mortality in sepsis. Dynamic changes in S1P may be clinically relevant beyond baseline levels.

articles.title: Early Valve Replacement vs Surveillance in Moderate Aortic Stenosis: Meta-Analysis of Randomized and Observational Evidence
articles.abstract: BACKGROUND: Moderate aortic stenosis (AS) is associated with excess mortality, and 2 randomized trials have tested early transcatheter aortic valve replacement (TAVR). OBJECTIVES: The authors sought to estimate the effects of early TAVR vs clinical surveillance and to compare randomized with observational estimates. METHODS: Six databases and registries were searched through November 3, 2026. Adjusted observational studies were synthesized separately from trials. Certainty was rated with GRADE. RESULTS: Two trials (922 patients; TAVR UNLOAD, n = 178, HF with reduced ejection fraction; PROGRESS, n = 744, 96.4% symptomatic) and 7 cohorts were included. Early TAVR did not detectably change death over approximately 2 years (HR: 1.05; 95% CI: 0.74-1.49; low certainty), with one-fifth of the deaths needed to detect a 20% reduction. Heart failure (HF) hospitalization was lower (RR: 0.53; 95% CI: 0.36-0.77; low certainty), or 70 fewer patients per 1,000 at 2 years. New pacemakers were more frequent (PROGRESS: 17.3% vs 9.3%; moderate certainty). About half of surveillance patients underwent valve replacement within 2 years. Observational cohorts estimated a 48% mortality reduction (HR: 0.52; 95% CI: 0.43-0.64; very low certainty), which differed from the randomized estimate (ratio of HRs: 2.01; 95% CI: 1.37-2.95). CONCLUSIONS: In older, predominantly symptomatic patients with moderate AS, early TAVR may make little or no difference to 2-year mortality and may reduce HF hospitalization, at the cost of more pacemakers. Because about half of patients under surveillance receive a valve within 2 years, the decision largely concerns timing. Observational survival estimates should not guide practice.

articles.title: Efficacy and Clinical Predictors of Topical NSAIDs as Bridging Therapy for Diabetic Macular Edema: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis
articles.abstract: Introduction & Objectives: Diabetic Macular Edema (DME) is a primary cause of vision loss. While anti-VEGF injections are the gold standard, prolonged referral delays in primary care settings often lead to irreversible photoreceptor damage. This study aims to evaluate the efficacy of topical Non-Steroidal Anti-Inflammatory Drugs (NSAIDs) as a temporary bridging therapy and to develop a new clinical scoring system to guide primary care physicians in early intervention. Methods: A systematic review was conducted to identify clinical predictors of responses to topical NSAIDs in DME patients, followed by a meta-analysis to calculate pooled Odds Ratios (OR) for each predictor. These values underwent natural log transformation (beta = ln(OR)) to derive a point-based clinical scoring system. Result: Twelve studies were analyzed. Predictor variables and assigned points derived from pooled ORs included: glycemic control (HbA1c < 8.0%; OR 2.41, 9 points), symptom duration (< 6 months; OR 2.11, 7 points), baseline visual acuity (> 6/12; OR 1.96, 7 points), and retinopathy stage (mild-to-moderate NPDR; OR 1.77, 5 points). The proposed 28-point scoring system categorizes patients into three tiers: High Probability (21-28 points) for immediate NSAID initiation; Moderate Probability (12-20 points) for combined systemic optimization; and Low Probability (0-11 points) for prioritized emergency referral. Evidence confirms that potent topical NSAIDs effectively stabilize macular thickness and prevent exudative progression during the referral window. Conclusion: This study concludes that the OR-derived scoring system effectively empowers primary care physicians to manage DME during referral windows. Topical NSAIDs serve as a safe, low-risk bridging strategy to mitigate permanent vision loss and reduce the burden of blindness in resource-limited settings.

articles.title: Epidemiology of acute respiratory infections in adult patients in Hospices Civils de Lyon, France, between October 2016 and April 2025
articles.abstract: Background Multiple viruses can cause acute respiratory infections (ARI), impacting morbidity, mortality and hospital resources. The objective of this study was to describe viral circulation among patients with ARI, patients characteristics and severity outcomes. Methods A retrospective cohort was assembled using electronic health records from the Hospices Civils de Lyon, France. Adult patients ([≥]18 years) hospitalised or presenting to the emergency department from October 2016 to April 2025 with either an ICD-10 diagnostic code for ARI or a laboratory-confirmed viral detection were included. Administrative variables and laboratory results collected during the stay were extracted. Results 103,011 hospital visits involving 82,077 patients were included. The number of eligible stays increased substantially since the COVID-19 pandemic, along with year-round laboratory testing. Following disruption during the pandemic, winter peaks of ARI incidence, influenza and RSV detections re-emerged after 2022. Influenza, rhinovirus and SARS-CoV-2 positivity rates peaked in younger adults (<65 years), whereas RSV and hMPV positivity rates were highest in patients aged [≥]80 years. Patients aged [≥]65 years had longer hospitalisations (median 10 vs 8 days, p<0.001), twice in-hospital mortality rate (14% vs 7%, p<0.001), less frequent ICU admission (21% vs 33%, p<0.001) and use of respiratory support than younger adults. Influenza was the virus associated with the shortest length of stays, hMPV was associated with the longest in younger adults. Conclusions Real-world hospital data are valuable for surveillance of viral circulation, early identification of patients at risk of deterioration, and may be used to evaluate the impact of preventive intervention in community.

articles.title: Epstein-Barr virus influences the induction of protective antibody responses in young African children vaccinated with the RTS,S malaria vaccine
articles.abstract: The RTS,S vaccine provides moderate protection against malaria in children, which may be due in part to environmental factors. Cytomegalovirus (CMV) and Epstein-Barr virus (EBV) infections are prevalent in Africa and potentially contribute to suboptimal vaccine responses. We evaluated whether latent CMV/EBV infections impact RTS,S-induced antibodies in 314 vaccinated children aged 5-29 months in West Africa. While no strong associations were observed for CMV, children seropositive for EBV had lower antigen-specific IgG and IgA, which have been linked with protective malaria immunity. These results may partly explain why malaria vaccines are suboptimal in populations where early CMV/EBV infections are prevalent.

articles.title: Estimated impacts of mandatory sodium reformulation targets on sodium consumption, health outcomes, health sector costs and health equity in Aotearoa New Zealand
articles.abstract: Aims Cardiovascular disease (CVD) is the leading cause of death in Aotearoa New Zealand (NZ), including for M[a]ori, the Indigenous population. Sodium intake is a modifiable CVD risk factor. In 2021, the World Health Organization (WHO) released sodium reduction benchmarks for 58 packaged food categories. We aimed to estimate the health, health-sector cost, and equity impacts of mandating these benchmarks in NZ. Methods Nationally representative data on household food purchases, packaged food sodium content, and dietary intake were used to estimate baseline sodium consumption (2011) and changes following implementation of the WHO benchmarks. A dietary multi-state life-table model estimated impacts on health-adjusted life years (HALYs) and health system costs (2011 NZ$, 3% discount rate) over the remaining lifetime of the 2011 NZ population (n = 4.4 million). Analyses examined impacts by sex and for M[a]ori. Results Mandatory reformulation was estimated to reduce sodium intake by 470 mg/day per person (1.18 g salt), a 22% reduction from baseline. Across population groups, age-standardised reductions ranged from 380 to 660 mg/day (22-23%), generating an estimated 55,600 HALYs (95% uncertainty interval 19,100-90,000) and NZ$535.2 million in health-system cost savings (95% UI: 183.0-914.6 million) over the population lifetime. M[a]ori gained 11,600 HALYs (95% UI: 4,900-17,700), equivalent to 17.2 HALYs per 1,000 population, compared with 11.8 per 1,000 among non-M[a]ori. Conclusion Mandating WHO sodium benchmarks in NZ could substantially reduce sodium intake, improve population health, reduce health sector costs, and advance health equity. Findings support adoption of this strategy in Aotearoa NZ.

articles.title: Estimation of fine-scale spatial heterogeneity in treatment effects in a large cluster-randomized trial
articles.abstract: Treatment effects in randomized trials may vary geographically, and estimating this variation is a broadly generalizable problem for large-scale, cluster-randomized trials. We conducted a secondary analysis of AVENIR, a cluster-randomized, placebo-controlled trial of biannual azithromycin distribution among children aged 1-59 months in Dosso, Niger (2020-2023). We assessed whether the survival benefit of mass azithromycin distribution varied geographically using Poisson models to estimate spatially continuous child mortality and average treatment effects (ATE). Among 1390 villages (276,452 person-years; 3635 deaths), the overall mortality rate was 13.1 and the ATE was -2.6 deaths per 1000 person-years. Mortality was highest in the south, whereas treatment benefit was concentrated in the southeast, following a northwest-southeast gradient. Aggregation of data to 160 primary health catchment areas preserved broad spatial patterns in mortality but attenuated local heterogeneity, suggesting that health catchment monitoring is sufficient for broad mortality surveillance. Examining unit-level, spatially predicted treatment effects as a function of mortality rate demonstrated that underlying mortality captured much, but not all, of the heterogeneity in treatment effects. The analysis demonstrates how to estimate localized treatment effects in large cluster-randomized trials and provides new insights into spatial heterogeneity in mortality and benefits of azithromycin distribution in Niger.

articles.title: Feeling Too Much or Too Little: Alexithymia Moderates How Self-Reported Physiological Hyperarousal Shapes Risky Decisions
articles.abstract: Background: Embodied cognition frameworks propose that physiological states shape decision-making, yet the contribution of sustained threat-related hyperarousal and individual differences in interoceptive integration remains poorly understood. This study examined whether self-reported physiological hyperarousal predicted Prospect Theory decision parameters: loss aversion, value sensitivity, and choice consistency; and whether alexithymia moderated these associations. Methods: Sixty-eight healthy young adults (M age = 18.94, SD = 1.46; 85% women) completed the DASS-21 anxiety subscale as a measure of hyperarousal, the TAS-20 as a measure of alexithymia, and a 64-trial Mixed Gambles Task; individual Prospect Theory parameters were estimated via hierarchical Bayesian analysis. Moderation analyses were conducted using Hayes' PROCESS macro with Johnson-Neyman probing. Results: Self-reported hyperarousal negatively predicted choice consistency and value sensitivity, but not loss aversion. Alexithymia moderated both effects through distinct conditional patterns: the self-reported hyperarousal-choice consistency association was significant only below a TAS-20 threshold of 51.05 (67.65% of the sample), reflecting monotonic buffering; the self-reported hyperarousal value sensitivity association was significant within a bounded TAS-20 range (45.31-66.08), suggesting that intermediate alexithymia constitutes a zone of maximal vulnerability, though this model only reached trend significance and should be treated as exploratory. No effects emerged for loss aversion. Conclusion: These findings indicate that sustained hyperarousal could selectively degrade evaluative precision and decision consistency, while leaving loss aversion intact. Alexithymia may operate as a stage-specific, conditional moderator of the body-decision relationship.

articles.title: Figure format and the accuracy of AI-assisted reconstruction of Kaplan-Meier survival data
articles.abstract: Reconstructing participant-level data from published Kaplan-Meier curves supports meta-analysis and other secondary survival analyses when original trial records are unavailable. Researchers may use original PDF figures or screenshots, which can look alike but retain different information. We assessed how converting vector figures to images affects reconstruction by a language model that can inspect files and execute code. We generated 64 independent two-arm datasets across four scenarios combining 100 or 1,000 participants per arm with proportional or crossing hazards. Each figure was supplied as a native vector PDF and a matched 300-dpi PNG to Opus 5.5 through Claude Code under the same instructions. Outcomes compared reconstructed records with the original observed records: time-averaged absolute curve error through 24 months, error in the between-group restricted mean survival time difference, and error in the Cox log-hazard ratio. Native PDFs had lower curve error in all 64 completed pairs, including replacements for incomplete runs. Mean errors were 0.000029 and 0.1047 percentage points for PDF and PNG, respectively; the paired difference was -0.1047 (95% confidence interval, -0.1194 to -0.0909). PNG errors in the restricted mean survival time difference and log-hazard ratio were small: mean absolute errors were 0.0084 months and 0.0027. Lower resolution and compression increased curve errors; embedding unchanged pixels in a PDF did not restore vector accuracy. Some PNG runs exceeded the instructed revision limit, so results describe the implemented workflow rather than performance under a strictly enforced limit. Preserving vector information improved reconstruction fidelity in this workflow, but the observed differences do not establish clinically consequential changes in treatment estimates. Validation against reported survival summaries and event counts remains necessary. Generalization to published clinical figures and other model workflows requires further evaluation.

articles.title: First-trimester nocturnal cardiorespiratory coupling during home sleep testing and later pregnancy complications: a secondary analysis of the nuMoM2b cohort
articles.abstract: We tested whether direction-specific nocturnal cardiorespiratory coupling (CRC) in the first trimester differed in pregnancies that later developed obstetric complications. The analysis included 2504 nulliparous women from the nuMoM2b cohort with valid level 3 home sleep recordings at 6-13 weeks' gestation. Bidirectional CRC between RR intervals and abdominal respiratory effort was quantified using bivariate phase-rectified signal averaging in consecutive 5-min segments. Coupling strength, local transition dynamics, and waveform irregularity were summarized by nightly mean and standard deviation. Associations with gestational diabetes mellitus (GDM; n = 111), preeclampsia (n = 149), preterm birth (n = 192), and fetal macrosomia (n = 186) were examined using proportional-odds models with CRC feature quintile as the ordered outcome. Models included all four complications simultaneously and adjusted for maternal age, pre-pregnancy body mass index, race and ethnicity, gestational age at recording, relevant medical and family history, medication use, and apnea-hypopnea index >5 events/h. Holm correction was applied across outcomes. GDM was associated with lower respiration-to-heart rate coupling strength (cumulative odds ratio, 0.45; 95% CI, 0.31-0.64; P < 0.001) and shallower slope at the anchor point (0.63; 0.45-0.89; P = 0.03). Fetal macrosomia was associated with lower within-night variability in heart rate-to-respiration waveform irregularity (0.59; 0.45-0.77; P < 0.001). No associations with preeclampsia or preterm birth remained significant after correction. Direction-specific differences in nocturnal CRC were detectable in the first trimester in pregnancies that later developed GDM or resulted in fetal macrosomia.

articles.title: Formal dissent in CHMP opinions on new medicines, 2020-2025
articles.abstract: Disagreement within medicines regulation is rarely visible in the public record at the point an opinion is adopted. We examined divergent positions formally appended to opinions of the European Medicines Agency's Committee for Medicinal Products for Human Use (CHMP) on new medicines from 2020 through 2025, both those opposing a positive opinion and those favoring authorization despite a negative opinion, describing how often they occurred, how large the dissenting minorities were, and which issues they raised. Divergent positions opposed 28 of 331 positive opinions (8.5%) and most often concerned efficacy and methodological limitations. Of 22 final negative opinions publicly available, 6 (27%) were accompanied by a divergent position favoring authorization. These records show when CHMP members disagreed about whether the evidence justified authorization. Indexing these disagreements and publishing vote outcomes with each opinion would make regulatory uncertainty visible and help clinicians, payers and health technology assessment bodies make better-informed decisions about treatment use and coverage.

articles.title: Germline Shelterin Loss of Function Predisposes to Lipoma and Uterine Leiomyoma: Population Evidence Bearing on Shelterin-Associated Sarcoma Risk
articles.abstract: Purpose Germline shelterin variants were linked to sarcoma in a case-enriched cohort. Whether shelterin loss of function predisposes to mesenchymal neoplasia in the general population is unknown. Methods We analyzed rare-variant collapsing associations for five shelterin genes across neoplasm phenotypes in UK Biobank exomes, with Genebass as a second pipeline. Prespecified shelterin and centrosome gene sets were tested by permutation-calibrated statistics against a TP53/RB1/NF1 positive control. Carrier risks were compared with telomere-lengthening predictions. Results Lipoma risk was increased in TERF1 (odds ratio [OR], 3.32; P = 8.4 x10⁻⁸), POT1, and TERF2IP carriers, and uterine leiomyoma risk in all four core shelterin genes, most strongly POT1 (OR, 2.23; P = 4.0 x 10⁻⁵); POT1 and TINF2 reproduced in Genebass. TERF1 was also associated with thyroid cancer and monoclonal gammopathy. Neither gene set nor the positive control was associated with self-reported sarcoma. Telomere lengthening accounted for POT1-associated chronic lymphocytic leukemia risk but not myeloma or TINF2-associated thyroid cancer, where observed risk exceeded prediction five- to seven-fold. Conclusion Shelterin loss of function is a population-level risk factor for lipoma and uterine leiomyoma, the benign counterparts of liposarcoma and leiomyosarcoma. TERF1 joins POT1 and TINF2 as long-telomere cancer genes. Sarcoma-specific penetrance remains untested.

articles.title: Housing Tenure and Mental Health Across Adulthood: Evidence from the 1970 British Birth Cohort
articles.abstract: Background In the UK, declining home ownership and delayed entry into the housing market have reshaped patterns of housing tenure (whether people own or rent their homes) across adulthood. Home ownership may reflect socioeconomic advantage, but may also provide greater housing security, stability and control, with implications for mental health. Using data from the 1970 British Cohort Study (BCS70), this study examines how home ownership trajectories, defined by whether, when and for how long individuals own their homes, are associated with mental health in midlife. Methods We analysed data from 8,016 BCS70 participants with information on housing tenure histories and mental health outcomes at age 51. Housing tenure was measured repeatedly from ages 26 to 46 and used to define prespecified patterns of home ownership across adulthood (referred to as ownership regimes), including sustained ownership and never owning. Mental health outcomes at age 51 were psychological distress and positive mental wellbeing. G-estimation of a structural nested mean model was used to estimate contrasts between these ownership regimes while accounting for time-varying confounding affected by prior exposure. Models were estimated in lavaan; non-response weights and full information maximum likelihood were used to address selective attrition and missing data. Results At age 51, 71% of participants owned their home (23% outright and 48% with a mortgage), while 24% were renting and 5% lived in other arrangements. Sustained home ownership across adulthood was associated with lower psychological distress at age 51 compared with never owning (ATE -0.21, 95% CI -0.47 to -0.03) and higher positive mental wellbeing (ATE 0.56 SD, 95% CI 0.38 to 0.67). In ownership-history regime contrasts, late ownership (first ownership in one's 40s) was associated with lower psychological distress than never owning (ATE -0.15, 95% CI -0.30 to -0.04), while the estimate for early ownership (first ownership in one's 30s) was in the same direction but imprecise (ATE -0.12, 95% CI -0.37 to 0.04). For wellbeing, both late and early ownership were associated with higher scores than never owning (ATE 0.17 SD, 95% CI 0.08 to 0.27 and ATE 0.40 SD, 95% CI 0.24 to 0.51, respectively), with the largest association observed for sustained ownership. Conclusion Home ownership across adulthood (age 26 to 46) was associated with better mental health in midlife (age 51) after accounting for time-varying socio-economic and health-related confounding. Findings suggest that both the timing and persistence of ownership may matter, particularly for positive mental wellbeing, with more sustained exposure to ownership associated with more favourable outcomes.

articles.title: Insulin genetic clusters and clinical outcomes in Hispanics/Latinos
articles.abstract: Increased fasting insulin reflects insulin resistance and is as a precursor to type 2 diabetes and a risk factor for kidney, heart and liver diseases and mortality. Cluster-specific fasting insulin polygenic scores (PS) characterize insulin resistance mechanisms based on insulin-related genetic associations with metabolic traits, and they have not been evaluated for liver outcomes. We calculated seven previously developed FI cluster-specific PS, including non-diabetogenic (Preserved Insulin Secretion, Elevated Insulin Secretion, Proinsulin) and diabetogenic clusters (Adiposity-driven Hyperinsulinemia, Visceral Adiposity, Lipodystrophy, Liver/Lipid) in 12,631 participants of the Hispanic Community Healthy Study/Study of Latinos (HCHS/SOL), and tested their association with type 2 diabetes, cardiovascular, kidney and liver outcomes. We also tested the association of FI clusters with indices of insulin homeostasis in additional 1,316 Hispanic individuals. Among HCHS/SOL participants (mean age 46 years, 59% women, 20% with diabetes), we validated associations of FI cluster-specific PS and the 19 traits used to generate clusters. The Lipodystrophy cluster was associated with type 2 diabetes (p-value =3.5 x 10-5). In addition, the Adiposity-driven Hyperinsulinemia cluster was associated with the hepatic steatosis index (p-value = 2.2 x1017) and the fatty liver index (p-value = 1.7 x1014), while the Liver/Lipid cluster with liver fibrosis (p-value = 1.5 x104) and lower kidney function (p-value = 5.2 x 10-5). The non-diabetogenic Elevated Insulin Secretion cluster-specific PS was associated with the disposition index (p = 0.0015). These results support insulin resistance mechanisms implicated in type 2 diabetes, liver and kidney outcomes.

articles.title: LOW-FREQUENCY DEEP BRAIN STIMULATION PROMOTES LONG-TERM OROFACIAL MOTOR RECOVERY AFTER TRAUMATIC BRAIN INJURY: A CASE STUDY
articles.abstract: Diffuse axonal injury (DAI), a subtype of traumatic brain injury (TBI), can disrupt corticobulbar pathways, leading to chronic deficits in speech and swallowing. We present a first-in-human case study demonstrating the long-term therapeutic potential of low-frequency continuous deep brain stimulation (DBS) of the motor thalamus to restore corticobulbar function in a patient with severe DAI and persistent dysarthria and dysphagia. The patient underwent bilateral motor thalamus DBS implantation one-year post-injury for treatment of post-traumatic action tremor, and stimulation was delivered chronically at 55 Hz over three years of follow-up. We assessed orofacial motor outcomes using kinematic analysis of facial movements, videofluoroscopic swallowing studies, and speech tasks to dissociate the immediate assistive effects of stimulation (DBS ON versus OFF) from its long-term therapeutic effects (DBS OFF over time). Continuous DBS led to progressive recovery of facial symmetry, resolution of laryngeal penetration, and marked improvements in respiratory and phonatory control and speech intelligibility. While improvements in gross orofacial motor function persisted in the absence of stimulation, fine articulatory control remained dependent on ongoing stimulation or adjunct speech therapy for optimal performance. Stimulation-induced improvements in cervical posture may also have contributed to enhanced biomechanics of swallowing and voice production. These findings provide early evidence that low-frequency motor thalamus DBS may promote therapeutic benefits and extend the window of functional recovery in chronic TBI patients.

articles.title: Large Language Model-Enhanced Electronic Frailty Assessment and Prognostic Performance in Hospitalized Adults: A Retrospective Cohort Study
articles.abstract: Background: Electronic frailty indices (eFIs) derived from structured electronic health record (EHR) data may incompletely capture functional deficits. Large language models (LLMs) can extract frailty-related information from clinical notes, but whether improved frailty ascertainment improves prognostic performance is uncertain. Objective: To compare frailty ascertainment and prognostic performance between standard and LLM-enhanced eFIs among hospitalized adults. Design: Retrospective cohort study Participants: Adults aged 50 years or older enrolled in two studies at an academic medical center and affiliated community hospital between February 2022 and April 2024. Main Measures: A validated 35-deficit diagnosis-based eFI and an LLM-enhanced eFI incorporating deficits extracted from physical therapy (PT) documentation using GPT-4o. Frailty was defined using an index threshold of 0.20 or more. The primary outcome was a composite of discharge to a facility, readmission, or death within 90 days. Multivariable logistic regression models assessed associations with the outcome, and discrimination was compared using area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUROC). Secondary analyses examined threshold-based classification and PT-documentation availability; prespecified sensitivity analyses evaluated population and outcome restrictions. Results: Among 616 hospitalizations, mean (SD) age was 70.9 (10.2) years, 329 (53.4%) had PT documentation, and 320 (51.9%) experienced the composite outcome. Standard and LLM-enhanced eFIs classified 216 (35.1%) and 362 (58.8%) hospitalizations as frail, respectively. Both were independently associated with the outcome (standard eFI: adjusted OR, 1.98 [95% CI, 1.39-2.83]; LLM-enhanced eFI: adjusted OR, 2.46 [95% CI, 1.75-3.47]). Discrimination did not differ significantly (AUROC, 0.636 vs 0.660; difference, 0.024 [95% CI, -0.006 to 0.053]; p=0.12). LLM enhancement increased sensitivity (42.5% to 69.4%) but decreased specificity (73.0% to 52.7%). Conclusions: LLM enhancement substantially increased frailty ascertainment and sensitivity for adverse outcomes but did not significantly improve prognostic discrimination. Thus, LLM-enhanced frailty assessment may depend on whether the intended use prioritizes broad identification of functional vulnerability or prediction of adverse post-hospital outcomes.

articles.title: Memory Self-Awareness Phenotypes are Associated with Alzheimers Disease Biomarker Burden and Clinical Progression in Amnestic Mild Cognitive Impairment
articles.abstract: Background: Altered memory self-awareness is common in mild cognitive impairment (MCI), but its relationship to Alzheimer's disease (AD) pathology and progression remains unclear. Methods: Using 590 amnestic MCI ADNI participants, memory self-awareness was derived from participant-informant discrepancies on the memory subdomain of the Everyday Cognition questionnaire. Heightened awareness and unawareness subscores were calculated, and k-means clustering identified four phenotypes. Associations with cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) and positron emission tomography (PET) were examined, and clinical progression was assessed using Cox models. Results: Aware and Unaware groups showed lower CSF amyloid-B, and higher CSF phosphorylated tau and PET amyloid. The Unaware phenotype was associated with increased progression risk (hazard ratio 2.41, 95% CI 1.48-3.92), whereas the Worried Well phenotype showed reduced risk (hazard ratio 0.58, 95% CI 0.34-0.99). Conclusions: Multidimensional assessment of memory self-awareness identifies biologically and prognostically distinct subgroups within MCI and may improve risk stratification in prodromal AD.

articles.title: Overall Outlook on Life and Cardiovascular Health Behaviors among Adolescent and Young Adult Females: A Cross-sectional Study
articles.abstract: Background: Cardiovascular disease is the leading cause of death among women, with risk factors commonly emerging during adolescence. Emerging evidence indicates that psychological factors, such as optimism, affect cardiovascular health, yet this remains understudied among young women. To assess the association between overall outlook on life and preventive cardiovascular health behaviors among young women. Methods: We conducted a secondary analysis of a cohort of 331 young women aged 15 to 24 years who completed the modified American Heart Association Women?s Health Survey (2017-2018), using multivariate regression adjusted for confounding. Results: Over 50% of young women felt their outlook on life may impact their likelihood of developing a serious illness such as heart disease. Outlook on life was associated with prioritizing and taking care of health (?=0.18-0.19, 95% Confidence Interval (CI) [0.09, 0.29]; P=0.002) and usually following recommended healthy eating (?=0.12, 95% CI [0.03, 0.23]; P=0.016). Young women who identified as black (27.5%; N=91) felt that their outlook on life had a lower impact on their likelihood of developing a serious illness such as heart disease (Odds Ratio (OR)=0.80; 95% CI [0.65, 0.98]; P = 0.04), compared to other racial groups. Conclusion: Our findings support previous observations indicating a cardioprotective role of optimism in cardiovascular health. However, this association may not hold among young women of color, potentially reflecting constraints in their lived environment that limit how much a positive outlook translates into perceived control over health outcomes. Strategies to reduce cardiovascular disease in women should address young women?s cardiovascular health and psychological and contextual factors, with particular attention to young women of color.

articles.title: Peak Agricultural Pesticide Spray Periods are related to Real-World Cognition Using an Ecological Momentary Assessment Burst Design over Two Years
articles.abstract: Objective: Emerging evidence suggests that exposure to organophosphate, neonicotinoid, and other pesticides may transiently impair cognition; however, traditional "snapshot" laboratory-based cognitive assessments fail to capture fluctuations in cognitive performance. This study used ecological momentary cognitive testing (EMCT) to evaluate whether real-world cognitive performance differs between peak and low floricultural pesticide spray seasons, thereby evaluating the potential cyclical effects of agricultural production and related pesticide exposures. Material and Methods: From 2022 to 2024, 15,063 EMCT assessments were completed by 494 participants (ages 17 to 25; 50% female) enrolled in the ESPINA cohort study in Ecuador. Participants completed nine 10-day burst assessments every 2 to 3 months during high and low pesticide spray seasons. EMCTs (NeuroUx) assessed processing speed, executive function, and visual working memory. Mixed-effects models examined associations of peak versus off-peak pesticide spray seasons, floricultural work or occupation (vs not) with EMCT performance, adjusting for socio-economic and other variables, and including participant- and burst-level random intercepts. Results: Peak pesticide spray season, compared to off-peak, was associated with higher T-scores on processing speed tests, including Matching Pair (B= 0.62) and Odd One Out (B= 0.88), but showed no significant association with other tests or the overall cognitive composite. Conversely, direct floricultural employment was significantly associated with lower cognitive performance overall (B= -0.59), with the largest differences observed in Memory Matrix (B= -0.78) and Matching Pair (B= -0.70). Conclusion: Peak pesticide spray seasons were associated with modestly higher processing speed scores, consistent with prior findings in this population suggestive of enhanced cognitive performance associated with neonicotinoid and sulfoximine exposures. In contrast, floricultural employment was associated with significantly lower memory and overall cognitive performance. These results suggest that occupational and seasonal pesticide exposure may have distinct associations with cognitive functioning, highlighting the importance of repeated cognitive testing for characterizing potentially transient effects.

articles.title: Place-based structural disadvantage and mortality inequality across 379 Polish counties, 2010-2025: a spatial Mundlak analysis
articles.abstract: Place-based mortality inequalities may persist even as short-term associations with local conditions change. We examined age-sex-standardised all-cause mortality in 379 harmonised Polish counties (2010-2025), asking whether durable between-county differences or lagged within-county deviations better characterise mortality geography. Spatial Mundlak generalised additive models allowed non-linear associations and county-specific spatial modification; a pre-COVID model (2010-2019) was compared with overlapping models through 2022 and 2025. In the pre-COVID model, median county average partial slopes per standard deviation were -26.1 deaths per 100,000 for higher education, +29.4 for primary/lower-secondary education and +30.2 for PM2.5. Directions of these between-county gradients persisted across analytical windows. By contrast, within-county associations were less stable and sometimes reversed sign in pandemic-inclusive models. County-level uncertainty indicated stronger and more coherent pre-COVID spatial patterns for education, PM2.5 and population density than for several health-care and migration terms. Strict leave-one-year-out validation revealed weak temporal transportability, particularly for the 2010-2022 model, limiting predictive interpretation. Outcome-defined comparisons further showed that educational composition remained an important separator of high- and low-mortality counties after COVID-19, while the fitted PM2.5 contribution contrast diminished. These findings distinguish durable configurations of place-based disadvantage from period-dependent ecological co-movement. They support geographically sensitive, multi-domain approaches to reducing mortality inequalities, while not establishing individual-level causal effects.

articles.title: Prediction of elective surgical red blood cell transfusion reveals surgeon-level variation
articles.abstract: BACKGROUND Preoperative prediction of red blood cell (RBC) transfusion in elective surgery serves two complementary purposes: enabling patient blood management (PBM) interventions before surgery and supporting blood product supply planning for elective lists. Beyond patient risk factors, individual surgeon practice may also contribute to transfusion rates, but this effect has not been fully quantified. STUDY DESIGN AND METHODS In a retrospective cohort of 279,905 elective surgical procedures at Helsinki University Hospital (2021-2025), we trained four gradient-boosted tree (CatBoost) models crossing patient factors with procedure group and pseudonymised surgeon identity. All predictors were restricted to data available seven or more days before scheduled surgery. The primary outcome was any allogeneic RBC transfusion from operating-room entry through seven postoperative days. Discrimination was assessed by the area under the precision-recall curve (AUPRC) on a held-out 20% test set. Surgeon-level effects were characterised by Shapley additive explanation (SHAP) values. RESULTS The transfusion rate was 2.2%. The patient-only model achieved AUPRC 0.261 (no-skill baseline 0.022). Adding surgeon identity to the procedure-adjusted model increased AUPRC from 0.440 to 0.472 (+0.032; 95% CI 0.020-0.044), raising lift from 20.3 to 21.7. Surgeon identity was the third most important of 72 features by permutation importance. DISCUSSION The operating surgeon was associated with RBC transfusion beyond patient and procedure factors, and surgeon identity was the third most important predictor in a deployment-realistic model using only data available a week before surgery. This information is readily available from routine records and could support PBM audit and blood supply planning for elective surgery.

articles.title: Prenatal Prediction of Delayed Abdominal Closure in Isolated Congenital Diaphragmatic Hernia Using Observed-to-Expected Lung-to-Head Ratio.
articles.abstract: Objective: O/E LHR is a well-established prenatal severity marker in congenital diaphragmatic hernia (CDH), but its capacity to predict the postnatal need for delayed abdominal wall closure (DAC) remains undefined. We aimed to determine its predictive capacity. Method: Retrospective analysis of neonates with isolated left-sided CDH (2015-2026), comparing primary closure with DAC. Discriminative capacity was assessed by ROC analysis and the optimal cut-off was determined by bootstrap-aggregated approach. Logistic regression estimated univariate and liver herniation adjusted multivariate odds ratios (OR). Result: 45 neonates were included, 28 underwent primary closure and 17 required DAC. DAC was associated with lower gestational age, higher rates of liver herniation, greater ECMO requirement, and higher mortality than primary closure (all p < 0.01). O/E LHR showed excellent discriminative ability for DAC (AUC 0.939), with an optimal cut-off of 34.1% (sensitivity 82.35%, specificity 82.14%, positive predictive value 73.68%, negative predictive value 88.46%). O/E LHR was independently associated with DAC after multivariate analysis (OR 0.821, 95% CI 0.668-0.939, p = 0.002). Conclusions: O/E LHR was independently associated with DAC risk beyond liver herniation. These preliminary findings suggest a potential role for O/E LHR in prenatal risk stratification for DAC, pending external validation.

articles.title: Quantifying the contribution of policy measures to COVID-19 dynamics across 126 countries
