articles.title: Bacterial Surfaces and Barriers: Biogenesis and Pathogen–Host Interactions
articles.abstract: The bacterial surface represents the primary interface between pathogens and hosts, yet its chemical and architectural complexity challenges conventional classification. This Review examines structural organization, molecular composition, and biogenesis of bacterial surface components across the Gracilicutes and Terrabacteria clades, linking mechanistic detail to pathogenic function. We describe lipid diversity, integral membrane protein biogenesis, and lipoprotein processing at the inner membrane and how these components support surface remodeling, secretion, and virulence. We then examine the peptidoglycan layer and its role in immune recognition and surface protein display, teichoic acids and their contributions to antimicrobial resistance and immune evasion, and S layers, whose crystalline arrays mediate adhesion and immune modulation. The outer membrane section covers lipopolysaccharide biosynthesis, outer membrane protein biogenesis and folding, lipoprotein trafficking, and contributions to pathogenicity, while the mycobacterial section addresses the mycolyl-arabinogalactan-peptidoglycan complex and virulence factors. We discuss bacterial capsule diversity, biosynthesis, and use as vaccine antigens, along with adhesive surface structures such as fimbriae, pili, and curli fibers and their roles in colonization and biofilm formation, before covering secretion systems types I through XI and their contributions to virulence. This Review provides a framework for understanding how bacterial surface diversity shapes infection and identifies chemical vulnerabilities for therapeutics.

articles.title: Mapping Local Environments in Single-Atom Catalysts
articles.abstract: Single-atom catalysts (SACs) offer exceptional structural resolution for investigating how local environments govern catalytic behavior and, ultimately, for controlling these effects through catalyst design. Yet, atomic dispersion does not imply a single or fully defined catalytic environment. The behavior of atomically dispersed active centers is shaped by a hierarchical local environment comprising persistent and transient contributions, while also being influenced by an extended reaction environment that intersects with the local environment in controlling reactivity and can become integrated into it. Establishing these boundaries and understanding how these contributions evolve and interact are central challenges in the interpretation and design of SACs. Here, we critically examine how local environments are generated and controlled, experimentally and theoretically resolved across spatial and temporal scales, transformed from synthesis through operation and deactivation, and linked to catalytic performance through structural, energetic, and electronic descriptors. By integrating aspects that are often considered separately and highlighting those that remain insufficiently addressed, we provide a roadmap toward the predictive, environment-driven design of SACs and a deeper understanding of catalytic phenomena.

articles.title: Regenerated Cellulose for Sustainable Electronic Devices
articles.abstract: Regenerated cellulose (RC), derived from natural cellulose through dissolution and regeneration processes, has emerged as a sustainable, versatile, and cost-effective material for advanced electronic devices. With unique hierarchical structures, abundant hydroxy groups, and excellent mechanical and thermal properties, RC allows extensive customization of its characteristics, offering biocompatibility, flexibility, processability, and environmental friendliness. This review systematically summarizes recent advances in RC-based electronics, focusing on its multiscale molecular configuration, dissolution and regeneration mechanisms, and functionalization and engineering strategies. It first provides a detailed molecular-level analysis of RC structures and formation mechanisms. The principles and strategies of cellulose dissolution and regeneration are then discussed, with emphasis on solvent systems and structure-regulating mechanisms essential for processing control. Functionalization strategies are categorized into direct modification and hybridization with functional materials. Notably, the hybridization approach involves the development of conductive, semiconductive, and insulating RC composites, evaluated from the perspectives of material selection, interfacial design, and processing techniques. Subsequently, engineering approaches to enhance mechanical strength, electrical conductivity, and optical transparency are explored. Applications of RC in sensors, actuators, circuits, energy harvesting and storage devices, and electromagnetic shielding devices are highlighted, demonstrating its potential to drive sustainable innovation in electronics. Finally, future directions are proposed to address remaining challenges, paving the way for RC to contribute to eco-friendly, high-performance electronic devices.

articles.title: Hole-selective self-assembled monolayers: a molecular platform for high-performance perovskite photovoltaics
articles.abstract: Classification of donor–acceptor molecular components used to identify key self-assembled monolayers (SAMs) as HTLs for overcoming efficiency limitations in solar cells.

articles.title: Layered superlattices: from physical assembly to chemical synthesis and emerging applications
articles.abstract: This review summarizes the classification, physical and chemical synthesis, and structure–property relationships of layered superlattices, with emphasis on emerging applications, structural control, dynamic characterization, and device integration.

articles.title: Liquid hydrocarbon separation membranes: mechanistic insight, material design and microenvironment engineering
articles.abstract: This review proposes a mechanism-based unified framework for liquid hydrocarbon separation membranes and discusses the fabrication- and application-oriented regulation strategies in microenvironment engineering.

articles.title: Density Functional Theory and Data-Driven Insights into Hydrogen Incorporation and Transport in Ternary ABO3 Perovskites
articles.abstract: Hydrogen is a promising energy carrier due to its clean and versatile nature, offering opportunities for decarbonizing diverse sectors. Hydrogen utilization in many applications relies on identifying and understanding materials with exceptional hydrogen storage and transport properties. In this study, we conducted a comprehensive investigation of the thermodynamic and kinetic properties of hydrogenation reactions in ternary ABO3 perovskites using density functional theory (DFT) calculations and machine learning (ML) screening. We performed DFT simulations for a diverse range of perovskites featuring a variety of A-site cations (Ca, Sr, Ba) and B-site cations (Co, Fe, Mn, Ce, Ti, Zr) across various phases (cubic, tetragonal, orthorhombic, and hexagonal). By computing all data at the same theoretical level, we establish a consistent framework to compare how crystal phase, lattice-site chemistry, and host electronic structure govern hydrogen incorporation and diffusion. Therefore, we identify hexagonal SrMnO3, cubic SrFeO3, and hexagonal BaFeO3 as particularly promising candidates, combining favorable hydrogenation thermodynamics (ΔG < 1 eV) with low rotation and hopping barriers (<0.2 eV), while orthorhombic phases, although thermodynamically preferred, suffer from proton trapping, highlighting the importance of phase engineering toward cubic/hexagonal frameworks. Ab initio molecular dynamics further support this phase-dependent kinetic picture by showing relatively facile H diffusion in cubic SrFeO3 but much slower proton motion in orthorhombic BaCeO3 under the same conditions. By incorporating spatial and electronic descriptors with the DFT data into our ML models, we further develop a mechanistically motivated ML model based on structural and electronic descriptors to screen hydrogenation thermodynamics across 111 ternary ABO3 compositions. This model led to the identification of two additional promising candidates, hexagonal BaPdO3 and cubic BaSnO3, which were subsequently validated by DFT calculations. These findings provide a foundation for the rational design of ABO3 perovskites and demonstrate the potential of ML-driven frameworks with chemical insights to accelerate materials discovery in energetic and catalytic applications.

articles.title: Limited potential of methane pyrolysis for energy production to reduce greenhouse gas emissions
articles.abstract: Although methane pyrolysis appears to be a promising technology for avoiding direct CO 2 emissions, growing dependence on natural gas and the high methane fugitive emissions associated with the process may offset its claimed benefits.

articles.title: Green synthesis of ZnO/Se nanocomposites: influence of selenium concentration on structural, optical properties with enhanced antimicrobial and photocatalytic performance
articles.abstract: The development of durable and multifunctional nanomaterials for water treatment continues to represent a significant challenge in the field of environmental nanotechnology. In this study, ZnO/Se nanocomposites were prepared via a completely green synthetic route, utilizing Raphanus sativus –leaf extract for the biogenic production of ZnO nanoparticles and Citrus limon –peel extract for the synthesis of Se nanoparticles. The effect of selenium incorporation on the structural and functional properties of ZnO was investigated by preparing several ZnO/Se nanocomposites with varying Se concentrations, which were analyzed by X-ray diffraction (XRD), Fourier transform infrared spectroscopy (FTIR), UV-Vis spectroscopy, energy dispersive X-ray analysis (EDX), and field emission scanning electron microscopy (FE-SEM). The photocatalytic activity of the prepared materials was evaluated based on the degradation of methyl orange under UV irradiation, and their antimicrobial efficacy was tested against clinically relevant microbial strains. Among the tested compositions, the nanocomposite containing 2 weight percent (wt%) Se showed superior performance: it achieved a superior performance of 83.4 ± 0.7% dye degradation in 120 min, compared to 62.4% for pure ZnO. This enhanced degradation efficiency was found to be statistically significant (p< 0.05) when compared against the pristine ZnO matrix control group, as validated by independent biological triplicates (n = 3). The same Se concentration also showed the most effective antimicrobial activity compared to the other tested formulations. The improved performance at low Se concentration can likely be explained by the strengthening of the interfacial contact between ZnO and Se, which promotes efficient charge separation and reduces electron–hole recombination. These results indicate that controlled Se incorporation can significantly modulate the structural and functional properties of biogenically produced ZnO. At the same time, they highlight the potential of ZnO/Se nanocomposites prepared via green synthesis as promising candidates for multifunctional water treatment applications.

articles.title: Direct and Trait‐Mediated Effects of Climate on Grassland Productivity Across the Alps
articles.abstract: Understanding how climate shapes ecosystem productivity through energetic constraints and changes in the functional properties expressed by vegetation remains challenging. This is central to trait‐based biodiversity–ecosystem functioning research in mountain grasslands where warming and environmental gradients interact. Here, we distinguish direct climatic controls on productivity from indirect pathways operating through changes in canopy functional composition, physiological state, and within‐plot spectral functional heterogeneity across the European Alps. Using Sentinel‐2 time series (2017–2024), we quantified canopy functional structure from spectral proxies of pigment investment and water status, within‐plot spectral functional heterogeneity using the functional richness (FRic) metric, and vegetation productivity using near‐infrared reflectance of vegetation (NIRv). We combined panel‐data models with piecewise structural equation modeling to partition climate associations into direct and trait‐mediated components operating through canopy functional properties and used varying‐coefficient models to evaluate how these pathways vary along environmental gradients. We identified two pathways linking climate to productivity. Warmer growing seasons increased productivity directly but were associated with a lower chlorophyll‐to‐carotenoid pigment balance, consistent with greater relative carotenoid investment, generating an opposing indirect pathway. Greater winter snow accumulation reduced productivity primarily through a direct pathway, while its canopy‐mediated pathways were uncertain. Climatic water deficit reduced canopy water status and within‐plot spectral functional heterogeneity, but its direct and total associations with productivity were not distinguishable from zero. Environmental context modulated climate–vegetation relationships. Baseline temperature and moisture availability strongly shaped climate effects on canopy traits and productivity, whereas canopy‐property–productivity relationships varied little across space. Positive productivity responses to warming were stronger in wetter and more seasonally variable climatic contexts, but weakened where baseline winter snow accumulation was greater. Together, our findings show that short‐term productivity responses in mountain grasslands reflect a balance between direct energetic constraints and indirect pathways through integrated canopy functional properties, and that this balance varies along macroclimatic gradients. RÉSUMÉ Comprendre comment le climat façonne la productivité des écosystèmes à travers des contraintes énergétiques directes et des voies indirectes médiées par la biodiversité demeure un défi majeur en écologie du changement global, en particulier dans les prairies de montagne où le réchauffement rapide interagit avec de forts gradients environnementaux. Nous démêlons ici les effets climatiques directs sur la productivité des écosystèmes de leurs effets indirects opérant via la structure fonctionnelle de la canopée, à l'échelle de l'ensemble des Alpes européennes. À partir de séries temporelles Sentinel‐2 (2017–2024), nous avons quantifié la structure fonctionnelle de la canopée à partir de proxys spectraux liés aux pigments et à l'état hydrique, ainsi que la richesse fonctionnelle, et estimé la productivité à l'aide de la réflectance proche‐infrarouge de la végétation (NIRv). Nous avons combiné inférence causale et modèles d'équations structurelles pour partitionner les effets climatiques totaux en composantes directes et médiées par les traits, puis utilisé des modèles à coefficients variables pour analyser la modulation de ces voies le long des gradients environnementaux. Nos résultats montrent que deux voies concomitantes relient le climat à la productivité.…

articles.title: Embracing macrophage complexity for research and translation
articles.abstract: Ginhoux, Mulder, Arcila-Barrera, and Amit argue that macrophage identity is best understood not as a set of discrete subsets or a binary M1/M2 axis but as combinations of modular gene programs. They propose an extensible, program-based classification of macrophage states and discuss how it reframes macrophage-directed therapy from targeting individual checkpoints toward program-level reprogramming.

articles.title: Redefining the thermal safety boundaries of ether-based sodium batteries
articles.abstract: Are ether electrolytes inherently hazardous? This perspective reveals they actually deliver markedly enhanced thermal safety over carbonates in sodium architectures alongside uniquely higher thermal resilience toward metallic sodium than lithium equivalents. However, this protective margin is fundamentally negated by oxygen-driven chemical autoxidation rather than mere electrochemical degradation. These insights establish the anode-free ether configuration as the definitive trajectory for future sodium batteries, perfectly balancing energy density with robust safety.

articles.title: What we measure matters: Trait choice shapes inferences about grassland functional diversity under altered precipitation
articles.abstract: Trait‐based approaches help reveal how ecosystems respond to global change, but trait selection and diversity metrics can lead to different conclusions. In a semi‐arid grassland, we show that methodological choices influence inferences about functional diversity and ecosystem stability under drought. Traits aligned with environmental mechanisms captured community responses differently than commonly used traits, highlighting the value of hypothesis‐driven trait selection. Abstract Trait‐based approaches are powerful tools for understanding ecosystem resistance and resilience under global change. Yet, relationships between global change drivers, functional trait diversity and ecosystem stability remain unclear. Some inconsistencies arise from differences in trait selection and diversity indices, which reflect distinct hypotheses and can lead to divergent interpretations. This complicates determining whether observed patterns stem from methodological choices or true ecological variation. We evaluated how methodological decisions influence ecological inference by comparing functional diversity metrics and community‐weighted means calculated from different trait subsets. Using a four‐year rainfall manipulation experiment in a semi‐arid grassland near Boulder, Colorado, USA, we quantified community responses to extreme drought, irrigation and ambient conditions. We measured nine leaf, root and whole‐plant traits and grouped them into six sets based on trait‐based literature: (1) all traits, (2) commonly used traits (e.g. specific leaf area, root dry matter content), (3) mechanistic drought traits, (4) economic spectrum traits, (5) above‐ground traits and (6) below‐ground traits. For each set, we assessed drought and irrigation effects on community composition using community‐weighted means and four functional diversity indices: richness, evenness, divergence and dispersion. We also examined how trait and metric selection influenced temporal biomass stability across treatments. Treatment effects varied across metrics: functional divergence was generally robust to trait selection, while evenness, richness and dispersion were more trait‐dependent. Relationships between functional diversity and biomass stability were both metric‐ and trait‐dependent: functional dispersion tended to decrease stability under drought and irrigation for above‐ground and commonly used traits. Functional evenness increased stability under irrigation for select sets, and functional divergence and richness showed weak or inconsistent relationships with stability across treatments and trait sets. Synthesis. Our results show that methodological choices in trait selection and metrics influence conclusions about functional diversity. Trait suites aligned with environmental drivers (e.g. mechanistic drought traits) captured community responses differently than commonly used traits, highlighting the value of hypothesis‐driven selection. We recommend prioritizing traits linked to the focal ecological mechanism and testing robustness across alternative trait subsets and diversity metrics. This approach improves mechanistic interpretation, clarifies when and where diversity stabilizes ecosystem function and increases comparability across systems and studies.

articles.title: Robust van der Waals diamond-like dielectric for two-dimensional electronics
articles.abstract: Next-generation two-dimensional electronics require robust insulating layers that effectively control current without compromising device performance. Here, we report fluorinated diamane, a diamond-like van der Waals material, as a high-performance gate dielectric. By combining a high dielectric constant, exceptional breakdown strength, and efficient heat dissipation, fluorinated diamane integrates seamlessly with diverse two-dimensional semiconductors and memory devices. This material platform addresses long-standing dielectric bottlenecks in ultra-scaled two-dimensional electronics.

articles.title: Building Field‐Ready Environmental RNA Panels
articles.abstract: Environmental RNA (eRNA) has been increasingly used to move beyond ‘who is there’ toward ‘who is active’ and ‘what is happening’ in ecosystems. Yet, most workflows have been optimised for laboratory sequencing, and decision‐grade field use has remained sporadic. In this article, field‐ready eRNA panels are defined as curated sets of transcripts paired with process controls and a transparent scoring rule, and a build–test pathway is described from marker discovery to deployment. Candidate markers are prioritised with field constraints in mind (abundance, specificity, persistence, and confounding seasonality), and RNA class choice (mRNA, rRNA, small, and other non‐coding RNAs) is treated as a design lever for robustness. Pre‐analytics are discussed as panel engineering, with emphasis placed on capture, rapid stabilisation, and inhibitor management to preserve multi‐marker relationships. Field readout options are then compared, including isothermal amplification, CRISPR‐assisted detection, portable qPCR, and portable nanopore sequencing for on‐site verification and panel refresh. Finally, minimum controls and staged validation levels are proposed to support defensible ecological claims. Deliberate attention is directed toward shared terminology and testable standards so that discussion within and between ecology, diagnostics, and conservation practice is stimulated and priorities for future investigations are sharpened.

articles.title: Chilling Out or Heating Up? Thermal Plasticity of Seminal Fluid Proteins in Drosophila melanogaster
articles.abstract: Seminal fluid proteins (SFPs) play crucial roles in reproduction by shaping female post‐mating physiology and behaviour, male sperm competition and sexual conflict between the sexes. However, we know little about how abiotic ecological factors regulate SFP expression and transfer. Here, we use quantitative proteomics in adult flies from a wild Drosophila melanogaster population to test how exposure to natural temperature variation (20°C, 24°C and 28°C) across two time scales (48 h and 13d), and under either no‐ or high‐sperm competition risk, interact to shape SFP production and transfer. Short‐term exposure to different temperatures resulted in lower SFP production and transfer at 24°C under no sperm competition risk, but no differences under high sperm competition risk. In contrast, both the production and transfer of SFPs were consistently reduced across sperm competition treatments after long‐term (13d) exposure to low (20°C) and high (28°C) temperatures, including for key proteins in the sex peptide and ovulin networks that mediate female post‐copulatory responses, sperm competition and sexual conflict. Our results show that natural temperature fluctuations can have a strong effect on SFP production and transfer, and thus on post‐copulatory sexual selection dynamics.

articles.title: Drift and Selection in a Recently Colonized Sea: The Genomic Basis of Adaptation to Low‐Salinity Waters in Baltic Harbour Porpoises
articles.abstract: Understanding how demography and natural selection interact during colonization of novel environments is a central question in evolutionary biology. The Baltic Sea region combines one of the world's strongest salinity gradients with a well‐characterized postglacial history of less than ~12,000 years. The harbour porpoise (Phocoena phocoena) is distributed across this gradient as three populations—the North Sea, Belt Sea and Proper Baltic Sea populations. Using whole genome resequencing data from 59 individuals, we reconstructed the demographic history of Baltic colonization and identified genomic signatures of local adaptation. Demographic modelling supported a sequential colonization in which the Belt Sea population diverged first from an ancestral North Sea population, followed by an independent divergence of the Proper Baltic Sea population, with two equally supported timing hypotheses placing initial colonization either during the Yoldia Sea (~11,800 years ago) or the Baltic Sea period (~8000 years ago). The Proper Baltic Sea population showed drift‐dominated divergence consistent with a founder effect, while two discrete genomic islands of differentiation with selective sweep signatures were identified between North and Belt Sea populations, pointing to recent positive selection. Both regions contain osmoregulatory candidate genes, most notably SCNN1D, encoding part of the epithelial Na+ channels, a key regulator of sodium homeostasis. A non‐synonymous mutation in SCNN1D showed striking allele frequency divergence along the salinity gradient, confirmed across ~400 individuals. Together, these results reveal how genetic drift and divergent selection interact to drive rapid adaptation to a brackish environment, and identify SCNN1D as a compelling candidate for cetacean osmoregulatory adaptation.

articles.title: Genomic Islands of Divergence Reveal Signature of Selection on the Alternate Homeolog in Upper Fraser River Sockeye Run‐Timing Groups
articles.abstract: Effective wildlife conservation and management depends on a thorough understanding of both neutral and adaptive intraspecific genomic variation. Population structure is often well understood in many ecologically or economically important species, but the extensive population genomic resources required to characterize putatively adaptive variation and punctuated genomic regions is typically only recently available for some species, if available at all. Here, we explore recently published whole‐genome resequencing data in the upper Fraser River and identify a large island of divergence separating Nechako Watershed populations with different return migration timings (i.e., run timing). The island of divergence at 56.3–58.0 Mbp of Chr18 has extended homozygosity and reduced Tajima's D in sockeye salmon Oncorhynchus nerka from the Nadina River, Stellako River and the Stuart‐Summer run timing group, but not the geographically proximal Early Stuart sockeye. In the populations without the Stuart‐Summer haploblock, genetic variation is similar to elsewhere in the chromosome. Gene content in the haploblock includes leucine rich‐repeat containing 9‐like (lrrc9‐like) and the surrounding homeologous region to the lrrc9 region of Chr12. lrrc9 is within a conserved and selected island of divergence associated with life history traits and run timing throughout the species range and lrrc9‐like has recently been associated with run timing in other salmonids. By also inspecting the samples in the present work at the Chr12 haploblock, three genotypic states were observed throughout the region, with the Stuart River run timing groups mainly comprised of the reference haplotype. No other regions of major differentiation were observed in the analysed samples in the Chilcotin or Quesnel River systems. These results provide additional evidence for the importance of both homeologous regions holding lrrc9 and lrrc9‐like in different geographic regions and underscore the uniqueness of upper Fraser River sockeye in this potentially adaptive island of divergence.

articles.title: Insight Into the Genetic Architecture of Local (Mal)Adaptation in Wild and Feral Brassica rapa Populations
articles.abstract: As climate change drives rapid environmental shifts, crops face significant challenges due to their limited adaptive genetic diversity, threatening food security. Crop wild relatives and potentially feral populations can serve as valuable reservoirs of adaptive diversity for breeding. Exploring and conserving this diversity is therefore essential, as it may encompass a wide range of adaptations. In this study, we investigate the genetic basis of local climate adaptation and the risk of maladaptation under future conditions in spontaneous populations—naturally occurring in the wild—of Brassica rapa (field mustard). A total of 62 populations were sampled, revealing strong differentiation between feral (France, Slovenia) and wild (Algeria, Sicily) populations. A genome–environment association analysis identified genomic regions associated with climatic variables, with broader patterns suggesting a polygenic architecture. Feral populations broadened the climatic range explored, but their reduced genetic diversity limited our ability to capture the full spectrum of adaptive variation in wild populations, indicating that the genetic architecture of climate adaptation is only partly shared between the two groups. We also used genomic offset (GO) analyses to assess mismatches between current and predicted‐optimal genetic composition under 2050 climate projections. A common garden experiment indicated that GO captures some component of fitness variation, with feral populations providing additional predictive information beyond the environmental space occupied by wild populations. These findings highlight the complex genetic architecture of climate adaptation in B. rapa, as well as the potential and limitations of genomic tools for guiding conservation and crop improvement under climate change.

articles.title: Parallel Genomic Responses to Ecological Gradients in the Phalaenopsis amabilis Complex
articles.abstract: There are multiple mechanisms that can underlie parallel adaptation to similar habitats at the genetic level, including de novo mutations, introgression, and shared standing variation. While evidence for each pathway is emerging, few studies have directly examined how demographic processes, range expansion and introgression interact to shape the fate of adaptive alleles. In the Phalaenopsis amabilis complex, we applied a dimensionality reduction approach to identify environmental extremes and link alleles to ecological gradients. By combining gene–environment association analyses with demographic inference and historical gene flow reconstruction, we evaluated whether repeated adaptation arises from de novo convergent mutations or introgression. The candidate SNP set departed strongly from neutral expectations in DMC analyses; standing variation was the best‐fitting model, although its separation from migration was modest. We also found heterogeneous allele sharing and historical introgression involving range‐margin populations, coinciding with demographic expansion. These findings suggest that standing variation, demographic history, and heterogeneous introgression may jointly contribute to repeated genomic responses across ecological gradients. A limited subset of environmentally associated candidates also overlapped with floral morphology‐associated candidates, but the magnitude of overlap was strongly threshold‐ and denominator‐dependent. These overlaps identify hypotheses concerning ecological and floral trait differentiation, but do not establish pleiotropy or a shared causal architecture. This work highlights how parallel adaptation in plants may emerge from the interplay of neutral and adaptive evolutionary mechanisms in recently diverged lineages.

articles.title: Static Expression of Major Histocompatibility Complex Genes Across Life‐Stages, Generations and Tissues in a Songbird
articles.abstract: The extraordinarily polymorphic Major Histocompatibility Complex (MHC) is an iconic genomic region that has been associated with, for example, disease susceptibility, mate choice, and fitness. Both the MHC class I and II gene families have expanded considerably in songbirds (Passeriformes) compared to other bird orders, but our understanding of the functional relevance of the large number of gene copies in songbirds is hampered by lack of data on gene expression. We therefore took advantage of longitudinal data from our wild long‐term monitored population of great reed warblers Acrocephalus arundinaceus as well as a long‐term experiment to study patterns of MHC class I (MHC‐I) gene expression during individuals' lifetimes and across generations, and between tissues. As could be expected within a species, the expressed diversity increased linearly with genomic MHC‐I diversity. However, most MHC‐I alleles were expressed at low levels, with only a handful of alleles showing moderate to high expression in each individual. The MHC‐I expression patterns in blood were highly consistent (i) over an individual's lifetime, (ii) between parents and offspring, and (iii) among siblings, and (iv) were strongly correlated with expression in other tissues. The moderately to highly expressed MHC‐I genes likely play a key role in antigen presentation in adaptive immunity and thus comprise primary targets for studies of host‐pathogen coevolution.

articles.title: The Genomic Landscape of Metallic Colour Variation in Ground Beetles
articles.abstract: The metallic colour variation of beetles is a spectacular feature that has inspired diverse human cultures. However, little is known about the genetic basis of this trait or its ecological importance. In this study, we characterize the geographical distribution, optical mechanism, genetic basis and ecological and evolutionary importance of metallic colour variation in the Nebria ingens complex, an alpine ground beetle in the Sierra Nevada, California. We find that elytral colour varies continuously across two allopatric species (from black N. ingens to green N. riversi), with hybrid populations showing intermediate coloration, and we demonstrate that the metallic colour is generated from multilayer reflectors in the epicuticle of the elytra. By applying association mapping in natural populations (wild‐GWAS) using high‐density genotype variants, we identify five promising candidate genes covarying with metallic variation, with known roles in cuticle formation and pigmentation pathways. This finding, together with a significant correlation between colour variation and water availability, suggests that metallic variation evolves as a local adaptation to environmental variation in the N. ingens complex.

articles.title: Stereochemical preorganization directs triple-helical assembly of Au4 nanoclusters
articles.abstract: Translating local stereochemical information into higher-order helical architectures is a central challenge in materials design. Now it has been shown that stereochemically preorganized Au4 nanoclusters assemble into homochiral triple helices through directional aurophilic interactions, providing a design strategy for chiral nanocluster materials with amplified chiroptical responses.

articles.title: Unidirectional rotation in a molecular motor driven by angular-momentum transfer via helical orbitals
articles.abstract: Molecular motors typically rotate by cycling through excitation and relaxation to ground states. Now it has been shown that a molecular motor can be driven by angular-momentum transfer. Circulating positive and negative currents flowing through orbitals of opposite helicity along a carbon–carbon triple bond enable unidirectional rotation.

articles.title: A reality check for autoimmune CAR T cells
articles.abstract: The hope with CAR T cell therapies for autoimmune disease is that they can reset the immune system and induce deep remission. But recent trial pauses have renewed concerns about safety, patient selection and acceptable risk.

articles.title: Conversational brain AI for adaptive epilepsy care
articles.abstract: A small study shows that patients can help fine-tune their own seizure detectors by chatting with an AI agent. However, the more difficult challenge ahead is to build AI that responds appropriately.

articles.title: EGFR-targeted antibody−toxin conjugate in recurrent glioma: a phase 1 trial
articles.abstract: Results of a phase 1 trial of the antibody−toxin conjugate D2C7-ATC targeting EGFR/EGFRvIII in patients with recurrent malignant glioma show encouraging safety and efficacy signals, with translational analyses of patient samples indicating intratumoral and systemic immune activation.

articles.title: Only time will tell
articles.abstract: Chronotherapy promises to improve medicine by aligning treatment with the body’s internal clock. As this idea moves into clinical trials, a high-profile retraction reveals the ups and downs of circadian medicine.

articles.title: Real-world, digital-first delivery of GLP-1 receptor agonist therapy in women
articles.abstract: Glucagon-like peptide-1 receptor agonists (GLP-1RAs) have demonstrated substantial weight reduction and cardiometabolic benefit in randomized trials; however, prospective implementation evidence from digital care models and female sex community populations remains limited. Here we report outcomes from an observational study of 8,127 women initiating GLP-1RA therapy (99.8% tirzepatide) through a structured digital program incorporating mandatory biochemical monitoring, weekly video-supported follow-up and clinician-guided dose titration in the UK. Mean weight reduction was 16.1 kg (95% confidence interval 15.9 to 16.2; P < 0.001), representing 15.5% of baseline weight; 83.1% achieved ≥10% and 22.4% achieved ≥20% weight loss, with consistent responses across age, baseline weight and socioeconomic strata. Among participants with paired biomarker data, mean glycated hemoglobin decreased by 3.3 mmol mol−1 (95% confidence interval 3.1 to 3.4; P < 0.001), normalizing in 84.5% of those with baseline diabetes-range values and 96.3% with prediabetes, and lipid parameters improved significantly (reductions in total cholesterol of 0.77 mmol l−1, low-density lipoprotein cholesterol of 0.61 mmol l−1 and triglycerides of 0.47 mmol l−1). Retention was 91.4% at 6 months, with no serious treatment-related adverse events. These findings support the feasibility of delivering structured, digitally enabled obesity pharmacotherapy at scale and provide prospective real-world implementation evidence for this care model. Interpretation is limited by the observational design, absence of a comparator group, self-pay population and 6-month follow-up. At 6 months, a cohort of 8,127 women in the UK initiating GLP-1 receptor agonist therapy via a digital platform showed mean weight reduction comparable to that in randomized clinical trials.

articles.title: AmpliconSuite: an end-to-end workflow for analyzing focal amplifications in cancer genomes
articles.abstract: Here we present AmpliconSuite, a toolkit for focal amplification analysis from cancer whole-genome sequencing that identifies extrachromosomal DNA (ecDNA), breakage–fusion–bridges and other amplification modes. Its ecContext module categorizes ecDNA structures to understand formation mechanisms. Validation across 175 metaphase fluorescence in situ hybridization-probed genes in 72 models demonstrated accurate predictions. Analysis of 6,506 patient pan-cancer samples revealed ecDNA-mediated oncogene co-amplification preferences. To democratize data sharing, we created AmpliconRepository, a community-contributable platform, enabling investigation of results across >15,000 publicly hosted samples.

articles.title: Recent developments of fluorescent proteins and biosensors driven by cross-disciplinary insights
articles.abstract: This Review summarizes recent developments in fluorescent protein technology, including the engineering of fluorescent biosensors.

articles.title: Millisecond phonon lifetimes in piezoelectric nanomechanical resonators
articles.abstract: When defect-mediated losses are mitigated, lithium niobate phononic crystal nanomechanical resonators can have intrinsic phonon lifetimes of up to 21 ms at gigahertz frequencies.

articles.title: Cavity-less Brillouin strong coupling in a solid-state continuous system
articles.abstract: Strong coupling between two systems allows them to exchange coherent information before the systems decohere. This important regime in light–matter interactions has predominantly been reached in optical resonator configurations. Here we demonstrate strong coupling between optical and acoustic fields within a continuum of modes in a cavity-less configuration after a single pass through an optical waveguide. The underlying physical effect of anti-Stokes Brillouin–Mandelstam scattering in a highly nonlinear fibre at cryogenic temperature allows us to experimentally demonstrate strong coupling in a waveguide scenario. We show the splitting of the optoacoustic spectral response and introduce a technique to measure the avoided crossing of hybrid optoacoustic modes via forced detuning. This demonstration opens a path towards in-line acoustic-wave-based quantum signal processing in waveguide systems.

articles.title: Chaos control with broken symmetries
articles.abstract: By breaking both material and cavity symmetries, waves can be funnelled into robust closed-loop patterns. This dual-symmetry-breaking approach enables the development of a new class of devices for wave-based signal processing and sensing.

articles.title: The extraction of work from hidden degrees of freedom
articles.abstract: Thermodynamics establishes that information acquired through measurement can be converted into work, as exemplified by Maxwell’s demon and Szilard engines. Most experimental realizations of information engines, however, implicitly assume Markovian environments, in which information exchanged with the surroundings is irreversibly lost. Many physical systems instead exhibit environmental memory, with hidden degrees of freedom retaining correlations with the history of the system and giving rise to non-Markovian dynamics. Whether and how such concealed memory can be harnessed as a thermodynamic resource has remained an open question. Here we experimentally demonstrate the extraction of work from environmental memory. Using time-resolved measurements on an optically trapped Brownian particle in equilibrium, we implement a time-delayed double-measurement protocol that retrieves information through backflow from hidden bath degrees of freedom. We show that this information backflow alters the relaxation dynamics, can be quantified independently of initial state effects and—when appropriately exploited—enhances work extraction. Notably, we identify regimes in which the extracted work exceeds the energy stored in the observable degree of freedom alone. Our results establish environmental memory as an experimentally accessible thermodynamic resource and reveal how non-Markovian dynamics can be systematically explored to improve the performance of information engines operating in time-correlated environments.

articles.title: Lean, mean, breast cancer-fighting machine
articles.abstract: Obesity is a modifiable risk factor associated with increased tumour incidence and aggressiveness. Curtin et al. identify an oxylipin secreted by lean adipocytes that suppresses breast cancer progression.

articles.title: Translating base editors: a decade of progress from the bench to the clinic
articles.abstract: Base editing, a gene editing technology capable of installing point mutations with high efficiency and precision, was first reported a decade ago. This Review examines the evolution of base editors and their road to clinical translation, highlighting key advances, ongoing challenges and the current clinical trial landscape.

articles.title: Hydrogel-confined environment for aqueous-compatible perovskite crystallization
articles.abstract: Confining water within a polymeric hydrogen-bond network creates a controlled aqueous reaction environment that stabilizes precursors and directs the growth of dense, crack-free perovskite thick films. The resulting X-ray detectors achieve an ultralow detection limit of 19.8 nGyair s−1.

articles.title: Introducing chemical gradients into crystalline porous membranes
articles.abstract: Diffusion-limited conversion of pre-formed covalent organic framework membranes creates a continuous chemical gradient across their thickness, with linkage conversion increasing from one face to the other while preserving aligned crystalline nanochannels. This asymmetry directs selective ion transport and increases salinity-gradient energy conversion, while the formation of robust linkages improves acid stability.

articles.title: Reversible zinc oxidation as a route to on-demand hydrogen delivery
articles.abstract: Reversible zinc oxidation, enhanced by lactate coordination, enables a self-sustained, circuit-free pathway for high-density hydrogen storage and delivery. By overcoming solubility limits under ambient conditions, this system delivers higher volumetric capacity and safety than existing carriers, providing a robust alternative to high-pressure infrastructure for decentralized, on-demand green hydrogen delivery.

articles.title: Synthesis of covalent organic frameworks through hydrogen-bonding catalysis
articles.abstract: Covalent organic frameworks (COFs) are a class of crystalline, porous networks constructed by polymerization of organic building blocks. However, most COF syntheses developed so far rely on acid- or base-catalysed reactions that are sensitive to monomer structure, require extensive condition screening, proceed under harsh conditions over several days and often yield low-quality products. Here we report a general hydrogen-bonding catalysis strategy enabled by benzimidazole and its derivatives, acting as both hydrogen-bond donors and acceptors, to produce high-quality COFs. Distinct from conventional catalysis, these catalysts interact with monomers, intermediates and transition states, thereby reducing energy barriers at each step and promoting reversibility. This approach enables control through catalyst-to-monomer ratios and allows the rapid synthesis, within hours, of imide-, imine-, hydrazone- and sp2-carbon-linked COFs with high crystallinity and porosity. The method further supports catalyst reuse and 1,000-fold scale-up, producing COFs with benchmark proton conductivity, establishing hydrogen-bonding catalysis as a versatile route for scalable COF synthesis and applications. Covalent organic frameworks (COFs) are typically synthesized under harsh acid- or base-catalysed conditions. Here a hydrogen-bonding catalysis strategy based on reusable benzimidazole enables the rapid and scalable production of COFs with high crystallinity and porosity, offering a general route to imide, imine, hydrazone and sp2-carbon-linked COF synthesis.

articles.title: The synthetic evolution of porous liquids
articles.abstract: Porosity has long been considered a property exclusive to solids, yet a new class of materials now combines permanent, well defined pores with the ability to flow. Realizing the full promise of these materials as ‘supersolvents’ will require a deeper understanding of the liquid–pore interface and continued exploration of understudied designs, alongside their translation into separation, catalysis, sensing and therapeutic applications.

articles.title: Topotactic synthesis of gradient-encoded covalent organic framework membranes
articles.abstract: A diffusion-limited topotactic exchange strategy transforms vertically aligned imine-linked covalent organic framework membranes into gradient-encoded frameworks across multiple linkage chemistries while preserving crystallinity and channel orientation. The built-in chemical asymmetry enables directional ion transport, enhanced osmotic energy conversion and robust operation under strongly acidic conditions.

articles.title: A shock wave in the Cygnus constellation
FYI science policy news
Glycome remodeling programs pathogenic γδ T17 cell responses in autoimmunity
articles.abstract: Glycans play fundamental roles in T cell biology; however, the glycome landscape of γδ T cells remains to be unlocked. Despite the growing importance of γδ T cells in host defense, tissue homeostasis, and diseases, the glycosylation mechanisms guiding their activation, commitment, and function remain poorly defined. By performing single-cell RNA sequencing, we revealed that type 3/γδ T17/interleukin-17A (IL-17A)–committed γδ T cells rely on ( N-acetylglucosaminyltransferase 1 ) MGAT1 – MGAT5 –mediated branched N-glycosylation. We further demonstrated that the absence of branched N -glycans on γδ T cells acts as a peripheral signal, driving an IL-17A–pro-inflammatory phenotype, alongside a shift to a Vγ4 + subset and the imprinting of innate-like properties. This altered glycoform of type 3 γδ T cells was shown to induce severe psoriasis. γδ T cells from patients with autoimmune and inflammatory diseases exhibited a deficiency in branched N -glycans. Glycan supplementation can reprogram γδ T cells toward a less-pathogenic state, highlighting N -glycans as a previously unrecognized immune checkpoint for γδ T cells.

articles.title: STAT3 operates as an inflammation-dependent transcriptional switch in antiviral NK cells
articles.abstract: The immune system integrates signals to regulate immune responses, forming complex context-dependent networks where identical cues produce distinct outcomes. Signal transducer and activator of transcription (STAT) transcription factors convert cytokine receptor engagement into transcriptional responses, serving as central regulatory hubs. How concurrent STAT activation across different environments shapes immune cell function remains unclear. Here, we show that STAT3 plays a context-dependent role in antiviral natural killer (NK) cells, either promoting or impairing adaptive responses depending on the inflammatory milieu during mouse cytomegalovirus (MCMV) infection. STAT3 is recruited to distinct genomic loci depending on IL-15 or type I interferon availability, thus driving alternative transcriptional programs. Mechanistically, STAT3 differentially regulates downstream transcription factors MYB and B lymphocyte–induced maturation protein-1 (BLIMP-1) to shape NK cell differentiation during homeostasis and infection. STAT3 relocation is governed by epigenetic mechanisms and preferred relocation toward distinct STAT motifs. Thus, STAT3 functions as a cytokine-sensing transcriptional switch integrating IL-15 and type I interferon signals to control lymphocyte adaptation during viral infection.

articles.title: Structural analysis of de novo-designed binders targeting the closed state of HSP90
articles.abstract: Srivastava et al. show that de novo-designed protein binders can selectively recognize the closed state of HSP90. The binders stabilize this conformation and provide new tools to study the HSP90 chaperone cycle and suggest a potential approach to HSP90 inhibition.

articles.title: [Correspondence] China–Nepal border catastrophic floods: a planetary health alarm
articles.abstract: The Hindu Kush Himalayan region, also known as the Third Pole, is warming faster than the global average, with mountain environments experiencing particularly rapid climatic change and climatic extremes.1 The potential risks of glacial lake outburst floods (GLOFs) have been documented for decades, with 47 glacial lakes at risk of expansion and causing GLOFs located in the Hindu Kush Himalayan region, including 21 in Nepal.2 The Rasuwa-Bhote Koshi flood of Aug 26, 2026, near the China–Nepal border, resulted in a catastrophic flood travelling at a speed of 188 km/h from its source; the flood covered 20 km within 7–8 min and reached the China–Nepal border at Rasuwagadhi.

articles.title: [Correspondence] Health care criminalised in Italian immigration detention centres
articles.abstract: Immigration detention centres in Italy constitute a substantive health risk for detainees, including risks of infectious and non-communicable diseases and mental health problems1,2 A 2024 report3 highlighted poor material conditions, an excessive focus on security alongside inconsistent health-care quality, over-medication of detainees with the use of psychotropic drugs, poor-quality food, and minimal transparency in the management of immigration detention centres.4 The report further warned about the excessive use of force by police officers and psychological and physical ill-treatment.

articles.title: [Correspondence] Thirlwall, Bier's spots, and the Letby murders
articles.abstract: The Thirlwall Inquiry1 was set up to examine events at the Countess of Chester Hospital (Chester, UK) and their implications following convictions for murder and attempted murder of babies by nurse Lucy Letby. The inquiry's terms of reference are mainly about the needs of bereaved parents and hospital safety;1 both are important, but are secondary to the prevention of the murders that led to such needs. When babies continue to die unexpectedly and clinical and postmortem explanations are uncertain, police involvement should follow and questions must begin with diagnosis.

articles.title: Carbamate post-translational modifications: bridging CO2 biology and protein regulation
articles.abstract: Carbon dioxide (CO2) is a bioactive gas essential for several physiologically important biological processes, including metabolism, acid–base homoeostasis, and chemosensing. CO2 can directly modulate these processes by stimulating or inhibiting specific cell signalling pathways, including the nuclear factor-κB, calcium, and Wingless (Wnt) pathways. One mechanism by which CO2 interacts with proteins to modulate cell signalling is through the reversible and nonenzymatic modification of α- N-terminal and lysine ε-amino groups to form the carbamate post-translational modification (PTM). Identifying carbamate PTMs is technically challenging because these modifications are readily reversible. However, emerging techniques have now made possible their identification and functional characterisation. Here, we review recent advances in experimental and computational methods to identify CO2-mediated PTMs.

articles.title: Enzyme proximity sequencing: mapping multidimensional enzyme fitness at scale
articles.abstract: Enzyme function is multidimensional, condition-dependent, and difficult to map at scale. Enzyme proximity sequencing (EP-Seq) is a deep mutational scanning method that combines a barcoded enzyme library, yeast surface display, fluorescence-activated cell sorting (FACS), and high-throughput DNA sequencing to measure enzyme expression and catalytic activity.

articles.title: A sulfur-doped nano-hydrangea-like S-NiFe-OH electrocatalyst for efficient and stable alkaline oxygen evolution reaction at industrial-grade current densities
articles.abstract: Scalable thiourea-assisted electrodeposition grows S-doped nano-hydrangea-like NiFe-OH catalysts. Thiourea acts as S source and morphology director, forming a 3D structure for mass transfer. S doping tunes Ni/Fe electronic structure, boosting OER.

articles.abstract: SrTiO 3 (STO), a perovskite-type oxide, is a low cost and nontoxic photocatalyst for H 2 production.

articles.abstract: Selective conversion of glycerol to triacetin can be achieved using mixtures of synthesized novel 2D/3D SnO 2 microbars with surface 2D nanostructures (MB) and SnO 2 quantum dots (QD) hybrid catalysts.

articles.abstract: Synthesis of functionalized oxymethylene ethers (f-OMEs) with unsaturated end groups as valuable building blocks in the chemical industry. This study includes experiments performed in a batch reactor, kinetic modeling and product characterization.

articles.title: A phenome-wide structural variant map from 467,152 UK Biobank genomes
articles.abstract: By studying nearly half a million human genomes, this work shows that structural variants, large changes in DNA sequence greater than 50 base pairs, are an important and previously underrecognized source of human disease risk. The resulting resource reveals rare and regulatory structural variants linked to disease, providing insights into human biology and accelerating the development of medicines.

articles.title: An opioid efficacy switch for reversible optical control of analgesia
articles.abstract: Azo-morphine-3 (AM-3) is a photoswitchable ligand that toggles between low and high efficacy states to control mu-opioid receptor activity in vitro and in vivo both in the brain and periphery. AM-3 provides a powerful tool to probe the structural basis of opioid efficacy and enables spatiotemporally precise control of analgesia across pain models with reduced side effects compared with systemic drugs.

articles.title: Cellular self-organization orchestrates ferroptosis propagation
articles.abstract: Local cell-cell interactions give rise to emergent cellular patterns that encode ferroptosis-sensitive and -resistant fates and establish polarized lipid organization within cells. These coupled biochemical and biophysical properties enable self-organized cell populations to orient and confine otherwise isotropic, unbounded ferroptosis propagation, revealing a systems-level mechanism that regulates collective cell fate.

articles.title: Functional diversification of the cephalopod proteome by RNA editing
articles.abstract: Coleoid cephalopods edit their RNA at a level far beyond other animals, but the functional consequences to the proteome have been largely unknown. Proteomic detection of recoded sites reveals that single amino acid edits alter protein stability, subcellular localization, post-translational modification, and organelle function.

articles.title: Mitochondria-targeted tetraoxanes initiate lipid peroxidation to drive ferroptosis and tumor suppression
articles.abstract: Pan et al. report tetraoxane-containing compounds WMK-1/2 as first-generation mitochondrial lipid peroxidation inducers that bypass GPX4- and retinol-mediated defenses to trigger a distinct “mito-ferroptosis” sub-pathway, demonstrating potent bioavailable tumor-suppressive activity across multiple in vivo models.

articles.title: Multi-omics atlas of chronic exercise
articles.abstract: A 22-tissue multi-omics atlas of chronic exercise is generated, detailing tissue-, sex-, and time-dependent molecular adaptations and cell-type-specific epigenetic remodeling in skeletal muscle. The atlas reveals coordinated transcriptomic, epigenetic, proteomic, and metabolic remodeling across the body.

articles.title: A pangenomic method for establishing a synthetic somatic variant resource in HapMap mixtures
articles.abstract: Kong et al. present a comprehensive resource for benchmarking somatic variant detection across variant classes and allele fractions. Using HapMap mixtures and pangenome graphs, they establish standardized benchmarking sets for evaluating sequencing technologies and variant-calling methods.

articles.title: Detecting low-allele-fraction mosaic mutations: A multi-institution benchmarking with cell-line mixtures
articles.abstract: Ha et al. benchmark detection strategies for mosaic mutations with low variant allele fractions (VAFs) using short- and long-read whole-genome sequencing. By cross-validating Illumina-based calls against PacBio HiFi data using cell-line mixtures generated across five institutions, they construct stratified reference sets, define realistic detection limits, and establish best practices for genome-wide analysis of low-VAF (<2%) variants in non-cancer tissues.

articles.abstract: Lana Mediavilla et al. present NeoBridge, a biophysics-informed machine learning ensemble that prioritizes immunogenic neoantigens. articles.abstract: Qu et al. show that the Akkermansia muciniphila (AKK) protects against endometritis by promoting production of the microbial metabolite tyrosol, which reaches the uterus and suppresses inflammation. These findings reveal a metabolite-mediated gut-uterus axis linking the intestinal microbiota to reproductive health.

articles.title: Gemella morbillorum promotes colorectal tumorigenesis through barrier disruption and invasion-dependent DNA damage
articles.abstract: Meyers, Medina Evora, Molina Tijeras, et al. show that the colorectal cancer-associated oral bacterium Gemella morbillorum (Gm) promotes tumor progression. Colonization of the colon by Gm increases intestinal permeability, enables epithelial cell invasion, reshapes host lipid metabolism, and triggers DNA damage, collectively accelerating disease progression.

articles.title: Prediction of immunotherapy response using live tumor fragments from routine clinical biopsies
articles.abstract: Predicting which patients will benefit from cancer immunotherapy remains challenging. Braun et al. use live tumor tissue from routine needle and forceps biopsies to measure ex vivo immunotherapy response. Results are consistent with clinical outcomes in a small patient cohort, including patients misclassified by current biomarker tests.

articles.title: Living on the Edge: Ecological and Evolutionary Dynamics Along Invasion Fronts
articles.abstract: Invasion fronts are the advancing edges of non‐native species' ranges and represent dynamic, non‐equilibrium boundaries where colonization, biotic interactions and rapid evolutionary processes interact. Although biological invasions are increasingly well studied, the ecological and evolutionary mechanisms operating at invasion fronts remain conceptually fragmented despite their disproportionate influence on spread dynamics, exerted impact and management. Here, we synthesize how invasion‐front geometries arise from interactions among propagule pressure, landscape permeability, long‐distance dispersal and environmental heterogeneity, producing continuous (including satellite colonies), patchy/fragmented or coalescing fronts that shift with invasion stage and spatiotemporal scales. We integrate ecological and evolutionary evidence from macro‐organisms to show how gradients from core to front can result in declining population density, increased trait divergence, spatial sorting, serial founder effects, expansion load, and behavioural and physiological differentiation. We further draw parallels with climate‐driven range expansions, while emphasizing the stronger disequilibrium and novel biotic contexts characteristic of non‐native invasion fronts. Finally, we map these dynamics onto impact trajectories, demonstrating how trait‐mediated interactions, resource reallocation and system‐level reconfiguration can emerge sequentially along the invasion gradient. By unifying ecological and evolutionary processes across appropriate spatial and temporal scales, we establish invasion fronts as powerful natural laboratories and critical leverage points for predicting, monitoring and managing biological invasions.

articles.title: Chemical ecology in conservation biological control: status and emerging challenges
articles.abstract: Over the past decade, chemical ecology has become increasingly integrated into the development of biological control programs, particularly Conservation Biological Control (CBC). Conservation Biological Control exploits a set of habitat manipulation practices to maintain and enhance the reproduction, survival, and efficacy of arthropod natural enemies that prey upon or parasitize insect pests. Specifically, chemical cues that convey information between living organisms, named semiochemicals, can enhance the management of herbivore populations by mediating interactions among plants, herbivores, predators, parasitoids, and their surrounding habitats. Nevertheless, translating mechanistic knowledge of chemically mediated interactions into reliable control of pest insect populations remains a major challenge. A central constraint is the persistent gap between results obtained under simplified laboratory conditions and outcomes observed in dynamic agroecosystems, where background odors, meteorological conditions, crop phenology, and multispecies interactions can modify semiochemical production and transmission, receiver responses, and ultimately, biological control agent efficacy. Additional priorities include moving from the study of individual compounds to ecologically realistic blends of bioactive volatiles; identifying non-target and food-web effects; integrating semiochemical-based interventions with habitat management and selective crop-protection practices; and developing standardized field metrics that connect natural enemy recruitment with predation, parasitism, herbivore population control, and reduction in crop damage. Progress will therefore require multiscale experimentation, closer integration of analytical chemistry with behavioral and field ecology that balance efficacy, ecological safety, and operational feasibility. From this perspective, CBC involves more than enhancing the abundance or activity of arthropod natural enemies: it requires the deliberate management of information flow across multitrophic levels to establish a more predictive and mechanistically grounded framework for biological herbivore population control. Here, are reviewed the principal issues that chemical ecology should address to advance CBC, focusing on how semiochemical production, transmission, and perception vary across plant genotypes, herbivore communities, natural-enemy guilds, microbiomes, agricultural practices, and landscape contexts.

articles.title: Editorial: Intensively monitored watersheds – a tool to help us understand how ecological processes function and are effected by stream and watershed restoration
articles.abstract: How much is watershed management and the protection and restoration of habitat restoration contributing to salmon and steelhead population recovery? This question has led to expansion of research and monitoring programs whose goal is to understand and quantify the contribution watershed management and habitat restoration is making to salmon populations (Diefenderfer et al. 2016). One component of this evaluation effort has been the establishment of a network of watersheds where habitat treatments are coupled with intensive, long-term monitoring to evaluate physical and biological responses to these treatments (Bennett et al. 2016). These sites have been labeled Intensively Monitored Watersheds (IMWs) (Bilby et al. 2005;Bennett et al. 2016). Data required to evaluate the ecological response to habitat actions are expensive to collect and must be gathered over many years to provide confidence in their conclusions (Roni et al. 2008). Because they are costly to implement, IMWs occur in a few select locations with the goal of enabling enough data collection over a sufficient period to develop an understanding of fish and habitat response that can be applied more broadly to restoration efforts.The IMW approach has been used for over six decades to evaluate aquatic ecosystem response to land use practices and habitat restoration. The Alsea Watershed Study, which was initiated in the 1950s, evaluated the response of Coho salmon and Cutthroat trout to alternative logging methods in three small watersheds on the Oregon coast. Results from this study provided much of the technical rationale for the establishment of forestry regulations intended to protect aquatic habitat in the Pacific Northwest. In the 1970s, an ambitious watershed-level project was initiated at Carnation Creek on Vancouver Island, British Columbia, that evaluated the response of hydrology, water quality and salmonid fish populations to logging of a previously unlogged watershed (Tschaplinski, this volume). The results of this study led to a revision of the forestry code for B.C. and influenced revisions to forestry practice rules in other areas of the Pacific Northwest. In the early 2000s multiple IMWs were established in the Pacific Northwest to evaluate the response of habitat and fish populations to freshwater and estuarine salmon habitat restoration efforts. Similar long-term studies have been undertaken in other parts of the world where salmon recovery is an important societal objective.The IMW approach as it has been applied is not without flaws and complications (Bisson et al., 2024). Logistical challenges to implementing study designs due to differences between treated and references watersheds, complexity of statistical study designs, permitting, funding, and implementing habitat treatments have all been identified over the years, but despite these difficulties IMWs have generated information useful for improving restoration strategies (Bilby et al. 2022). Furthermore, intensive. long-term monitoring at watershed scales remains one of the few tools available for empirically quantifying the contribution habitat restoration can make to salmon population recovery.What were the objectives of this special issue?The goal of this issue, "IMWs -A tool to help us understand how ecological processes of stream ecosystems and how these processes are affected by stream and watershed restoration", was to identify ecosystem changes resulting from stream and watershed habitat restoration using the IMW framework and assess salmon and steelhead response to these changes.…

articles.title: Reconstructing early hominin behavioural ecology: a modelling approach
articles.abstract: IntroductionWe use a reverse engineering approach to develop a linear programming model for the behavioural ecology of early hominins (australopithecines).MethodsOur models are based on a recently developed family of empirical models that use climate to predict how animals allocate time to core activities and, from this, whether or not they can balance their activity budget at a specific location as a guide to whether they could survive there. We first use models developed for baboons and chimpanzees to predict whether australopithecines could have survived at sites where they are known to have been present, had they been ecological baboons or ecological chimpanzees. We show that none of the hominins behaved ecologically like either baboons or chimpanzees: the models for these genera fail to predict their known distribution. We then use the equations from the baboon and chimpanzee models to build a model that predicts the known distribution of the australopithecines more precisely.ResultsThe results suggest that they had evolved their own distinctive response to environmental parameters that seems to be related to exploiting a habitat (lacustrine and riverine flood plains) that no other living primate exploits. Our analysis suggests that, in exploiting open flood plain habitats, australopithecines likely foraged as a single group for protection against predators rather than living in fission-fusion communities like modern chimpanzees. The models indicate that climate change post 2.4 Ma resulted in declining group sizes leading to eventual extinction, associated with the appearance of early Homo with novel adaptations for coping with a warmer, drier climate.DiscussionOur analyses suggest that exploiting quantitative models can offer novel insights into the behavioural biology of extinct species, thereby providing rich insights into the forces that drove evolution within particular lineages.

articles.title: Plant invasion in mountain ecosystems reduces soil micro‐food web complexity at higher elevations
articles.abstract: Read the free Plain Language Summary for this article on the Journal blog. Abstract Anthropogenic activities have accelerated plant invasions in mountain ecosystems, impacting the structure and functions of native plant communities. Changes in above‐ground vegetation can drive shifts in below‐ground biota, yet the effects of plant invasions on soil micro‐food web structure and complexity along elevational gradients and the underlying mechanisms remain poorly understood. This study examined the differences between the communities of native herbaceous plants invading Ageratina adenophora along an elevational gradient in the Gaoligong Mountains. We surveyed the composition of the plant community, measured the physicochemical properties of the soil and the enzyme activities of carbon and nitrogen acquisition. The complexity of the soil micro‐food web complexity index (including bacteria, fungi, nematodes and protists) using high‐throughput sequencing and network analysis. Structural equation modelling and two‐way ANOVA were used to analyse the effects of elevation, invasion and their interaction on the micro‐food web. We found that native plant diversity, soil micro‐food web complexity and soil carbon‐ and nitrogen‐acquiring enzyme activities all increased significantly with elevation. However, invasion by A. adenophora both reduced native plant diversity and altered the original elevation pattern of the soil micro‐food web. At the highest elevation (2300 m), the complexity index of the soil micro‐food web in native communities was approximately 4.8 units higher than in invaded communities, while the activities of the C‐acquiring enzymes of the soil were 135% higher and the activities of the N‐acquiring enzymes 119% higher. The complexity of the soil micro‐food web was directly influenced by plant diversity, soil nutrient cycling capacity and multitrophic diversity, whereas environmental factors such as mean temperature and soil moisture exerted indirect effects through soil nutrient status and cycling processes. Our findings demonstrate that the invasion of A. adenophora primarily affects high‐elevation ecosystems by reducing native herbaceous plant diversity, thus reducing the complexity of the micro‐food web of the soil and altering the carbon and nitrogen cycling of the soil. This study advances the mechanistic understanding of how plant invasions impact soil food webs and associated mountain ecosystem processes, providing insights into invasion management and control strategies. Read the free Plain Language Summary for this article on the Journal blog. 摘要 人为活动加速了山地生态系统中的植物入侵，影响了本地植物群落的结构和功能。地上植被的变化可以驱动地下生物群落的转变，但植物入侵沿海拔梯度对土壤微食物网结构和复杂性的影响及其潜在机制仍不清楚。本研究考察了高黎贡山紫茎泽兰(Ageratina adenophora)入侵群落与本地草本植物群落沿海拔梯度的差异。我们调查了植物群落组成，测定了土壤理化性质以及碳氮获取酶活性，并利用高通量测序和网络分析评估了土壤微食物网(包括细菌、真菌、线虫和原生动物)的复杂性。采用结构方程模型和双因素方差分析解析海拔、入侵及其交互作用对微食物网的影响。研究发现，本地植物多样性、土壤微食物网复杂性以及土壤碳氮获取酶活性均随海拔升高而显著增加。然而，紫茎泽兰入侵既降低了本地植物多样性，也改变了土壤微食物网的原有海拔格局。在最高海拔(2300 m)，本地群落的土壤微食物网复杂性指数比入侵群落高约4.8个单位，而土壤碳获取酶活性高135%，氮获取酶活性高119%。土壤微食物网复杂性直接受植物多样性、土壤养分循环能力和多营养级多样性的影响，而平均气温和土壤湿度等环境因素则通过土壤养分状态和循环过程发挥间接效应。本研究推进了对植物入侵如何影响土壤食物网及相关山地生态系统过程的机制理解，为入侵管理和控制策略提供了科学依据。

articles.title: Dan Kastner (1951–2026)
articles.abstract: Daniel L. Kastner, physician-scientist, geneticist, mentor, and scientific leader, transformed our understanding of human inflammatory disease. His death is a profound loss not only to the immunology community but also to the numerous patients and families whose illnesses he elucidated—and for whom, in many cases, he developed effective treatments. Called the “father of autoinflammatory diseases,” Dan did more than discover individual disorders: he defined an entirely new category of human disease.

articles.title: Lactate dehydrogenase A-dependent redox control of selective mRNA translation directs monocyte fate commitment
articles.abstract: Metabolic reprogramming regulates immune cell function; however, how metabolic signals instruct early monocyte fate commitment remains unclear. Yang et al. show that LDHA-dependent cytosolic NAD+ regeneration promotes selective HIF1α translation, supporting commitment to a protective NOS2+ macrophage fate and revealing a broader link between redox metabolism and cell fate decisions.

Polarization switching modulates the junction depletion region and enables nonvolatile memory operation. The Fe-JFET also supports analog conductance modulation and synaptic functions for neuromorphic computing.

articles.title: Inherent electrochemical activity of extrachromosomal DNA hub shapes spatial redox environment in nucleus
articles.abstract: Qin et al. demonstrate that extrachromosomal DNA hubs function as inherent electrochemical reactors. By non-enzymatically generating a localized antioxidant shield, these hubs protect themselves from oxidative damage. Disrupting this spatial redox balance triggers ecDNA degradation, exposing a distinct vulnerability in ecDNA-positive cancers.

articles.title: Molecular mechanism of residue-specific nucleosome acetylation
articles.abstract: Müller, Kolesnikova, Doudin, et al. reveal a structural mechanism for residue-specific nucleosome acetylation by capturing the MSL histone acetyltransferase during catalysis. Their findings provide a foundation for understanding how H4K16 acetylation links transcription to changes in chromatin structure, a mechanism essential for Drosophila dosage compensation and implicated in human disease.

articles.title: The binding of OTULIN restrains LUBAC activity to prevent TNF-driven immunopathology
articles.abstract: Lyu et al. show that the interaction between the deubiquitinase OTULIN and the ubiquitin ligase LUBAC restrains LUBAC autoubiquitination and activity. Disrupting this interaction enhances Met1-linked ubiquitination at the TNF receptor complex, which increases NF-κB signaling and sensitizes mice to TNF-dependent toxicity. Thus, the OTULIN-LUBAC interaction restricts Met1-linked ubiquitin signaling.

articles.title: Lyman continuum escape during the onset of galactic winds in compact starbursts
articles.abstract: UV spectra of six similar galaxies show that stronger, faster, multiphase outflows accompany lower escape of ionizing radiation. Thus Lyman continuum escape may peak before strong galactic winds develop and then decline as the wind-column density grows.

articles.title: Structural variant detection across sequencing technologies
articles.abstract: HitSV models the interaction between genomic repetitiveness and signature intensity to improve structural variant detection.

articles.title: Operando resolution of CO2 electrolysis interfaces at application-relevant current density reveals water gating
articles.abstract: Understanding the dynamic interplay between all components in complex electrocatalytic systems is crucial to advancing their performance. Here operando Raman spectroscopy is used in combination with molecular dynamics simulations to establish the role of water ordering in the mechanism of electrocatalytic CO2 reduction over a range of current densities and under practical conditions.

articles.title: Author Correction: Type A cholesterol-dependent cytolysins translocate to the trans-Golgi network for NLRP3 inflammasome activation
articles.abstract: Author Correction: Type A cholesterol-dependent cytolysins translocate to the trans-Golgi network for NLRP3 inflammasome activation

articles.title: Tuning T cells to give cancer the blues
articles.abstract: On 26–29 May 2026, the first ‘ImmunoMemphis in May’ conference took place at St. Jude Children’s Research Hospital in Memphis, Tennessee, bringing together scientists to catch up on recent advances in T cell immunotherapy.

articles.title: Hidden race disparities in cancer treatment toxicity
articles.abstract: Large-scale analysis of real-world data reveals racial disparities in the occurrence of immune-related adverse events during cancer immunotherapy — which were not evident in trial data, owing to the enrollment of mostly white patients.

articles.title: Interlayer sliding controls magnetism in tetralayer graphene
articles.abstract: The crystal structure of tetralayer graphene can be switched between rhombohedral and Bernal stacking through interlayer sliding controlled by gate voltages. This sliding transition now enables ferromagnetic states present only in the rhombohedral stacking to be turned on and off through structural control.

articles.title: Your battery may not be a battery
