Such interdisciplinary collaboration facilitates the recognition of new diseases and elucidation of the causes of previously unclassified disorders. Improving patient care requires not only aetiological and mechanistic insight to enable development of targeted therapies but also strengthened cross-specialty expertise to optimise diagnosis and management.

articles.title: Climate change: aggravation and adaptation in neurology
From syndrome to antibody-defined autoimmune encephalitides

Neurotrauma as a chronic disease: a call for integrated care
Progress in exon skipping for Duchenne muscular dystrophy
Reframing traumatic brain injury and spinal cord injury as chronic multisystem disorders: toward integrated, long-term care
articles.abstract: Traumatic brain injury (TBI) and spinal cord injury (SCI) affect more than 220 million people worldwide and are associated with cardiometabolic, endocrine, neurological, and psychiatric sequelae for years to decades after an acute injury. However, most health systems still treat neurotrauma (TBI and SCI, collectively) as a time-limited event, leaving long-term surveillance of these patients fragmented or absent, which leads to preventable mortality and avoidable readmissions. TBI and SCI in adults should be reclassified as acute-onset multisystem chronic-risk conditions. Existing cardiovascular, endocrine, and psychiatric services do not capture neurotrauma-specific risks, including trauma-induced hypopituitarism, autonomic dysregulation, accelerated ageing, and cognitive-behavioural impairment, so neurotrauma care is best framed as a missing node in chronic neurological care. We propose a risk-stratified pathway of care navigation, multisystem screening, and telehealth; convergence with adjacent stroke, cardiometabolic, memory, psychiatric, pain, and epilepsy services; and the financing, workforce, and registry reforms needed to deliver measurable reductions in 5-year mortality, avoidable rehospitalisation, and long-term disability.

articles.title: Safety and efficacy of delpacibart zotadirsen in Duchenne muscular dystrophy mutations amenable to exon 44 skipping in the USA (EXPLORE44): a randomised, placebo-controlled, double-blind, phase 1/2 trial
articles.abstract: BackgroundThere are no approved exon skipping therapies to treat Duchenne muscular dystrophy due to DMD variants amenable to exon 44 skipping (DMD44). Delpacibart zotadirsen (del-zota, also known as AOC 1044) is a first-in-class antibody-oligonucleotide conjugate designed to deliver an exon 44-skipping phosphorodiamidate morpholino oligomer to muscle to restore dystrophin expression for individuals with DMD44. EXPLORE44 was a first-in-human trial to evaluate del-zota's safety, tolerability, pharmacokinetics, pharmacodynamics, and efficacy.MethodsEXPLORE44 was a two-part randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled, phase 1/2 study in healthy adult men (aged 18-55 years; part A) and ambulatory and non-ambulatory male participants with DMD44 (aged 7-27 years; part B) at ten clinical research sites in the USA. Dosing in part B was informed by safety, pharmacokinetic, and pharmacodynamic data from part A. In part B, participants with DMD44 were randomised (3:1 del-zota:placebo) within two dose cohorts to receive three intravenous doses of del-zota (5 mg/kg every 6 weeks, or 10 mg/kg every 8 weeks) or matching placebo. A computer-generated permuted-block randomisation schedule was prepared by an independent statistician with no further role in the study. Infusions were prepared by an unmasked pharmacist under supervision of the masked investigator; other site staff, participants, and sponsor team members were masked to allocation. The primary objective was safety and tolerability measured by the incidence of treatment-emergent adverse events. Secondary endpoints assessing target engagement were change from baseline in exon skipping (ie, defined as the percentage of dystrophin mRNA transcripts in which exon 44 is excluded from the mature mRNA relative to total dystrophin mRNA transcripts) and dystrophin level to month 4 (5 mg/kg cohort) or month 5 (10 mg/kg cohort). The trial was registered with ClinicalTrials.gov (NCT05670730) and is complete.FindingsBetween Dec 5, 2022, and June 27, 2024, we enrolled and randomly assigned 45 healthy volunteers and 26 men and boys with DMD44. In part A, three (30%) of ten healthy volunteers who received placebo and 21 (62%) of 34 who received del-zota reported at least one adverse event, none of which were severe or serious. In part B, nine participants with DMD44 received del-zota at 5 mg/kg, ten at 10 mg/kg, and seven received placebo; mean age 13·3 years (SD 4·2). 16 (84%) participants with DMD44 treated with del-zota and six (86%) treated with placebo reported at least one adverse event, most of which were mild or moderate; two participants, both in the 5 mg/kg del-zota group, discontinued due to adverse events (anaphylactic reaction and infusion-related reaction). Mean increases from baseline in exon 44 skipping were 36·6% (95% CI 20·8 to 52·4, SD 17·1, nominal p=0·0013) at 5 mg/kg, 43·4% (32·8 to 54·0, 14·9, nominal pInterpretationDel-zota had an acceptable safety profile, produced increases in exon 44 skipping and dystrophin expression, and decreased biomarkers of muscle damage in participants with DMD44. Findings from this study support further investigation of del-zota in a phase 3 study to assess efficacy and long-term safety.FundingAvidity Biosciences, A Novartis Company.

articles.title: Staged bilateral focused ultrasound pallidothalamic tractotomy for Parkinson's disease
Staged bilateral focused ultrasound pallidothalamic tractotomy for Parkinson's disease – Authors' reply
Beyond attention: performance pressure shifts information-processing complexity
articles.abstract: Why does performance pressure sometimes cause choking but sometimes elicit exceptional performance? We propose that pressure shifts the complexity of information-processing rules that guide action. Performance improves when shifts move processing toward task-matched complexity and deteriorates when they promote maladaptive simplification, overcomplexification, or the use of rules that exceed available processing resources.

articles.title: From ‘magic traits’ to diversification mechanisms
articles.abstract: Species richness is markedly uneven across the tree of life, and traits have long been invoked to explain this pattern. Expanding phylogenetic and trait datasets enable broader comparisons, but trait–diversity associations alone do not reveal how differences in richness arose. We argue that such associations should be reframed as process hypotheses about three non-exclusive processes: lineage origin, access to ecological or geographic opportunity, and persistence. Mixed trait–diversity associations are expected when the same trait influences multiple processes whose relative contributions vary across contexts. This process-based framework makes alternative diversification histories explicit and specifies contrasting temporal predictions that can be evaluated with complementary evidence. It clarifies what findings would weaken each hypothesis and when available data leave alternative histories unresolved.

articles.title: Precipitation timing matters for flowering communities
articles.abstract: Flowering times have long been a harbinger of the changing seasons and, more recently, of a changing climate. Among the cues that trigger flowering, precipitation timing has been relatively little-studied. Tsafon et al. show that the timing of precipitation shapes flowering in complex ways. Much work remains to disentangle this complexity.

articles.title: A high-dimensional population code in the bat motor cortex during natural dexterous flight
articles.abstract: Bats use their hand-like wings to reproduce natural flights with wingbeat-level precision. Rather than mainly tracking the wingbeat cycle, the wing motor cortex generates sparse, distinct population states with little shared variance across wingbeats, resulting in a high-dimensional code distinct from that typically observed in constrained tasks.

articles.title: Mechanisms of transcription control by distal enhancers from single-gene nanoscopy
articles.abstract: High-resolution real-time imaging of enhancer-promoter communication reveals how the two genomic loci are actively brought together through cohesin-mediated loop extrusion and how E-P interactions are temporally coordinated with transcriptional bursts. Unexpectedly, components of the RNA Pol II general machinery form nanoscale clusters at distal enhancers, and embedding the promoter into such clusters boosts GTF activities and triggers burst initiation.

articles.title: PTPRS mediates invasion of tetanus neurotoxin into the central nervous system
articles.abstract: Tetanus neurotoxin enters the central nervous system through motor neurons. This study identifies PTPRS as the long-sought retrograde transport receptor that directs toxin trafficking in motor neurons into the spinal cord, uncovering a host pathway that can be targeted for post-exposure treatment and for drug delivery into the central nervous system.

articles.title: Rare k-mers reveal centromere haplogroups underlying human diversity and cancer translocations
articles.abstract: By defining centromere haplogroups from rare k-mer variation, Shiraishi et al. uncover extensive hidden diversity and link centromere structure to human evolution and disease-associated genomic instability.

articles.title: Structural basis and rational engineering of a thermophilic Cas13a for robust RNA detection
articles.abstract: Oladeji et al. determined the cryo-EM structure of the TccCas13a ternary complex and leveraged structural insights to engineer a thermophilic Cas13a variant with 100-fold enhanced sensitivity. The engineered nuclease retains programmability and thermostability, enabling highly sensitive RNA detection in different biological matrices.

PrimeCAR cells maintain stemness-associated and proliferative responses with reduced myeloid-activating inflammation, and early-phase studies in B cell malignancies demonstrate encouraging clinical activity with few severe cytokine release syndrome (CRS) or immune effector cell-associated neurotoxicity syndrome (ICANS) events.

articles.title: Single-cell CRISPR screen maps epigenetic regulators of lineage specification and malignancies in human HSPCs

The atlas identifies regulators associated with long-term repopulation and lineage-biased outputs and nominates PRDM10 as a candidate AML dependency.

Kinetic Monte Carlo simulations of solid-state photon upconversion describe an anticorrelation between emission yield and threshold intensity
articles.abstract: Kinetic Monte Carlo simulations are used to model solid-state triplet-triplet annihilation photon upconversion, which consists of a sensitizer doped into an annihilator matrix. The simulations incorporate solid-state activated processes, where the process of Förster resonance energy transfer is independently benchmarked against experimental data. Our results show that both upconversion efficiency and threshold intensity are coupled through the sensitizer concentration, limiting their simultaneous optimization. Thus, the triplet-state lifetime is a key parameter in solid-state upconversion.

articles.title: Ultrafast water transport through densely fluorinated foldamer channels
articles.abstract: Extensively fluorinated aramid polymers fold into discrete single-chain nanoparticle tubes with continuous internal lumens. Stabilized by F–H–F interactions, these abiotic channels enable ultrafast and highly selective water transport across membranes, surpassing natural aquaporins while maintaining excellent salt rejection.

articles.title: Marine Carbonate System Observing and mCDR: New Processes, Needs, and Systems
articles.abstract: Marine carbon dioxide removal (mCDR) techniques have the potential to remove legacy emitted carbon dioxide from the atmosphere and store it durably in ocean reservoirs. While the ocean’s vast surface area and buffering capacity offer benefits for scaling removal, monitoring remains challenging. This comprehensive review of marine carbonate system observing and monitoring technologies finds that mCDR processes span multiple scales, often at the edges of existing platform and sensing capability. While some mCDR observing and monitoring is possible today, challenges will arise as experiments and operations expand. Leaps forward in assessing the novel scales of mCDR processes will emerge from low-energy, low-cost, highly durable sensors; innovative deployment platforms; cooperative sensing networks; dedicated model validation programs; and decision support tools. This review is intended to serve as a guide to the history, ongoing innovation, and transformative vision of future marine carbonate system observing and monitoring informed by mCDR.

Individual bumblebee foraging repertoires: Implications for disease persistence
articles.abstract: Read the free Plain Language Summary for this article on the Journal blog. Abstract Generalist species may be comprised of individual specialists. Individual specialization can impact disease transmission at shared resources by shaping contact patterns. Mathematical models of pollinator diseases that spread via flowers have shown that R 0 can be greatly amplified when each forager specializes on one flower species at a time with slow turnover. Yet, such behaviour has not been empirically demonstrated in generalist bumblebees. Here, we used palynology from sequential pollen loads of individual common eastern bumble bees (Bombus impatiens) to assess their foraging preferences over time. We used an automated monitoring system to greatly improve recapture rates, hence allowing a more complete characterization of each bee's foraging behaviours. Individuals in a bumblebee colony exhibited unique foraging repertoires of two to three flower species while the full-colony diet breadth was up to three times larger depending on time of year. Individual repertoires exhibited roughly 50% turnover, on average, over 10 days. Implications for disease transmission when individual repertoire sizes are greater than one may differ from specialization on a single flower species. Hence, we developed mathematical models where each bee has an effective repertoire size of two, and found that ignoring individual specialization still resulted in an underprediction of R 0, although to a smaller extent compared to a single-specialty model. Our results provide novel insights into the foraging behaviours of social bumblebees and improve predictions of how diseases are transmitted and persist in complex plant–pollinator networks. Read the free Plain Language Summary for this article on the Journal blog.

articles.title: Milder winters alleviate seasonal challenges for a migratory goose facing Arctic warming
articles.abstract: By combining extensive body mass records with population‐wide migration counts spanning several decades, this study uncovers long‐term improvements in body condition associated with progressively milder winters, alongside earlier spring departure in an Arctic migrant, highlighting the importance of the full annual cycle in determining species' responses to climate change. Abstract Many migratory birds now reach their Arctic breeding grounds earlier in response to advancing springs and shifting nutrient peaks, either by departing earlier from non‐breeding grounds or by travelling faster. For dark‐bellied brent geese, there is limited potential to travel faster, as their spring migration is already among the fastest of Arctic geese and swans. Earlier departure would require reaching departure body mass earlier, either through a faster accumulation of energy stores during spring staging in the Wadden Sea or via adjustments earlier in the annual cycle. We examined long‐term shifts in spring staging phenology and changes in winter and spring body mass trajectories of brent geese at the population level, with particular emphasis on the effects of winter temperature on body mass and spring body mass on departure timing. We used more than five decades of body mass measurements from individuals caught in the United Kingdom and France and in the Dutch Wadden Sea to reconstruct changes in winter and spring mass trajectories, respectively. These data were combined with over five decades of migration counts in the Netherlands and more than two decades of counts in Denmark to quantify changes in arrival and departure timing, respectively. We found that brent geese were heavier during and after milder winters and that their body mass trajectories flattened over the years: they no longer lose body mass during winter; during spring staging, fuelling rates have declined (in the so‐called ‘fattening phase’), while they also no longer lose body mass in the 1–2 weeks prior to departure (‘plateau phase’). Brent geese have not shifted their spring arrival in the Wadden Sea but have advanced departure timing. Annual variation in body mass was not related to annual departure timing. These results suggest that milder winters have relaxed energetic constraints and improved body condition in brent geese throughout the non‐breeding season. Our findings highlight the importance of considering the full annual cycle when assessing how migratory animals respond to global change, in particular those with limited capacity to adjust migration timing or speed.

articles.title: Legume presence outweighs functional group richness in determining community invasibility under nitrogen enrichment
articles.abstract: These findings reveal that FGR provides a structural template for biotic resistance, whereas functional identity determines whether this template translates into resource pre‐emption or community vulnerability. In nutrient‐enriched ecosystems, low‐biomass legumes can inadvertently convert nutrient pulses into invasion opportunities by elevating the baseline resource environment and presenting limited above‐ground suppression. Restoring invasion‐resistant communities under N enrichment therefore requires functional‐identity screening—prioritizing strongly competitive non‐legumes rather than relying solely on FGR. Abstract Anthropogenic nitrogen (N) enrichment often promotes plant invasions by increasing resource availability, yet why resident communities differ in their resistance to the same resource pulse remains poorly understood. Here, we manipulated native plant functional group richness (FGR = 1–3) and community composition while holding species richness constant and assessed the performance of the nitrophilous invader Bidens alba under ambient and N‐enriched conditions to determine whether biotic resistance is driven by diversity per se or specific functional identities. N enrichment consistently increased invader biomass, but its interaction with FGR was not significant across the full richness gradient, indicating that FGR alone was insufficient for predicting biotic resistance. Instead, functional identity strongly governed plant invasion outcomes. Non‐legume communities (grasses and forbs) sustained high biotic resistance under N enrichment through strong above‐ground neighbour suppression. Conversely, legume‐containing communities exhibited weak biotic resistance under N enrichment, permitting a considerable increase in invader biomass. Legumes facilitated plant invasion through a coupled below‐ and above‐ground mechanism: they maintained a high baseline soil nitrate availability while experiencing competitive suppression under N enrichment, resulting in low biomass and minimal physical canopy presence. Combined with N enrichment, this created a favourable resource window that enabled B. alba to reduce its root: shoot ratio—a morphological plasticity response constrained in non‐legume communities by dense native neighbour biomass. Synthesis. Our findings reveal that FGR provides a structural template for biotic resistance, whereas functional identity determines whether this template translates into resource pre‐emption or community vulnerability. In nutrient‐enriched ecosystems, low‐biomass legumes can inadvertently convert nutrient pulses into invasion opportunities by elevating the baseline resource environment and presenting limited above‐ground suppression. Restoring invasion‐resistant communities under N enrichment therefore requires functional‐identity screening—prioritizing strongly competitive non‐legumes rather than relying solely on FGR.

articles.title: Molecular regulation of Frenkel defect pairs enables phase-stable wide-band-gap perovskites for tandem photovoltaics
articles.abstract: Light-induced phase segregation limits the efficiency and stability of wide-band-gap mixed-halide perovskites. This work demonstrates that multi-site molecular regulation can cooperatively manage Frenkel defect-pair dynamics, thereby suppressing phase segregation. This stabilization is achieved by thermodynamically suppressing Frenkel defect-pair formation and dissociation while kinetically restricting subsequent halide redistribution.

articles.title: A feedback mechanism of m6A via PARP1-mediated ADP ribosylation of METTL3/METTL14
articles.abstract: Bai et al. reveal a PARP1-mediated m6A feedback mechanism involving IGF2BPs and the METTL3/METTL14 writer complex. They further show that combined targeting of ADP ribosylation and m6A leads to synergistic anti-tumor effects, providing a potential therapeutic strategy for cancer treatment.

articles.title: Reverse transcribed ssDNA derepresses translation of a retron antiviral protein
articles.abstract: Retrons help bacteria defend against phage by initiating a toxic response to restrict viral propagation. Here, Zhang et al. describe the non-canonical mechanism of Retron-Vpa2, which accumulates msDNA in response to phage triggers and regulates its toxic response on a translational level through a highly structured hybrid RNA.

articles.title: Structural basis of directionality control in large serine integrases
articles.abstract: Shin et al. present cryo-EM structures of the SPβ integrase along the integration and excision pathways that provide mechanistic insights addressing the long-standing questions of how large serine integrases enforce highly directional DNA recombination and how the cognate recombination directionality factor leads to a complete reversal of directionality.

articles.title: Transposable element splicing reveals a tumor-enriched class of gene-independent transcripts
articles.abstract: Li et al. systematically map splicing within and between transposable elements (TEs) across cancers and define TEtrans, a tumor-enriched class of gene-independent transcripts. TEtrans display distinct regulatory programs and can function as oncogenic RNAs or encode immunogenic tumor antigens, expanding the functional landscape of TE reactivation in cancer.

articles.title: A ∧-like metallicity profile in the disk of the Sagittarius dwarf galaxy
articles.abstract: N-body simulations decode the chemo-kinematic signatures of the Sagittarius stream, reproducing their vertical metallicity gradient. The findings reveal that the stream originated from a disk with a ∧-like metallicity profile.

articles.title: Two families of multi-planet systems with distinct architectures and stellar hosts
articles.abstract: The rapidly growing census of exoplanets now includes over a thousand multi-planet systems, revealing architectures that span more than four orders of magnitude in mass and five in orbital scale. Explaining the origin of this striking diversity remains a central challenge for planet formation theory, compounded by observational biases that limit access to Solar System-like regimes. Here we introduce architecture-agnostic metrics to uniformly analyse four independently defined samples of multi-planet systems, uncovering unifying patterns across their diversity. We identify a clear bimodality in system masses, dividing known architectures into two distinct families. The lower-mass family, predominantly hosted by subsolar-to-solar stars, exhibits tightly packed configurations with mass distributions consistent with the ‘peas-in-a-pod’ pattern and modal dynamical excitation comparable with that of the Solar System. By contrast, the high-mass family forms in metal-rich environments around solar-to-supersolar stars, displays gravitationally compact architectures and is an order of magnitude dynamically hotter than both the Solar System and the lower-mass counterparts. Their high level of dynamical excitation points to violent evolutionary pathways driven by global instabilities and planet–planet scattering. Together, these results show that the architectures of planetary systems are born from the combined influence of formation processes and host star properties. Signatures of these roots are preserved across the post-formation dynamical evolution that reshaped most known multi-planet systems.

articles.title: In vivo engineering of CAR natural killer cells for immunotherapy using ligand-directed lipid nanoparticles
articles.abstract: Chimeric antigen receptor natural killer cells to treat autoimmune disease and cancer are generated in vivo.

articles.title: Proteomic aging clocks go to trial
articles.abstract: Six proteomic aging clocks are deployed in a clinical trial for the first time, revealing more about the clocks than about the drug.

articles.title: A unique and equity-driven approach to immunology education in low- and middle-income countries
articles.abstract: We present a model for education that has proven transformative for faculty and students, fostering mentorship, inclusion and cross-border collaboration. By embedding training in local contexts, our framework builds confidence, skills and leadership among early-career scientists. These elements foster scientific autonomy and enable sustainable global engagement.

articles.title: Author Correction: Monocyte-derived galectin-1hi cells provide innate immune help in the generation of functional memory CD8+ T cells
articles.abstract: Author Correction: Monocyte-derived galectin-1hi cells provide innate immune help in the generation of functional memory CD8+ T cells

articles.title: Near-infrared photochromic miniprotein enables photoacoustic molecular imaging of acute inflammation and intracellular antigens
articles.abstract: Using near-infrared photoswitchable photochromic genetically encoded probes, differential photoacoustic tomography (PAT) enables deep-tissue imaging with high resolution and sensitivity; however, current bacteriophytochrome-based probes are bulky multidomain proteins exceeding 55 kDa, which constrains their use for designing PAT molecular reporters. Here we engineer rsmiRFPnano, a compact cyanobacteriochrome-derived photoswitchable PAT probe. With a molecular weight below 19 kDa, rsmiRFPnano efficiently incorporates biliverdin, exhibits high extinction coefficients in both photochromic states and demonstrates robust performance in live cells. We established rsmiRFPnano-based reporters for NF-κB and AP-1 pathways, which display low basal activity and strong activation-dependent responses. These reporters effectively visualized acute inflammation using noninvasive PAT in vivo, further validated through cellular-level spatial omics mapping. We then created photoswitchable nanobody probes, rsNIR-Fbs, stabilized upon antigen binding and rapidly degraded otherwise, enabling selective photoacoustic immuno-imaging of intracellular antigens in vivo. Together, these results establish rsmiRFPnano as an ultracompact and versatile platform for molecular PAT.

articles.title: The companion website
articles.abstract: How biologists can make the most of supplementary materials for impact.

articles.title: From DNA to full-length proteins through nanopore sequencing
articles.abstract: Nanopore protein sequencing has advanced from a theoretical ambition to a practical technology, overcoming major challenges in protein unfolding, transport and signal detection to achieve single-amino-acid and post-translational modification sensitivity. With both full-length and peptide-based approaches progressing towards commercialization, the field is now focused on scaling throughput and refining analysis tools to unlock a new generation of single-molecule proteomics.

articles.title: From a single atom to manufacturable quantum processors in silicon
articles.abstract: Two decades on from the first atomic-scale devices, atom-based silicon quantum computers have progressed from proof of concept to scalable quantum processors that are rapidly gaining commercial traction. What remains is largely a matter of industrial-scale engineering and 3D integration.

articles.title: From nano to technology
articles.abstract: As the journal turns 20, we reflect on the journey nanoscale science has undertaken over the past two decades and how nanoscience-enabled technologies have had a real-world impact.

articles.title: How display technology adopted quantum dots
articles.abstract: Quantum dots — semiconductor nanocrystals whose optical and electronic properties can be tuned by controlling their size, composition and surface chemistry — have found commercial success for display technologies. Their transition from nanophotonics research into an applied modern nanotechnology exemplifies the bottlenecks that many emerging technologies must overcome on the path to commercialization.

articles.title: How lipid nanoparticles evolved from models of biological membranes to systems that enable RNA therapeutics
articles.abstract: Curiosity-driven studies of lipid organization and lipid asymmetry in biological membranes led to scalable methods for making liposomes, efficient loading of drugs and ionizable cationic lipids. In turn, these advances led to lipid nanoparticles enabling the RNA medicine Onpattro and the COVID-19 mRNA vaccines, and they are now facilitating gene therapies that can potentially treat most human diseases.

articles.title: How single-atom catalysis transformed from a nanoscience curiosity into a new paradigm for heterogeneous catalysis
articles.abstract: Single-atom catalysis has reshaped heterogeneous catalysis by shifting its central focus from surface and interface to isolated atom-centred active sites. This transition establishes a new paradigm for understanding reactivity, integrating experiments and theory, and advancing heterogeneous catalysis from empirical observations toward a more predictive and precise science.

articles.title: How spin-transfer-torque magnetoresistive random access memory bridged spintronics research and the microelectronics industry
articles.abstract: Spin-transfer torque magnetoresistive random access memory has emerged as a leading non-volatile memory technology replacing embedded Flash in diverse fields including aerospace, automotive and healthcare applications.

articles.title: Where is my graphene battery?
articles.abstract: After years of hype and research, there is still no graphene battery electrode in mass production, but researchers say the material shows promise for energy storage.

articles.abstract: This study provides evidence that afforestation and reforestation can increase soil carbon storage and support soil microbial communities, thus highlighting their potential in nature-based climate solutions.

articles.title: Mosquito-based malaria control through genetic, microbial and immunological innovations
articles.abstract: In this Review, Dong and colleagues overview recent developments in mosquito-targeted malaria control, highlighting Anopheles population modification (rendering mosquitoes Plasmodium-resistant) and Anopheles population-suppression strategies based on gene drive technology, engineered microorganisms, vaccines and drugs, and discuss key knowledge gaps and the responsible implementation of these approaches in conjunction with existing malaria interventions.

articles.title: A general synthesis of tryptophan-crosslinked macrocyclic peptides enabled by a dual-functional directing group
articles.abstract: Tryptophan-crosslinked macrocyclic peptides display interesting therapeutic properties; however, methods for their synthesis are limited. Now a Rh-catalysed process enables their synthesis through the development of a dual-function directing group that promotes C–H activation and C–N bond formation. The method provides access to a range of macrocycles, including pharmacophores of micitide 982 and tryglysin.

articles.title: Synthesis of chiral allylic amines through regio- and enantioselective homologation of enamines using Ni catalysis
articles.abstract: Chiral allylic amines are key building blocks in the synthesis of bioactive molecules. Now a regio- and enantioselective method for their synthesis is reported. The Ni-catalysed process proceeds through homologation of enamines by cross-coupling with alkynes, forming a range of chiral allylic amines in good yield and with excellent enantioselectivity.

articles.abstract: Researchers establish a framework using local reversibility to correctly classify phases of matter in open and noisy quantum systems.

articles.abstract: Researchers demonstrate that bipartite Einstein-Podolsky-Rosen entanglement cannot be distilled from tripartite Haar random states by local operations.

articles.title: [Correspondence] Prioritising the future of youth is an urgent political choice
articles.abstract: Health professionals and policy makers should fully support the students currently protesting in France.1 Apart from the regrettable outbursts of violence happening during protests, this movement reflects the anger of youth at decades of successive policies, both at national and global levels, which have progressively widened educational inequalities. These educational inequalities have led to a cascade of further inequalities: access to employment and type of employment (manual or office-based); level of income—in the past 20 years, the Gini index in France increased from 0·27 to 0·30;2 living conditions and the environment (quality of food, water, noise, air, etc); and, eventually, health inequities.

articles.title: Degenerative cervical myelopathy: early detection and the potential for preventing disability
articles.abstract: Degenerative cervical myelopathy (DCM), the most common non-traumatic spinal cord injury, is a prevalent, progressive, and highly disabling neurological disease, causing heterogeneous impairment ranging from sensory loss and impaired hand dexterity to gait, balance, and autonomic dysfunction. Disability often persists despite surgical decompression, and untreated disease can progress to irreversible neurological injury, including tetraplegia. Current clinical management is largely reactive, with diagnosis and intervention typically only after neurological deterioration has become clinically apparent and radiographic evidence of cervical myelopathy is established. Advances in multimodal diagnostics over the past 5 years are now enabling the detection of subtle spinal cord injury, biological disease activity, and subclinical neurodegeneration before overt clinical disability. Quantitative spinal cord MRI, advanced neurophysiological assessments, dynamic biomechanical metrics, and sensitive functional testing provide complementary tools for early detection, risk stratification, and prognostication. Together, these approaches are redefining DCM as a disease that should be managed proactively. Evidence supports decompressive surgery in patients with moderate-to-severe disease, whereas in milder disease or in spinal stenosis that might develop into DCM, the management of patients should be interdisciplinary, with active surveillance to detect early deterioration or decompressive surgery in selected cases. Improved prediction of disease trajectories and clearer evidence on long-term outcomes could enable selective earlier intervention and help to prevent neurological disability.

articles.title: Emerging landscape of antibody–drug conjugates in lung cancer: a clinical review
articles.abstract: Lung cancer is a heterogeneous disease, and while targeted therapies and immunotherapies have improved patient outcomes, 5-year overall survival remains poor at approximately 20%. Antibody–drug conjugates (ADCs) target tumors using a targeted antibody that delivers a cytotoxic payload with clinically proven antitumor activity, and over a dozen ADCs are under consideration for solid tumors. Recent clinical trial data in metastatic non-small cell lung cancer have led to FDA approval of three ADCs: trastuzumab deruxtecan for patients with human epidermal growth factor receptor 2-mutated disease, telisotuzumab vedotin for MET-overexpressing tumors, and datopotamab deruxtecan for patients with epidermal growth factor receptor-mutated disease. In this article, we review the trajectory of individual ADC targets in lung cancer, describe the latest clinical trial results, and discuss future innovations in ADC therapies and potential mechanisms of resistance.

articles.title: Disease-causing helix-8 mutations reprogram parathyroid hormone receptor-1 effector selectivity
articles.abstract: Höppner et al. show that disease-associated substitutions in PTH1R helix-8 selectively rewire receptor coupling to G proteins and βarrestin. Distinct mutations bias PTH1R engagement toward either Gαq or βarrestin pathways and impair Gαs activation. These findings reveal mutation-driven shifts in effector selectivity as a previously unrecognized mechanism in PTH1R-associated disease.

articles.title: Orally delivered metabolically reprogrammed probiotics for cascade-activated antitumor immunity in colorectal cancer
articles.abstract: Wang et al. develop an oral metabolically engineered bacterial platform (EcN-HlpA-CGL [EHC]) for colorectal cancer immunotherapy, which triggers ferroptosis in colorectal cancer cells to boost immunogenicity, while the bacterial adjuvanticity reshapes the immunosuppressive microenvironment. This approach activates both systemic and gut mucosal immunity, effectively suppressing orthotopic tumor growth and metastasis.

articles.title: Continuous refrigeration and dehumidification using the lower critical solution temperature cycle
Exploring magnesium- and calcium-based compounds via solid-state metathesis reactions
Applications of Single-Atom Alloys in Thermal, Electro, and Photo Catalysis
articles.abstract: Single-atom alloys (SAAs) are an emerging class of heterogeneous catalysts that maximize atom efficiency by embedding isolated reactive metal atoms within a host metal surface, creating well-defined active sites. Atomic isolation imparts unique catalytic properties, including high selectivity, resistance to poisoning, coking, and sintering, and in some cases the ability to circumvent conventional scaling relationships that limit traditional catalysts. This article focuses on progress in the SAA field since our 2020 review (Chem. Rev.2020, 120, 12044−12088.), while incorporating earlier foundational studies where relevant. We first examine the fundamental principles governing SAA formation, stability, electronic structure, reactivity, and selectivity, drawing on insights from experimental single-crystal model systems and theoretical studies. We then review the application of SAAs in a wide range of industrially important reactions, including hydrogenation, dehydrogenation, selective oxidation, water–gas shift, Fischer–Tropsch synthesis, and dry reforming, among others. Beyond thermal catalysis, SAAs demonstrate great promise in electrocatalysis and plasmon-driven chemistry. Their structurally simple active sites have also enabled the rational design of novel catalysts and promoters that challenge conventional catalytic intuition. Looking ahead, recent advances in computing, including machine-learning potentials, offer the opportunity to explore vast compositional spaces and discover new alloy chemistries for challenging reactions using the SAA concept.

articles.title: Nonaqueous Redox Flow Batteries: Opportunities and Challenges for Sustainable Energy Storage
articles.abstract: Redox flow batteries (RFBs) have emerged as promising electrochemical energy storage technologies for long-duration stationary applications. Although aqueous RFBs represent the most commercially mature class, they are inherently limited by a narrow electrochemical stability window and high temperature sensitivity. Nonaqueous RFBs (NRFBs) expand the accessible voltage and temperature ranges, offering a promising route toward high-energy-density storage for long-duration and extreme-environment applications. However, their practical deployment remains impeded by several challenges, including high costs, insufficient power density, limited cycling stability, and safety concerns. This review offers a systematic synthesis of recent advances in key NRFB components, encompassing solvents, supporting electrolytes, membranes, electrodes, and redox-active molecules. We also highlight emerging methodologies expected to accelerate development, including machine-learning-enabled screening, advanced characterization, and life cycle assessment. Finally, this review compares aqueous and nonaqueous systems from commercialization and sustainability perspectives. Collectively, this review aims to advance design principles and optimization strategies for NRFBs, providing guidance for next-generation low-cost, high-energy-density flow battery technologies.

Retracing the olive (Olea europaea L. subsp. europaea) origin and its early history diffusion among the civilizations overlooking the Mediterranean coasts: an integrated approach
articles.abstract: The olive tree is one of the most important crops in the world, but even more, one of the most identitarian plant for the countries of the Mediterranean basin. In this article, the vast consultation of scientific literature, archaeological, historical and anecdotal sources, allowed to outline a global reasoned vision on the olive origin, its spread during early history and how olive fruit fly may represent as proxy for tracing its early diffusion. The reconstruction of the first forms of exploitation, propagation and trade routes yielded a chronologically coherent westward emergence of integrated olive-oil economies and cultures throughout the Mediterranean Basin, with the exception of some independent cultivation events tied to the widespread diffusion of the wild olive tree from the end of the last Glacial Period. Written sources, iconography, and archaeological installations further anchor this spatio-temporal narrative, leading to the transition from -wild- olives gatherers to olive growers.

articles.title: Correction to ‘Differential effects of pollen nutritional quality on male and female reproductive success within a diverse co‐flowering community’
The effect of prenatal environment on brain mitochondrial function and prey detection in a lizard
articles.abstract: Read the free Plain Language Summary for this article on the Journal blog. Abstract The ability to detect prey is crucial for survival in many animals. However, prey detection is a cognitive process that can be influenced by early life conditions such as prenatal stress or temperature. Mitochondrial function is likely to underlie these effects because cognitive abilities are energetically demanding (i.e. dependent on efficient metabolic function) and because metabolic‐derived oxidative stress and oxidative damage can impair cognitive function. Yet, whether prenatal stress and thermal environments affect prey detection, and whether mitochondrial function mediates such effects, remains poorly understood. Here, we investigated the links between prenatal environments, mitochondrial function and prey detection in the delicate skink (Lampropholis delicata). We manipulated egg corticosterone (CORT) levels—a key stress hormone in reptiles—and incubation temperature and assessed the ability of lizards to detect chemical and visual prey stimuli. Then, using flow cytometry, we measured metabolic function, oxidative stress and oxidative damage in the olfactory bulbs and optic tecta, two brain regions involved in sensory processing. While metabolic function and oxidative stress remained robust to early life conditions, CORT and temperature interacted to influence oxidative damage. Particularly, CORT decreased DNA damage in the olfactory bulbs of cold‐incubated lizards but had no effect on hot‐incubated lizards. In both brain regions, lipid peroxidation was lower in CORT‐treated lizards incubated at high temperatures compared to CORT‐treated cold‐incubated lizards, but no other between‐treatment differences were detected. Additionally, CORT‐treated lizards responded faster when presented with chemical cues but not visual stimuli. We did not find any relationship between mitochondrial function and prey detection. Our findings suggest that prenatal conditions have lasting effects on DNA damage and prey detection, but prey detection appears decoupled from mitochondrial function in L. delicata. Read the free Plain Language Summary for this article on the Journal blog.

articles.title: Phenological Flexibility in Nesting Grassland Birds Over a Half Century Informs Timing of Management
articles.abstract: The timing of biological events for wildlife species reflects and influences ecological and evolutionary processes and helps guide management actions to meet conservation objectives. Climate change may cause phenological shifts across trophic levels and ecosystems, which can have broad ecological impacts. Shifts may also result in mistiming between management practices based on historical conditions and current biological events, reducing the effectiveness of natural resource management and conservation efforts. We analyzed nesting phenology patterns over recent decades across North America for 44 species of grassland‐nesting birds, including waterfowl, upland gamebirds, shorebirds, and passerines, many of which have experienced precipitous population declines. Understanding nesting phenologies of these species is important to their conservation, as grassland management activities often conflict with reproductive periods leading to high nest and young mortality. We compiled a dataset of over 172,000 nest records spanning five decades and evaluated environmental factors influencing long‐term shifts and short‐term flexibility in nesting phenology. We found considerable variation in responses among species, with differences in both direction and magnitude of spatiotemporal effects on nest initiation dates. Notably, the community‐level nesting season lengthened over time, but shifts exhibited spatial heterogeneity within this community of grassland birds. Nesting dates shifted asymmetrically across the breeding season with differential changes in early, peak, and late nesting dates whereas long‐term changes were mediated by weather and geographic gradients. For example, nest initiation was earlier in warmer and wetter years. By applying a quantile‐based analysis, we provide estimates of the full nesting period that could serve as a flexible tool for scheduling monitoring efforts and balancing management and human activities with periods of reduced nesting activity. Our collaborative effort illustrates the challenges and opportunities of collecting long‐term data on avian communities necessary for answering questions across large regions but highlights the value of research coordination for bird conservation.

articles.title: Skin-resident CXCR6+ memory CD4+ T cells and dendritic cells form dermal perivascular hubs that drive relapse in allergic dermatitis
articles.abstract: Tissue-resident memory T (TRM) cells are heterogeneous, but how pathogenic subsets drive relapse in allergic dermatitis remains unclear. Asahina et al. identify a pathogenic CXCR6+ CD4+ TRM subset sustained through CXCL16-dependent clustering with CD301b+ cDC2s, revealing the TRM-DC niche as a potential therapeutic target for allergic dermatitis.

articles.title: Cost effectiveness of synthetic fuel and CO2 removal for net-zero aviation
articles.abstract: Aviation's climate impact goes beyond CO2, yet current policies such as the EU's ReFuelEU regulation push almost exclusively toward sustainable fuels, overlooking an alternative: permanently capturing CO2 from the air via DACCS while continuing to burn fossil jet fuel. Comparing long-term costs of both approaches, we find DACCS is 49%–69% cheaper than synthetic fuels and needs far less renewable electricity, suggesting that current policy may be locking aviation into a costlier decarbonization path than necessary.

articles.title: High-frequency inductively heated molten salt bubbling beds for methane pyrolysis
articles.abstract: Methane pyrolysis can produce hydrogen while sequestering solid carbon, but efficient high-grade heat delivery and coking management remain challenging. This study shows that high-frequency magnetic induction directly and volumetrically heats molten salt bubbling beds with stable power delivery, providing a scalable route for methane pyrolysis while managing solid carbon formation. These principles have applicability more broadly to molten salt chemical conversion and thermal energy storage systems.

articles.title: Host‐mediated filtering and interspecific associations structure strongyle parasite communities in Sable Island horses
articles.abstract: Using individual‐level nemabiome metabarcoding of 3147 samples from 916 horses on Sable Island over 10 years, we generate the largest dataset of its kind to date. This unprecedented scale enables a rare test of the processes structuring parasite communities in a natural system, revealing dominant host‐mediated filtering and predominantly positive species associations. Abstract Mixed‐species parasite infections are common in wildlife, yet the ecological processes that structure these communities remain poorly understood. We hypothesized that host‐mediated and extrinsic environmental filtering, alongside biotic interactions, act concurrently to shape parasite community composition, and that these structuring patterns would depend on parasite traits or evolutionary history. We applied nemabiome DNA metabarcoding to 3147 faecal samples from 916 feral horses with no history of anthelmintic treatment, collected over 10 years as part of a long‐term individual‐based study on Sable Island, Canada. Using joint species distribution models, we tested whether strongyle parasite communities were structured by host‐associated factors, extrinsic environmental variables or interspecific interactions. Host factors, particularly age and individual identity, explained the greatest proportion of variation in both parasite prevalence and infection intensity, indicating strong host‐mediated environmental filtering. In contrast, spatial location and year explained minimal variation, suggesting weaker effects of extrinsically mediated environmental filtering. Parasite traits such as body size and gut site preference had limited associations with species' environmental responses. Positive species associations were common, particularly among species occupying the same gut region, suggesting that strong, consistent competitive interactions were not prominently reflected in the residual covariance structure. Negative associations were less frequent but consistently involved Strongylus equinus, indicating potential context‐dependent biotic interactions involving this species. By integrating species‐level molecular data with hierarchical joint species models, this study quantifies patterns of host‐related filtering and species co‐variation within a natural parasite community and provides a framework for examining mixed infections in wild systems.

articles.title: Design and engineering of a sustainable, reusable Fe@ISCOF SPE catalyst with suppressed metal leaching for electro-organic Reppe sulfonation enabling efficient synthesis of phenylethane-1-sulfonate derivatives in DES matrix
Ground‐penetrating radar amplitudes to roots: A numerical modelling framework for mapping coarse root system architecture
articles.abstract: Observations of three‐dimensional (3D) coarse root system architecture remain limited because most measurement approaches require excavation. Here, we combined dense single‐ and multi‐channel 500 MHz ground‐penetrating radar (GPR) surveys with a flow‐guided connectivity framework to non‐destructively characterise the coarse root architecture of two trees. Migrated and depth‐normalised GPR amplitudes were treated as spatially variable hydraulic conductivities in a steady‐state numerical model. The resulting connectivity fields transformed spatially discontinuous, collapsed diffraction hyperbolae into continuous 3D representations of root architecture extending 10–15 m from the trunk. We applied this approach to a swamp oak (Quercus palustris) and a river red gum (Eucalyptus camaldulensis). The two trees were surveyed under different environmental conditions and acquisition parameters. The reconstructed architectures revealed shallow, laterally extensive coarse root systems and captured substantial variation in root structure between the two trees. The oak roots exhibited an asymmetrical architecture with preferential development towards the upslope, wind‐exposed side of the tree, whereas the river red gum displayed a more radially distributed root architecture with deeper roots near the trunk. Approximately 80% of reconstructed roots for both trees occurred within 6.2 m of the trunk and above 60 cm depth. Together, these results demonstrate that dense GPR surveys, coupled with connectivity‐based modelling, provide a non‐destructive and repeatable approach for characterising coarse root architecture.

articles.title: UNIQAT: An open‐source toolkit for reproducible image quality assessment in marine surveys
articles.abstract: Modern marine surveys generate tens of thousands of underwater images per expedition, yet many are unusable due to image quality deterioration. Manual quality screening is labour-intensive, subjective and inconsistent across observers and teams, hindering reproducible science, creating large backlogs of unprocessed imagery, and limiting real-time algorithmic and robotic applications. We present UNIQAT (UNderwater Image Quality Assessment Toolkit), an open-source Python toolkit for automated underwater image quality assessment. The toolkit computes reference-free quality metrics across nine categories of image characteristics relevant to underwater images, such as colour cast, turbidity and contrast loss. Metrics can be combined with user-defined weights into task-specific quality scores tailored to different ecological applications. High-performance computing (HPC)-aware multiprocessing and optional deep learning architectures for metric approximation support processing at scales matching modern survey data collection. We evaluated UNIQAT on 130,845 images from nine coral reef surveys conducted by the Australian Institute of Marine Science; every result reported in the main text was produced by the traditional metrics pipeline, with no deep learning model involved, and a separate training demonstration is reported in the Supporting Information. The traditional metrics pipeline, run as 48 CPU workers on a 64-core cluster node, processed 7.9 4K-images/s, with processing time scaling linearly with image count (r 2 = 0.98). The resulting quality scores captured expected patterns of image modulation based on the environmental context of the imaged scenes: All nine surveys showed negative depth–quality correlations (r = −0.16 to −0.89), consistent with the depth-dependent deterioration of image quality in underwater environments. Cross-survey metric profiles were highly consistent (mean Spearman ρ = 0.99 across all 36 pairwise comparisons, minimum 0.96), confirming measurement stability across different dates, locations, camera systems and environmental conditions. Synthesis. UNIQAT can help deliver objective and tunable image quality metrics in a versatile toolkit that enables transparent reporting and supports unsupervised quality assessment for applications in marine monitoring and robotics.

articles.title: A CK2-β-TrCP kinase-E3 ubiquitin ligase cascade is a metabolic sensor regulating tryptophan 2,3-dioxygenase stability
articles.abstract: How metabolic enzyme levels are regulated is poorly understood. Studying the tryptophan (Trp)-metabolizing enzyme TDO2, Thielen et al. discover a CK2 kinase-β-TrCP E3 ligase pathway that regulates stability in response to substrate availability. Trp occupation of an exosite restricts degron accessibility, whereas low Trp releases the degron for phosphorylation-ubiquitylation-mediated degradation.

articles.title: PHYHD1-mediated translational control regulates renal cell carcinoma progression
articles.abstract: Liang et al. identify phytanoyl-CoA dioxygenase domain containing 1 (PHYHD1) as a tumor suppressor that regulates protein production in kidney cancer. Loss of PHYHD1 promotes disease progression by increasing ceramide transporter 1 (CERT1) production, uncovering a regulatory pathway that may help predict patient outcomes and provide a therapeutic opportunity for PHYHD1-deficient tumors.

articles.title: Advancing Marine Mammal Conservation Through Omics Tools and Integration of Indigenous Ecological Knowledge
articles.abstract: Conservation of biodiversity is a global priority as human‐driven pressures continue to intensify and alter ecosystems worldwide. Marine mammals are vulnerable species, facing numerous escalating anthropogenic threats. Here, we evaluate how, as omics technologies become more accessible and affordable, established and emerging tools are advancing effective marine mammal research and conservation management. Assessments of genetic diversity, adaptive capacity, demographic history and local adaptation provide vital insights into how marine mammal populations respond to environmental change across contemporary and evolutionary timescales. Whole‐genome sequencing, functional genomics, epigenetics and multi‐omic integration enable deeper insights into the molecular basis of complex fitness‐related traits. Approaches like epigenetics, ancient DNA and environmental DNA offer new opportunities to study cryptic, rare, or historical populations and evolutionary processes. Yet, effective marine mammal conservation management cannot rely exclusively on increased availability of omics tools and data. We emphasize the need and obligation for genuine collaboration and integration of Indigenous perspectives with marine mammal genomics approaches to foster ethical, inclusive and effective conservation, and suggest best practices for this. Additionally, we highlight that translating omics data into practical conservation outcomes remains challenging, requiring clear communication, collaboration and integration into management. Using marine mammal genomics to address conservation challenges in a changing world requires innovation, partnership and the integration of diverse knowledge systems, such as Indigenous Ecological Knowledge.

articles.title: Chilling Injury to Algal Symbionts Induces Host Starvation and Metabolic Reorganization in a Temperate Cnidarian
articles.abstract: Global temperature anomalies increasingly disrupt the cnidarian‐algal symbiosis resulting in a phenomenon termed bleaching. In contrast to heat stress, the mechanisms underlying symbiotic breakdown under cold stress remain largely unknown. Combining physiological and metabolomic measurements, we investigated the response of the photosymbiotic sea anemone holobiont Aiptasia couchii to an experiment mimicking a cold spell in the Mediterranean Sea. Within 4 weeks, we observed the onset of symbiotic breakdown reflected in reduced algal endosymbiont density and chlorophyll a content. While photosynthetic efficiency remained largely unaffected, no gross photosynthesis was detectable in cold‐stressed anemones and decreases in glycosyldiacylglycerols and fatty acyl glycosides indicated chloroplast lipid remobilization. This breakdown of symbiotic carbon cycling was reflected in increased dipeptide and ceramide levels suggesting anemones catabolized protein reserves and induced pre‐apoptotic pathways. Taken together, these responses suggest a decoupling of light and dark reactions of photosynthesis in cold‐stressed endosymbionts, resembling chilling injury in higher plants and free‐living microalgae. This chilling‐induced collapse of symbiotic nutrient cycling eventually leads to host starvation in cold‐stressed Cnidaria. Hence, while cold and heat stress may invoke contrasting physiological effects on endosymbionts, our results suggest that both stressors destabilize the symbiosis through similar mechanisms culminating in host starvation.

articles.title: Host‐Associated Differentiation in a Parasitoid Wasp Connected to Venom‐Related but Not Chemosensory Genes
articles.abstract: The mechanisms driving the megadiversity of parasitic wasps remain a central question in evolutionary ecology. To investigate the genomic architecture underlying host‐associated differentiation in parasitic wasps, we generated a de novo genome assembly and performed whole‐genome re‐sequencing of 17 populations of the parasitoid wasp Asecodes parviclava (Eulophidae) across a latitudinal gradient and multiple Galerucella host species. Despite panmixia in host populations, we identified three genetically differentiated wasp lineages, with the most profound divergence separating Galerucella tenella‐associated wasps from other populations. Locus‐specific scans revealed that selection acts highly asymmetrically. We detected significant differentiation and copy‐number expansion clustered within venom‐related gene families, contrasting sharply with a near‐complete lack of divergence in chemosensory genes. This decoupled evolution suggests that host finding may rely on behavioural plasticity, whereas physiological compatibility is genetically hard‐wired via multi‐layered immune‐suppression mechanisms. Finally, asymmetrical gene flow in northern populations demonstrates that fine‐scale habitat overlap creates ecological connectivity without eroding specialized lineages, as intense host‐mediated selection purges maladapted hybrids. Ultimately, our study demonstrates that physiological barriers, rather than behavioural recognition, may maintain specialized parasitoid lineages, providing new insights into the genomic basis of speciation with gene flow in specialized natural enemies.

articles.title: Farewell NASA ADS
articles.abstract: After more than 33 years, NASA’s Astrophysics Data System will close its virtual doors in November 2026 and be replaced by its much-expanded successor, Science Explorer. While the core functionality and astrophysics database will remain the same, SciX will extend its relevance to a broader range of scientists.

articles.title: Transitioning from ADS to SciX to serve twenty-first century astronomy
articles.abstract: For decades, the NASA Astrophysics Data System (ADS) has been the foundational digital library for astronomy. As ADS now becomes the Science Explorer (SciX), the team prioritizes preserving this trusted experience while increasing their support for space and Earth sciences more broadly, without diluting its commitment to astrophysics.

articles.title: Alus harbor genetic variants that shape the human cortex
articles.abstract: The genetic changes associated with development of the human cortex are difficult to test functionally, especially in the context of gene regulation. In this issue, Matoba et al. show that variants that shape human cortical structure are hiding inside Alu transposable elements, co-opting their inbuilt machinery to rewire regulatory networks in the developing brain.

articles.title: Genome-wide analysis of common structural variants in Alzheimer’s disease identifies a risk-associated regulatory CCG repeat in FAM193B
articles.abstract: This study identifies common structural variants contributing to Alzheimer’s disease heritability. An expanded promoter CCG repeat increases FAM193B expression and disease risk, linking its expression to DNA damage and cell death pathways in neurons.

articles.title: Investigating molecular and hemodynamic effects of LSD in the human brain
articles.abstract: Using simultaneous PET–MRI, McCulloch, Larsen and colleagues quantify LSD’s dose–occupancy relationship at the serotonin 2A receptor and reveal hemodynamic effects of LSD that contrast with those of psilocybin.

articles.title: Chip-mediated manipulation of photonic quantum skyrmions
articles.abstract: Although photonic quantum skyrmions can be generated as entangled or single-photon states, a means to switch between the two is required for quantum information processing. Now, entangled skyrmions and their manipulation on chip is realized.

articles.title: Morphogenesis of a stratified cell mound at a vortex defect
articles.abstract: In cell monolayers with a vortex-like orientation defect, cells converge towards the core of the defect and form a highly organized three-dimensional mound. This mechanism may be relevant for morphogenesis and tumorigenesis.

articles.title: Filling the massive AI drug discovery data gap
articles.abstract: Charlotte Deane, co-leader of the OpenBind initiative, discusses the need for more protein–small molecule binding data.

articles.title: One-step skeletal editing of oxetanes to thietanes using thiourea
articles.abstract: Four-membered heterocycles are privileged scaffolds in medicinal chemistry, yet valuable thietanes remain underexplored compared with widely studied oxetanes and azetidines. Now a one-step skeletal editing strategy is reported that directly converts oxetanes into thietanes using thiourea.

articles.title: Photocatalytic tetrapeptides for enantioselective visible light-induced transformations
articles.abstract: Research on enantioselective photocatalysis has so far been focused on molecular photocatalysts or large yet easily adaptable photoenzymes. However, both catalysis classes display deficiencies either due to their limited adaptability or their high molecular weight. Here we show that small peptides can bridge the gap between the currently used photocatalysts by combining structural flexibility and low molecular weight. We constructed a small peptide that displays a pyroglutamic acid at its N terminus for substrate recognition. At the C terminus, a thioxanthone-based amino acid was installed to harvest photons and to act catalytically by energy transfer. Two amino acids were sufficient to link the two components, resulting in a photocatalytically active tetrapeptide that was used both for photochemical deracemization and enantioselective [2 + 2] photocycloaddition reactions. Our results demonstrate that small peptides with a molecular weight below 750 Da can act as efficient molecular catalysts for enantioselective photochemical transformations.

articles.title: Scrambling-free synthesis of heteroleptic silylium ions by halide abstraction from halosilanes
articles.abstract: Heteroleptic silylium ions with different substituents at the silicon atom are generally not accessible using established tools for producing such reactive intermediates because substituent exchange reactions occur in acidic media, leading to homoleptic silylium ions with three identical alkyl and aryl substituents, respectively. Here we report a broadly applicable route to heteroleptic silylium ions using halosilanes as silylium ion precursors, which are less prone to that scrambling process. While this deceptively simple method has failed so far owing to the lack of a suitable halide-abstracting agent, superhalophilic halogen-substituted silylium ions enable smooth halide abstraction from a diverse set of halosilanes at ambient temperature without substituent redistribution. Accordingly, this approach provides access to essentially any heteroleptic acyclic as well as cyclic silylium-ion motif from common halosilanes, including trialkyl-, dialkyl(aryl)-, alkyldiaryl- and triaryl-substituted congeners. Computational calculations reveal the mechanism of heteroleptic silylium-ion formation and the origin of the suppressed substituent-scrambling process.

articles.title: Jennifer Inman supports human spaceflight at NASA
