Molecular mechanism of KRAS binding to BRAF and its regulation by the BRAF-specific region
articles.abstract: Bonsor et al. determined the crystal structure of the KRAS-BRAF(RBD-CRD) complex, revealing reduced KRAS engagement by BRAF(CRD) compared with CRAF(CRD). They further show that the BRAF-specific region (BSR) attenuates RBD binding to KRAS, while inclusion of the CRD partially relieves this inhibition.

articles.title: [Comment] Hepatitis C—is discrimination preventing elimination?
articles.abstract: The UK (chiefly driven by England and Scotland) is expected to be the first country to meet WHO's goal for the elimination of hepatitis C virus (HCV) infection by 2030. In April, 2026, the UK Health Security Agency's analysis of progress by the National Health Service (NHS) towards elimination showed that 84·6% of people living with HCV had been diagnosed and prevalence in people who inject drugs had fallen to 5·2% in 2024, with an estimated incidence of 4·4 infections per 100 person-years, predicted to fall below WHO's target of two infections per 100 patient-years by 2030.

articles.title: [Comment] Tailoring levels of evidence in trials comparing common treatments
articles.abstract: In many disease settings, physicians and patients can choose between several treatment options that are in common use, but how should they make the choice? The problem is often not the absence of evidence but the absence of robust randomised controlled evidence directly comparing treatments that are already widely used in practice. Treatment options might have been directly compared with a common comparator, but not to each other; for example, in respiratory syncytial virus prevention in infants, both maternal vaccination and infant monoclonal antibodies have shown efficacy versus placebo but have not been directly compared.

articles.title: Thiol reactivity: lost in the crowd?
articles.abstract: Predictions of cysteine reactivity rely heavily on acidity (pKa) data from dilute solutions. However, the intracellular milieu is crowded and dynamic, with substrates, cofactors, and metabolites that modulate reactivity, thereby affecting cell signaling and metabolic adaptation. This forum argues that Cys pKa values are necessary but insufficient, proposing an integrated, microenvironment-dependent framework.

articles.title: From species richness to interaction architecture
articles.abstract: Biodiversity research has long focused on the number and identity of species, but recent advances suggest that ecosystem functioning depends on how species are connected. Predicting the consequences of biodiversity loss in the Anthropocene will therefore require moving beyond inventories of species toward a predictive ecology of interaction networks.

articles.title: Drought and soil macrofauna functional diversity effects on Mediterranean tree growth in an Ecotron ecosystem experiment
articles.abstract: Read the free Plain Language Summary for this article on the Journal blog. Abstract The intensity, frequency and severity of drought events are projected to increase in the Mediterranean region under ongoing climate change. This may impact plant growth and survival in Mediterranean forests leading to altered ecosystem dynamics. The functional diversity of soil macrofauna may have a critical role in mitigating negative climate change effects as it determines soil structure and regulates biogeochemical cycling as well as water retention. However, very little is known on how changes in climate and soil biodiversity conjointly influence plant growth. In a 5‐year experiment, we tested two levels of soil macrofauna functional diversity (Low and High), using combinations of endogeic and anecic earthworms, diplopods and isopods, and measured growth and biomass allocation in three tree species (Acer monspessulanum, Arbutus unedo and Quercus pubescens) as well as total tree biomass production. Our results showed that tree growth was overall only moderately affected by stronger drought and functional diversity of soil macrofauna. The effects of functional diversity of soil macrofauna differed among tree species. High functional diversity was associated with greater stem diameter in Q. pubescens. In contrast, low functional diversity was associated with greater stem diameter in A. unedo and proportionally greater biomass allocation to roots in A. monspessulanum. Individual macrofauna groups had stronger effects than overall functional diversity. Endogeic earthworm presence was associated with greater ecosystem‐level fine root and total plant biomass, but with lower fine root and total biomass in A. unedo. Diplopod presence was associated with greater stem diameter and higher total tree biomass in Q. pubescens. Overall, four consecutive summers of intensified drought had few significant effects on tree growth and biomass production, possibly because of high variability among individual trees. Most macrofauna effects were independent of drought, although drought modified the effect of diplopods on ecosystem‐level shoot biomass. These results show that macrofauna effects on tree growth depend on both macrofauna group and tree species identity. Read the free Plain Language Summary for this article on the Journal blog.

articles.title: HGTScanner: Detecting horizontal gene transfer at the fine scale using whole organelle genomes
articles.abstract: Horizontal gene transfer (HGT) has profoundly shaped eukaryotic organellar genomes like plant mitochondria. Yet no generalized tools are currently available to efficiently characterize HGT across these genomes due to both high structural complexity and low sequence divergence compared to prokaryotic HGTs. Accurate identification of HGT, including the genomic location and donor lineage, is critical for understanding its impact on genetic novelty and genome evolution as well as species interactions that generate HGTs. Here, we introduce HGTScanner, a Python tool to characterize HGT across whole organellar genomes. HGTScanner automatically establishes homology, produces alignments and phylogenies, and tests hypotheses of HGT based on BLAST, phylogeny and synteny. It contains a built‐in database of green plant (Viridiplantae) organellar sequences to facilitate the characterization of promiscuous mitochondrial HGTs and mitochondrial plastid DNAs (MTPTs) in plants but may also be adapted to other organisms like fungi which share many similar genomic features. Using benchmark data from the early diverging angiosperm Amborella and parasitic plant Orobanchaceae, we demonstrate that HGTScanner can effectively locate and identify the donor lineages of MTPT and HGT. In Amborella, we recovered the well‐documented fusion of moss and green algae mitochondria, and discovered prevalent HGTs from the New Caledonian parasitic plant Hachettea (Mystropetalaceae). In the parasitic Orobanchaceae, non‐native MTPTs are strongly linked with their sympatrically distributed host plants. HGTScanner is an efficient and flexible tool that can drive discoveries of HGT without a priori knowledge regarding the donor identity. The sympatric distribution of donor‐recipient pairs in HGT events suggests that HGTs can serve as valuable genetic markers for organismal interactions across time and terrain.

articles.title: Limited Lifetime Costs of Inbreeding in a Large Wild Population of Superb Fairy‐Wrens
articles.abstract: Inbreeding depression can have major negative effects on both individual fitness and population performance. The impact of inbreeding depression in wild populations remains poorly understood, and our knowledge is primarily based on estimations in insular populations with limited dispersal, which has been predicted to enhance the capacity for outcrossing. Limited migration and small population sizes, which make insular and endangered populations tractable models for fieldwork, often experience low genetic variation and may be subject to stronger inbreeding effects. Estimating inbreeding effects is difficult in many populations because pedigrees of migrants are unknown. Genomic data offer methods to estimate realised inbreeding even in migrants. Here, we apply genomic methods to a superb fairy‐wren (Malurus cyaneus) population that has been subject to detailed study of fitness variation over three decades. The population has sex‐biased dispersal, resulting in many immigrant females. We use genomic inbreeding estimates to explicitly test for inbreeding depression across several key components of individual fitness, including nestling condition, juvenile survival and adult traits. Genomic methods were able to recover previous pedigree‐based findings of inbreeding depression in early nestling condition and additionally identified some evidence for inbreeding depression in fledgling but not juvenile mortality. The only adult fitness trait affected, male extra‐pair paternity, is highly variable and under strong sexual selection. Our findings suggest that natural populations experiencing high effective population sizes and regular dispersal might be less affected by inbreeding depression than previously assumed based on studies of often insular and smaller populations.

articles.title: [Editorial] Rethinking threats to human survival
articles.abstract: Much health advocacy is driven by single-issue activism. Communities with a common interest—from AIDS to child health, climate to tobacco control—focus intensely on their own domain. And understandably so. Important progress has been made through often courageous direct action. But this sharply competitive approach is, according to a new Lancet Commission on 21st Century Global Threats to Health, dangerously flawed. Indeed, perhaps the most important contribution of this Commission is to move global health beyond the consideration of individual harms.

articles.title: [Health Policy] Strengthening health systems to prioritise, provide care, and prevent osteoarthritis: a roadmap for global health policy
articles.abstract: By 2050, almost 1 billion people are expected to live with osteoarthritis—a disabling musculoskeletal condition with currently no cure. Despite its burden and costs, osteoarthritis remains largely invisible in national and global health agendas, is poorly integrated within service models for other chronic health conditions, and is frequently perceived as inevitable with ageing and associated with limited therapeutic options. This context drives an osteoarthritis identity problem that fuels frustration among those living with the disease and health-care professionals, perpetuates stigma and inequities, undermines access to effective interventions, and crucially, deprioritises osteoarthritis in health policy.

articles.title: Emerging trends in redox-neutral phosphorus(V) organocatalysis
articles.abstract: Phosphorus-mediated reactions that leverage the thermodynamic driving force of phosphorus(III) oxidation are crucial in all areas of the chemical industry. While substantial progress has been made in phosphorus(III/V) redox organocatalysis to develop catalytic alternatives, the rising field of redox-neutral phosphorus(V) organocatalysis has revealed new modes of phosphorus-based reactivity in chemical transformations without requiring stoichiometric reductants. This review highlights key advances in redox-neutral phosphorus(V) organocatalysis with a focus on fundamental phosphorus(V) reactivity, organized by the catalyst structure and emphasizing its role as a Lewis acid, Brønsted acid/base, nucleophile, superbase, or single-electron transfer agent. We close with remarks connecting established reactivity paradigms that will likely be applied to new generations of phosphorus(V) catalysts capable of solving modern synthetic challenges.

articles.title: Spatial configuration of MXene in MXene-rGO sponges enhances electromagnetic wave absorption
Shrubs benefit from being functionally more conservative and distinct from neighbour trees
articles.abstract: Read the free Plain Language Summary for this article on the Journal blog. Abstract Multi‐strata forests can enhance ecosystem functioning, with interactions between overstorey trees and understorey shrubs playing a pivotal role. However, how the structure and composition of neighbouring trees, together with shrub traits, influence shrub growth remains poorly understood. In a large‐scale subtropical biodiversity experiment manipulating tree and shrub species richness, we inventoried 4411 shrubs and their surrounding trees after 11 years of interactions. We found that individual shrub biomass declined with increasing neighbour tree species richness, basal area and functional diversity, but exhibited a U‐shaped trend with the proportion of ectomycorrhizal‐associated neighbour tree individuals. Shrubs with more conservative resource‐use strategies attained higher biomass, particularly when surrounded by trees with low functional diversity and a high proportion of ectomycorrhizal associations. Biomass was also greater when shrubs were more resource‐conservative and functionally distinct from the neighbouring trees. Our findings highlight how shrub functional traits, combined with tree diversity, competition and functional traits, shape tree–shrub interactions, with shrubs benefiting more from resource‐conservative and functionally distinct traits relative to their neighbouring trees. Read the free Plain Language Summary for this article on the Journal blog.

articles.title: Why don't all birds lay early? Causes and consequences of breeding timing for a long‐lived migratory seabird
articles.abstract: Why don't all birds lay early? Our 16‐year study of Manx shearwater behaviour shows that selection on breeding timing fluctuates among years. We also find that lay dates are influenced by persistent individual differences, variation in non‐breeding duration, and pair synchrony, potentially constraining breeding phenological advancement under ongoing climate change. Abstract The relationship between earlier laying and higher breeding success is well‐established in avian species. However, a wide distribution of breeding timings is often maintained within a population, and the causes and consequences of this variation require further exploration, particularly as many avian species advance breeding phenology in response to climate change. Using a 16‐year dataset combining colony observations and biologging of Manx shearwaters (Puffinus puffinus), we show that earlier laying does not always result in higher breeding success, with later laying becoming less costly in recent years. We additionally report a slight advancement in breeding timing within breeding pairs, despite finding no temporal trends in spring bloom onset. Nonetheless, birds adjusted lay date in response to interannual variation in phytoplankton bloom timing, and years with stronger Celtic Sea blooms exhibited stronger selection for early breeding. Breeding timing was also influenced by repeatable individual differences in migratory behaviour, with birds undertaking generally earlier, shorter migrations to less southerly destinations laying earlier across years. However, lay date was not determined solely by individual behaviour. In this long‐lived species with stable pair bonds, the arrival date of the second‐returning bird constrained advancement in laying. This study suggests that variation in breeding timing is maintained through the combined effects of fluctuating selection, persistent individual differences, variation in non‐breeding duration and pair‐level processes. [Comment] 21st century global threats to health are not what you think
articles.abstract: The Lancet Commission on 21st century global threats to health's report by Christopher J L Murray and colleagues uses forecasts based on expected cumulative amenable disability-adjusted life-years (DALYs) to quantify and compare threats from 2025 to 2100.1 The Commission's intent is to equip governments with the tools to make smart long-term decisions that reduce risk based on “systematic, repeatable risk assessment and preparedness planning” as opposed to “short-termism and localism”.

articles.title: [Lecture] 50 years of Ebola research and response
articles.abstract: These are two lectures that form the Virchow Prize Lecture given by the authors in October, 2026. The first lecture was given by Peter Piot. The second lecture was given by Jean-Jacques Muyembe-Tamfum.

articles.title: [Perspectives] John Wong: making an impact on population health at scale
articles.abstract: “I’m concerned that the narrative now around ageing populations is one of doom and gloom. But long-lived populations are not the problem. The problem is that we haven’t allowed people to get to an older age healthy”, says John Wong, Executive Director of the Centre for Population Health at the National University of Singapore (NUS) and Executive Director of The Yong Pung How and Yong Wei-Woo Centre at the National University Health System (NUHS), Singapore. “Two-thirds of the world is now below the fertility replacement rate, and unless we keep our populations healthy throughout their whole lifespan, we’ll have this major challenge of more and more unwell older people”, continued Wong, who is also Isabel Chan Professor in Medical Sciences in the Division of Haematology-Oncology at the Yong Loo Lin School of Medicine, NUS, and Emeritus Consultant in the Department of Haematology-Oncology, National University Cancer Institute, NUHS, Singapore.

articles.title: [Review] Addressing threats to future global health—what is the right timeframe?
articles.abstract: Our decisions today can support or threaten future human health. Insofar as we protect the planet or invest in fruitful research on pandemic countermeasures, we promote future wellbeing and health, sometimes at the present generation's expense. As we warm the planet, accelerate antibiotic resistance, or consume finite natural resources, we might serve present-day wellbeing or health at the expense of future generations. To decide which such trade-offs are legitimate or advisable, we need to know how to balance the health interests of future generations against each other and against our own.

articles.title: [The Lancet Commissions] The Lancet Commission on 21st century global threats to health
articles.abstract: This report from the Lancet Commission on 21st century global threats to health lays out a foresight-driven, health-focused approach to identifying and prioritising major threats to global health over the remainder of the century. We argue that recent global shocks (including COVID-19, Ebola Bundibugyo virus disease, major geopolitical conflict, accelerating climate impacts, rapid shifts in development assistance, and the emergence of powerful artificial intelligence [AI] systems) show how quickly assumptions about stability can be overturned—and why governments and multilateral institutions must counter short-termism and localism with systematic, repeatable risk assessment and preparedness planning.

articles.title: Mapping transcriptional responses to cellular perturbations with RNA fingerprinting
articles.abstract: RNA fingerprinting is a statistical framework that infers causal regulators from single-cell experiments by mapping their transcriptional responses onto reference perturbation dictionaries.

articles.title: A modular platform for in cellulo target engagement profiling of chromatin reader inhibitors
articles.abstract: Chromatin reader inhibitors require robust cellular assays for target-engagement profiling. Recchia et al. develop modular Acyl-eCR reporters that enable scalable live-cell measurement of bromodomain inhibitor specificity and PROTAC activity, providing a versatile platform for chromatin-targeted drug discovery.

articles.title: AI-integrated RNA therapeutics in precision oncology
articles.abstract: Symmans et al. review how artificial intelligence supports RNA therapeutic development in precision oncology, spanning multi-omics target prioritization and RNA design to delivery, patient stratification, manufacturing, and clinical translation. They distinguish clinically supported applications from preclinical and speculative approaches, outlining validation, governance, and regulatory requirements.

articles.title: Anti-HDGFL2 cryptic protein antibodies provide a sensitive readout of TDP-43 pathology and clinical disease features
articles.abstract: Citrano, Maheswari Jawahar et al. develop sensitive immunoassays using second-generation polyclonal and monoclonal antibodies against HDGFL2-CE proteins and show that their levels in brain tissue associate with pTDP-43 pathology, earlier symptom onset, and shorter survival in patients with FTLD-TDP and FTLD-TDP/MND.

articles.title: Breastfeeding and maternal microbial reservoirs are associated with infant gut phageome development during the first year of life
articles.abstract: Cabello-Yeves et al. use longitudinal metagenomic analysis of mother-infant dyads to show that infant gut phageomes diversify during the first year of life and are associated with feeding-related variables and maternal microbial reservoirs. Persistent bifidophages dominate early communities, highlighting the potential relevance of phages in microbiome-targeted early-life interventions.

articles.title: Microbiota-regulated TCDCA associates with Parkinson’s disease severity and promotes BBB dysfunction through VSMC TGR5 signaling in mice
articles.abstract: Zhao et al. show that circulating TCDCA associates with Parkinson’s disease severity and that TCDCA administration worsens neurovascular and motor outcomes in mice. VSMC TGR5 deletion and BSH-active L. reuteri interventions implicate a microbiota-regulated TCDCA-BBB pathway while defining its translational limitations.

articles.title: Spatially tuned localization of interleukins and OX40 agonists enhances synergistic anti-tumor immunity
articles.abstract: Klich et al. use a hydrogel to deliver immunotherapy combinations intratumorally and peritumorally. Rational selection of the site of administration drives tumor clearance and long-term survivors.

articles.title: Asymmetric Dipolar Cycloadditions toward Chiral Medium-Sized Rings under Palladium and Iridium Catalysis
articles.abstract: Chiral medium-sized rings, defined herein as 7- to 11-membered cyclic frameworks, are common in bioactive molecules and occupy an important but still underexplored region of drug-like chemical space. Their asymmetric synthesis remains formidably challenging, as conformational flexibility, transannular interactions, and unfavorable entropic and enthalpic factors collectively complicate ring formation and stereocontrol. In recent years, palladium- and iridium-catalyzed asymmetric dipolar cycloadditions and related cascade processes have emerged as effective strategies for building structurally diverse and stereochemically complex medium-sized rings. As such, this review aims to summarize the advances in this emerging field from the perspectives of metal identity, precursor class, and dipole-generation mode, with emphasis on their effects on chemo-, regio-, diastereo-, and enantioselectivity. We also highlight the distinct yet complementary features of Pd and Ir catalysis, as well as current limitations in generality, selectivity, and substrate scope. By combining mechanistic insight with representative applications, this review aims to define the foundations, boundaries, and future opportunities of this rapidly evolving area.

articles.title: Overcoming the Charge Confinement-Transport Trade-Off in Perovskite Light-Emitting Diodes
articles.abstract: Nanocrystalline metal halide perovskites are promising light emitters for light-emitting diodes (PeLEDs) because they suppress the intrinsic problem of exciton dissociation through charge confinement within nanocrystalline domains. Although these nanostructures have enabled high-emission efficiencies, such confinement strategies typically result in significantly reduced charge transport. This limitation is attributed to numerous grain boundaries, which induce severe charge carrier scattering and trapping, alongside insulating organic ligands typically introduced for defect passivation and size reduction. Poor charge transport increases the required operating voltage and accelerates device degradation pathways under an electrical bias, leading to limited operational lifetimes. This Review examines material design strategies intended to mitigate the competition between charge confinement and transport across various nanocrystalline perovskites. Specifically, we investigate fundamental crystal nucleation and growth mechanisms and evaluate methods to optimize grain size, aiming to minimize the grain boundary to increase charge transport while maintaining charge confinement. Passivation strategies for defect states are also evaluated, emphasizing the engineering of organic ligands to enhance their electrical conductivity while maximizing the passivation efficacy. In addition, the integration of core/shell architectures is discussed as a promising strategy. By controlling the shell composition, these structures promote efficient charge transport while maintaining high radiative recombination rates. Together, these material design strategies aim to overcome the confinement and transport trade-offs in PeLEDs.

articles.title: Photochemical Hetero-cycloadditions
articles.abstract: Hetero-cycloaddition reactions are powerful, atom-economical strategies for the rapid construction of heterocyclic frameworks from readily available building blocks. Over the past two decades, advances in photochemistry, photocatalysis, and modern excitation strategies have driven remarkable developments in the field. By accessing electronically excited states, light enables cycloaddition pathways inaccessible under classical thermal conditions, providing access to reactive radical, ionic, or excited-state intermediates under mild conditions. Technological advances in light sources and photocatalyst design have improved reaction efficiency, site-, regio-, and stereoselectivity, while considerably expanding the accessible chemical space. Beyond established hetero-[2 + 2], hetero-(3 + 2), and hetero-[4 + 2] processes, new reaction classes, including π–σ hetero-cycloadditions exploiting strained small-ring systems, have emerged as powerful approaches to structurally complex saturated scaffolds of increasing relevance in medicinal chemistry. In this Review, we critically examine the evolution of photochemical hetero-cycloadditions from 2000 to 2026, discussing fundamental concepts and terminology, cycloaddition classes, heterocyclic targets, and activation mechanisms. We highlight the conceptual advances that have shaped modern photochemical hetero-cycloaddition chemistry and conclude by discussing current limitations and future directions for the field.

articles.title: Inter-flake modulation of MXenes for advanced sensing applications
articles.abstract: This review highlights the role of inter-flake structure in MXene-based sensing and discusses how spacing, orientation, porosity, and inter-flake chemistry can be controlled to influence its sensing performance.

articles.title: Pyrodiversity and Phylodiversity: Insights on Post‐Fire Forest Communities
articles.abstract: Fire is a fundamental process that structures community assembly and biodiversity patterns; however, altered disturbance regimes associated with anthropogenic change present a major threat to fire‐adapted systems. Reintroducing fire to increase pyrodiversity (spatiotemporal diversity in fire) has been identified as an important step in restoring fire‐adapted western temperate forests. Here, we utilize phylogenetic and taxonomic metrics to assess how pyrodiversity influences plant community assembly dynamics and diversity patterns in the central Sierra Nevada, California, USA. Compared to fire exclusion, regional taxonomic and phylogenetic diversity generally increased after fire. Further, with increased pyrodiversity, community assembly mechanisms diversified and occurrences of diverse plant lineages and local phylogenetic endemism increased, illustrating how evolutionary history influences responses of plants to pyrodiversity. These results demonstrate the importance of restoring mixed‐severity fire to these systems and how phylogenetic tools can provide a valuable way to understand and monitor restoration impacts.

articles.title: Long‐term demographic study reveals stabilizing mechanisms of salt marsh plants under climate change
articles.abstract: Read the free Plain Language Summary for this article on the Journal blog. Abstract Despite its critical importance for biodiversity conservation, population persistence in multiple habitats under climate change has rarely been evaluated using long-term demographic data. Furthermore, the drivers of population growth and the contributions of different demographic rates to population growth rates are likely to vary across habitats. Here, we parameterized size-dependent integral projection models (IPMs) using 23 years of data on the clonal salt marsh plant Spartina alterniflora in two habitats at eight sites in coastal Georgia (USA) to investigate spatiotemporal variation in population dynamics and the driving mechanisms. Compared with environmental factors, population density was the strongest predictor of asymptotic population growth rates (λ) of S. alterniflora in nearly all creekbank and mid-marsh habitats, with population dynamics exhibiting pronounced negative density dependence. Creekbank populations compensated for a low contribution of clonal reproduction number to population growth by increasing recruit size, resulting in effective demographic compensation and similar population fitness between habitats at most sites. Together, negative density dependence and demographic compensation acted as key mechanisms promoting population persistence, allowing most S. alterniflora populations to maintain positive cumulative population growth rates (λ c) across habitats. This study highlights the value of demographic analyses in clarifying population trends of species exhibiting high spatiotemporal variability and provides robust evidence for population persistence of salt marsh plants under climate change, emphasizing the crucial role of intrinsic population regulatory mechanisms in maintaining population stability. Read the free Plain Language Summary for this article on the Journal blog.

articles.title: Correction to “Status of Polar Blue Carbon: Toward Recognition and Integration in Marine Policy”
Woodland Decline Undermines Resilience in Fire‐Adapted Landscapes
articles.abstract: Open‐canopy forests and woodlands are a foundational component of historically fire‐adapted landscapes, yet their persistence under contemporary climate and fire regimes remains poorly understood. Here, we leverage historical aerial photogrammetry integrated with contemporary satellite imagery to assess landscape change, vegetation transitions, and ecological stability over a century (1930s–2020s) for a large regional landscape of the Interior Northwest. We found woodlands declined by more than 40% across the region and exhibited high rates of type conversion, with roughly half converting to closed‐canopy forests and a quarter transitioning to grass‐ and shrub‐dominated ecosystems. Forest area, in contrast, remained relatively stable over the same period as woodland‐to‐forest conversion compensated for forest losses. The widespread decline in woodlands demonstrates that they exist as a metastable state, created and maintained only under stable, low‐ and mixed‐severity fire regimes. The loss of these keystone ecosystems portends the erosion of landscape resilience—as remaining woodlands disappear, their ability to buffer for forest losses will decline as well, increasing the risk of abrupt and persistent ecosystem transitions under shifting fire regimes and warmer future climates.

articles.title: Lymphatic constraint of germinal centers optimizes protective antibody responses
articles.abstract: Lymphatic vessel networks remodel during infection to regulate antigen and immune cell dynamics, yet whether these changes impact humoral immunity remains unknown. Mudianto et al. demonstrate that lymph node lymphangiogenesis encapsulates activating germinal centers to constrain their size, which enhances clonal selection and protective antibody responses, establishing lymphatic vessels as structural determinants of germinal center fitness.

articles.title: Single-cell analyses of global cohorts outline determinants of immune aging and link the ratio of GZMK+ to GZMB+ Tem cells to health trajectories
articles.abstract: Terekhova et al. assemble a single-cell PBMC atlas of 8 datasets, 2,609 individuals, and over 12 million cells to dissect variable and conserved features of human immune aging. CD8+ Tem GZMK+ to GZMB+ ratio distinguishes healthy from disease-associated trajectories and predicts mortality risk. This work provides a clinically relevant marker for monitoring human aging.

Machine learning accelerated exploration of the global high pressure phase diagram
40S ribosome remodeling triggers 18S rRNA U-tailing and DIS3L2-dependent decay
articles.abstract: Translational perturbations trigger ubiquitination and turnover of 40S ribosomes, yet how these events are coupled remains unclear. Shah et al. reveal that RIOK3 remodels ubiquitinated 40S subunits, exposing the 3′ end of 18S rRNA for uridylation and subsequent DIS3L2-mediated degradation. These findings link ribosomal protein ubiquitination to selective rRNA turnover.

articles.title: Oligo(uridine) tailing and exonucleolytic decay drive 40S ribosome degradation in response to stress
articles.abstract: 40S ribosomes are degraded in diverse stress conditions. Diehl et al. find that in response to stress, TUT7 is recruited to ubiquitylated 40S ribosomes and adds 3′ oligo(U) tails to the 18S rRNA. Iterative uridylation and 3′-5′ decay by the exonuclease DIS3L2 drive 18S rRNA and ultimately 40S ribosome degradation.

articles.title: Bottlenecked but Booming: Strong Inbreeding in a Highly Invasive Freshwater Mussel
articles.abstract: The ‘genetic paradox of invasions’ refers to successful invasive populations originating from low founder numbers. Theory predicts that such invaders should exhibit reduced genetic diversity and increased inbreeding, which should restrict their evolutionary potential and often lead to inbreeding depression. Here, we provide evidence for an invader succeeding against these odds by demonstrating strikingly strong inbreeding in a highly successful, invasive freshwater mussel. Using whole‐genome resequencing data, we show that zebra mussels (Dreissena polymorpha) from thriving invasive populations carry numerous and long runs of homozygosity (ROH) in their genomes, reflecting severe, sequential founder events followed by inbreeding during the invasion process. Additionally, predicted genetic load (accumulation of deleterious mutations) is correlated with inbreeding levels: more inbred invasive populations exhibit lower masked (i.e., heterozygous) but higher realised (i.e., homozygous) load compared to less inbred populations. These genomic consequences of inbreeding would be expected to decrease the fitness of invasives, but here have not prevented their success. Our study thus challenges conventional expectations that inbreeding and high numbers of putatively deleterious alleles should limit biological invasion success. This research provides a compelling example of an invader that defies genetic expectations, and is therefore broadly relevant for understanding invasion success and dynamics across taxa.

articles.title: Host and Environmental Factors Outweigh Pathogen in Shaping Skin Microbiome of a Threatened Andean Amphibian Community
articles.abstract: The fungal pathogen Batrachochytrium dendrobatidis (Bd) has driven severe amphibian declines across the Neotropics, yet some species persist under enzootic pathogen conditions following epizootics. We investigated whether skin bacterial communities and host mucosome activity contributed to the persistence of seven amphibian species in a once megadiverse Chocó‐Andean community that experienced drastic Bd‐associated declines. Across dry and wet seasons, we characterized skin bacterial communities using 16S rRNA metabarcoding and assessed mucosome‐mediated inhibition of a local Bd lineage using in vitro challenge assays. Host species identity was the strongest predictor of bacterial community composition, while season and reproductive mode, which were strongly associated with habitat use, also contributed to microbiome structure. Host phylogeny was associated with broad‐scale bacterial community patterns, whereas Bd infection status and intensity explained little variation. Putative Bd‐inhibitory bacteria were detected in all host species and occurred at greater relative abundance during the dry season and in species with aquatic larvae, but neither their richness nor abundance was associated with Bd infection or load. Mucosome assays showed little to no inhibition of Bd growth in most species; only Pristimantis laticlavius, one of the few species whose abundance increased following the historical Bd epizootic, exhibited slight inhibition. Overall, host identity, seasonality, and habitat‐associated reproductive mode, rather than current Bd infection, were the principal drivers of amphibian skin bacterial community composition. The widespread occurrence of putative Bd‐inhibitory bacteria and their enrichment in some persistent hosts are consistent with a potential microbiome‐mediated response, but limited mucosome activity indicates that the microbiome alone is unlikely to explain host persistence. Integrating host immune traits, pathogen characteristics, and environmental conditions will be necessary to understand long‐term host–pathogen coexistence in this threatened amphibian community.

articles.title: Spatial and Ecological Drivers of Diversification in the World's Southernmost Gecko
articles.abstract: Understanding the mechanisms driving genetic differentiation—and ultimately, speciation—is central to evolutionary biology, particularly in widespread species inhabiting environmentally complex landscapes. Homonota darwinii, a member of the H. whitii group, is the southernmost gecko in the world, distributed across the Patagonian Steppe—a vast, heterogeneous landscape with a complex geoclimatic history. This system offers an opportunity to assess the relative roles of geographic distance, environmental variation, and landscape resistance in diversification. We present a comprehensive dataset of > 700 geckos sampled over 20 years across > 1,000,000 km2 of southern South America. Using phylogeographic, landscape genomics and coalescent approaches, we examined patterns of population divergence and connectivity. Genomic data revealed geographically consistent groups and admixture in transitional zones. We identified three putative species‐level lineages corresponding to regional phylogeographic breaks shared by other taxa. Landscape genomic analyses indicated that isolation‐by‐environment (IBE), particularly climatic gradients related to aridity, temperature, and seasonality, was the primary driver of genetic divergence. We also identified genomic variants associated with local adaptation. Our results suggest that H. darwinii expanded into the Patagonian Steppe during the Pliocene, with persistence facilitated by adaptations to arid conditions. Within the H. whitii group, we found evidence supporting a hybrid speciation model for Homonota williamsii, involving roughly equal genomic contributions from two H. darwinii genetic groups. This study highlights the interplay of spatial, ecological and historical factors in shaping genetic structure and adaptation. It also provides a framework for taxonomic and conservation initiatives, especially given prior projections of climate‐driven population decline in H. darwinii.

articles.title: Breaking symmetry for better catalysis
articles.abstract: Sulfides catalyse aromatic halogenations but often struggle with less reactive arenes. Now, breaking the symmetry of existing sulfide catalysts allows sulfur orbital interactions that can expand the scope of these reactions.

articles.title: Unanticipated intermediates during isopenicillin N synthase catalysis identified by time-resolved X-ray free-electron laser studies
articles.abstract: The structural basis of key intermediates in isopenicillin N synthase catalysis, underlying β-lactam biosynthesis, has remained incomplete. Now time-resolved X-ray free-electron laser studies capture transient states and reveal how protein dynamics and solvent networks govern oxygen activation and ring formation.

articles.title: Reversible Sn4+/Sn0 anode for high-energy-density flow batteries
articles.abstract: Tin-based aqueous flow batteries offer high-capacity anodes due to the potential four-electron redox reactions, but irreversible Sn4+/Sn2+ electrochemistry has hindered battery development. Now it has been shown that iodide-mediated intermediate complexes enable reversible Sn4+/Sn2+ conversion and four-electron Sn4+/Sn0 chemistry, yielding a high anolyte energy density and stable long-term operation.

articles.title: Lift from the flow
Order from chaos with adaptive circuits on quantum hardware
articles.abstract: Programmable quantum devices provide a platform for controlling the coherent dynamics of quantum wave functions. Monitoring and feedback can control classically chaotic dynamics, but extending these approaches to quantum systems is challenging because chaotic evolution amplifies perturbations and is sensitive to noise and decoherence. Here we demonstrate adaptive monitored quantum circuits that incorporate conditional feedback into non-unitary evolution, using local mid-circuit measurements and resets to control quantum chaotic dynamics. We perform the experiments on an IBM superconducting quantum processor with up to 100 qubits, implementing a quantum version of the classically chaotic Bernoulli map. The map scrambles quantum information, whereas local measurements and feedback attempt to steer the dynamics towards a fixed point of the map. This competition drives a dynamical phase transition between quantum and classical dynamics, which we observe experimentally and describe theoretically using noisy simulations, matrix product states and mappings to statistical mechanics models. By successfully applying up to nearly 5,000 entangling gates and 5,000 non-unitary mid-circuit operations on systems up to 100 qubits, the quantum processor yields accurate estimates of the universal critical properties. Controlling quantum chaos requires using measurement and feedback that survive noise and decoherence. Such control is now achieved in a superconducting quantum processor and reveals a critical transition between quantum and classical dynamics.

You should advertise your conference
articles.abstract: Participation in conferences is a great way to learn about a new field and make connections across international and disciplinary boundaries. However, that can only happen if people know where to go.

articles.title: The urgent challenge of gastroesophageal cancer
articles.abstract: Gastric and oesophageal cancers caused more than 1 million deaths worldwide in 2024. In this Comment, Cancer Grand Challenges explain how they have launched two targeted challenges to address this unmet need, inviting global interdisciplinary teams to apply for up to US $34 million in funding from the Torrey Coast Foundation and Cancer Research UK and move the dial towards the prevention of gastroesophageal cancer.

articles.title: LAG3 checkpoint function and its mechanism of action in therapeutic targeting
articles.abstract: This Review explores how the immune checkpoint receptor lymphocyte activation gene 3 (LAG3) suppresses T cell activity through newly defined signalling mechanisms, including tonic and ligand-induced pathways. The Review highlights therapeutic advances, biomarker strategies and emerging opportunities to target LAG3 in cancer and autoimmune disease.

articles.title: Metastasizing cancer cells leave an immunogenic trail
articles.abstract: Metastasizing cancer cells release migrasomes containing tumour-specific antigens that can promote T cell responses.

articles.title: The role of the respiratory microbiome in acute and chronic respiratory diseases
articles.abstract: In this Review, Heinzinger, Segal and Dickson summarize recent advances in our understanding of the respiratory microbiome in health, examine how it is altered in acute and chronic respiratory diseases, and discuss its diagnostic and therapeutic potential.

articles.title: Breakdown of the Kerr-Cat Qubit Tunneling Time Induced by Auxiliary Circuit Modes
articles.abstract: Researchers show that auxiliary circuit modes trigger multiphoton resonances that break down Kerr-cat qubit coherence under strong driving.

articles.title: Fluidic Hysterons and Memory in Flow Networks
articles.abstract: Soft elastic fibers in microfluidic channels can create a fluid system with memory of previous actions through a flow-structure feedback.

articles.title: Next-generation materials and devices by combustion processes
B1-like innate B cells are present in adult human organs in homeostasis
articles.abstract: Innate-like B cells produce natural antibodies and include marginal zone (MZ) B cells and B1 cells. B1 cells are well characterized in mice, where they prenatally seed serous cavities and produce regulatory cytokines. Putative B1 cells have been identified in human prenatal organs, but whether they persist into adulthood remains unclear. Here, we identified B1-like cells in the IgM + and IgA + memory compartment across adult human organs. These cells transcriptionally resembled murine and human prenatal B1 cells but not MZ B cells. They expressed canonical murine B1 cell markers, including AHNAK , and spontaneously secreted IgM. B cell receptor sequencing of paired kidney-spleen samples revealed lower diversity and mutation rates in kidney IgM/IgA clones, suggesting spleen-independent seeding. Adult B1-like cells expressed the regulatory cytokine TGFB and had abundant inferred interactions with tissue myeloid cells, which reciprocally expressed B cell prosurvival cytokines. These findings support the presence of B1-like cells across adult human organs in homeostasis.

articles.title: Follicle-associated epithelial tuft cells amplify type 2 mucosal immunity and IgA production
articles.abstract: Peyer’s patches (PPs) in the intestinal mucosa coordinate antibody responses to luminal microbes and dietary antigens. The follicle-associated epithelium (FAE) is traditionally recognized by the presence of microfold cells (M cells) that mediate antigen sampling in PPs. By analyzing Gfi1b -eGFP reporter mice and human PP biopsies, we identified tuft cells as an additional, evolutionarily conserved FAE population that regulates mucosal immunity. Using mouse models and intestinal organoids, we demonstrate that M cells and tuft cells are distinct lineages arising from Pou2f3 + progenitors, whose differentiation is reciprocally regulated by RANKL and interleukin-13 (IL-13), respectively. Tuft cell–derived IL-25 activates type 2 innate lymphoid cells (ILC2s) in PPs. Furthermore, IL-13 production by ILC2 enhances immunoglobulin A class switching and antigen-specific immunity. These findings reveal a dual surveillance system in the FAE, where developmentally related epithelial lineages use distinct mechanisms to coordinate mucosal immunity.

articles.title: The IKK complex and TBK1/IKKε are recruited to STING through distinct mechanisms to activate NF-κB signaling
articles.abstract: Stimulator of interferon genes (STING) is a highly conserved signaling molecule that coordinates an antiviral innate immune response through activation of the nuclear factor κB (NF-κB) and interferon regulatory factor 3 (IRF3) signaling pathways. In addition to an antiviral response, STING-mediated NF-κB signaling also leads to an inflammatory response, which can cause substantial pathology. However, the molecular mechanism whereby STING drives inflammation is poorly understood, and this has hindered the development of anti-inflammatory strategies targeting this pathway. Here, we define an evolutionarily conserved mechanism whereby STING activates NF-κB signaling via recruitment of inhibitor of NF-κB kinase subunit γ (IKKγ) in an M1-linked ubiquitin-dependent manner. We also show that the more recently evolved carboxyl-terminal tail of STING cooperates with the IKKγ-IKK complex for NF-κB–dependent expression of pro-inflammatory genes in mammalian cells through the kinases TBK1 (TANK-binding kinase 1)/IKKε. Thus, the expression of the key inflammatory genes CCL3 and CCL4 requires the formation of M1-linked ubiquitin and the activation of NF-κB, but we do not detect a role for IRF3 in STING-driven NF-κB signaling.

articles.title: Invasive interval breast cancer rates after digital breast tomosynthesis plus synthesised mammography versus digital mammography screening (TOSYMA): 24-month follow-up of the multicentre, open-label, randomised, controlled, superiority trial
articles.abstract: BackgroundDespite high invasive breast cancer detection rates, the effectiveness of digital breast tomosynthesis screening is still uncertain. We aimed to compare the invasive interval cancer rates in women screened with digital breast tomosynthesis plus synthesised two-dimensional (s2D) mammography with those screened with digital mammography.MethodsTOSYMA is a multicentre, open-label, parallel-group, randomised, controlled, superiority trial done at 17 screening sites across two federal states in Germany. Women aged 50-70 years were randomly allocated (1:1) to digital breast tomosynthesis plus s2D mammography or digital mammography. The first primary endpoint of TOSYMA (TOSYMA-1) was the detection rate of invasive breast cancer and has been previously reported. The second primary endpoint (TOSYMA-2) was the invasive interval cancer rate, defined as the proportion of women who developed an invasive breast cancer in the 24-month interval after being negative at screening (ie, no ductal carcinoma in situ or invasive breast cancer detection) in TOSYMA-1. The primary endpoint was analysed in all participants with a negative screening result in TOSYMA-1. The cumulative incidence of invasive interval cancers at 12 months in screen-negative women was the prespecified secondary outcome. Suspected interval cancers were identified by data linkage to cancer registries. The study is registered on ClinicalTrials.gov (NCT03377036) and is closed to accrual but follow-up is ongoing.FindingsBetween July 5, 2018, and Dec 30, 2020, 99 689 women were enrolled in TOSYMA-1 and 99 558 participants included in the modified full analysis set of TOSYMA-1. The median age was 57 years (IQR 53-62) in the TOSYMA-2 modified full analysis set and all participants were female. 49 299 (99·1%) of 49 762 women assigned digital breast tomosynthesis plus s2D mammography screened negative in TOSYMA-1, as were 49 456 (99·3%) of 49 796 women assigned digital mammography who had evaluable data and were included in the TOSYMA-2 modified full analysis set. Invasive interval cancers were detected in 70 of 49 299 women in the digital breast tomosynthesis plus s2D mammography group (invasive interval rate 14·2 cases per 10 000 women screened with a negative result) and in 92 of 49 456 women in the digital mammography group (18·6 cases per 10 000 women screened with a negative result; adjusted odds ratio [OR] 0·76 [95% CI 0·55-1·06]; p=0·11). Invasive interval cancers were detected within 12 months in 22 women in the digital breast tomosynthesis plus s2D mammography group (4·5 cases per 10 000 women screened with a negative result) and in 31 women in the digital mammography group (6·3 cases per 10 000 women screened with a negative result; OR 0·71 [95% CI 0·52-0·97]).InterpretationTOSYMA-2 indicates that about a quarter of invasive interval cancers occurring with digital mammography over 2 years might be avoided with digital breast tomosynthesis plus s2D mammography screening. Although the primary outcome of TOSYMA-2 did not reach statistical significance, this large, randomised trial adds substantial evidence to the use of digital breast tomosynthesis plus s2D mammography in breast cancer screening.FundingDeutsche Forschungsgemeinschaft (German Research Foundation).

articles.title: Time to say goodbye to full-field digital mammography in population-based screening?
Metabolic enzymes moonlighting as protein kinases and phosphatases
articles.abstract: Protein phosphorylation is a central and reversible mechanism regulating virtually all cellular processes and is classically mediated by the canonical protein kinome and phosphatome. However, beyond their traditional roles as metabolic catalysts, a subset of metabolic enzymes also exhibits noncanonical ‘moonlighting’ activities as protein kinases or phosphatases, directly linking metabolic states to phosphorylation-dependent signaling. These unexpected functions of enzymes involved in glucose, fructose, lipid, nucleotide, and creatine metabolism influence a broad spectrum of cellular processes, including chromatin remodeling, transcription, cell cycle progression, metabolism, autophagy, cell survival and death, and immune responses. As a result, metabolic enzymes are increasingly recognized as key regulators that bridge cellular metabolism and signaling networks, with important implications for both normal physiology and disease.

articles.title: Improving the promise of drone seeding for restoration
articles.abstract: Drone seeding is expanding as a restoration tool, yet evidence of ecological effectiveness remains limited and outcomes are highly variable. Our synthesis of global initiatives suggests drone seeding should target landscapes where conventional restoration is constrained and ecological conditions support seedling recruitment. Standardized monitoring and reporting of outcomes are essential.

articles.title: Trait-based inference of fragmentation-driven extinction risk
articles.abstract: Habitat fragmentation is a leading cause of plant extinctions, yet predicting which species are most vulnerable remains a key challenge. We propose that population connectivity, and thus gene flow via pollination and seed dispersal, can be inferred from plant traits. We integrate these traits into a connectivity–trait dimension, which, together with breeding system, life-history traits, and landscape context, ranks species at risk of genetic erosion and local extinction, providing an early-warning triage tool. By linking traits to gene flow mechanisms, the framework helps prioritise investment in detailed population genetic analyses and provides a scalable tool to identify species most at risk of genetic inbreeding and extinction in fragmented landscapes.

articles.title: A fluctuation test for gastruloid heterogeneity
articles.abstract: Organoids grown side by side under identical conditions vary unpredictably, a longstanding obstacle to their use. Adapting the logic of a classic fluctuation test to gastruloids grown from single stem cells shows that this variability is largely inherited rather than induced and is traceable to fluctuations in the state of the founding cell.

articles.title: Arabidopsis uses distinct coumarins and bacterial pathways for pH-adaptive iron acquisition
articles.abstract: Arabidopsis coordinates Fe acquisition with its root microbiota by releasing distinct coumarin chemotypes in response to environmental pH. These root-exuded specialized metabolites interact with root-associated bacteria to mobilize Fe either through bacterial siderophore-dependent chelation at circumneutral pH or through bacterial redox-sensing-controlled reduction at acidic pH.

articles.title: Comprehensive lineage tracing maps the landscape of cell fate decisions in mouse embryogenesis
articles.abstract: We use PEtracer to reconstruct high-resolution lineage histories for >1.4 million cells from E7.5 to E10.0 during mouse development, providing a quantitative view of fate bias, restriction timing, and clonal output. Across diverse tissues, these data reveal highly reproducible lineage architectures and define general and tissue-specific strategies of cell fate specification.

articles.title: Immunoregulatory gene GIMAP6 suppresses lethal atherosclerotic vasculopathy and ischemic heart failure
articles.abstract: By destabilizing the endothelium and promoting macrophage lipid loading and inflammation, GIMAP6 deficiency drives atherosclerosis and ischemic heart disease through a mechanism that operates without hyperlipidemia, yet hyperlipidemia significantly exacerbates disease progression.

articles.title: Disrupting BRD4-BD1-p62 engagement restores protective autophagy
articles.abstract: Autophagy is impaired in idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis. Zhang et al. identify a BRD4-BD1-selective inhibitor that disrupts BRD4-BD1–p62 engagement, restores protective autophagy, and attenuates pulmonary fibrosis, revealing a druggable mechanism linking epigenetic regulation to autophagy.

articles.title: Native pathogen-phage networks reveal multilayered defense and gut-active anti-phage immunity
articles.abstract: Wang et al. map >1,000 interactions between Salmonella isolates and bacteriophages to measure the relative contributions of surface features and intracellular defense to phage resistance across a major human pathogen. They further identify AppA, which blocks DNA packaging by targeting the large terminase and restricts phage replication within mammalian hosts.

articles.title: A spatiotemporal atlas of radiation-induced brain injury reveals dysfunction of the blood-CSF barrier
articles.abstract: Quan et al. construct a spatiotemporal transcriptomic atlas of radiation-induced brain injury and show that loss of radiosensitive Tmsb4x+ choroid plexus epithelial cells triggers blood-CSF barrier dysfunction and macrophage infiltration that sustains interferon-responsive microglial activation. These findings position the blood-CSF barrier as a potential target for mitigating post-irradiation neuroinflammation.

articles.title: Human genetic evidence challenges NCOA1 as a monogenic obesity gene
articles.abstract: Delplanque et al. combine large-scale human genetics with functional analyses to reassess the role of NCOA1 in obesity. Despite its biological plausibility within the melanocortin pathway, pathogenic NCOA1 variants were not associated with adiposity, questioning their relevance for precision obesity therapies targeting this pathway.

articles.title: Lipid-engineered antibody-based therapeutics target inflamed joints and lymph nodes to enhance rheumatoid arthritis treatment
articles.abstract: Zhao et al. attach multiple lipid motifs to antibody-based biologic disease-modifying anti-rheumatic drugs (bDMARDs), enabling them to engage multiple albumin molecules in vivo and enhancing their accumulation in inflamed joints and lymph nodes. This generalizable strategy can target therapeutics larger than albumin to inflammatory sites for improved rheumatoid arthritis treatment.

articles.title: Microbiota-mediated naringenin release limits postoperative acute gastrointestinal injury by suppressing ferroptosis
articles.abstract: Deng et al. show that reduced preoperative fecal naringenin and β-glucuronidase activity associate with postoperative acute gastrointestinal injury after cardiopulmonary bypass. Mechanistically, microbial β-glucuronidase promotes naringenin release and limits epithelial ferroptosis, highlighting candidate noninvasive biomarkers and a potential microbiota-based intervention axis.

articles.title: Prognostic value of cfDNA methylation in locally advanced esophageal squamous cell cancer treated with neoadjuvant immunochemoradiotherapy
articles.abstract: Chen et al. track cfDNA methylation during neoadjuvant immunochemoradiotherapy for esophageal squamous cell carcinoma. Methylation signals decline with treatment and are associated with pathological response and disease-free survival. The decline is reproduced in a separate 30-patient cohort, supporting further evaluation of cfDNA methylation for noninvasive monitoring.

articles.title: Reviving low-affinity glycan-targeting CAR with combinatorial design
articles.abstract: Forcados et al. develop and test a combinatorial CAR strategy against B cell lymphoma, in which they combine CD75s and CD19 targeting. This combinatorial approach overcomes the limited efficiency of CD75s mono-targeting and lowers the risk of CAR-related toxicity seen with CD19 single targeting.

articles.title: Interfacial reaction-network catalysis: steering complex transformations through physical mixing
articles.abstract: Physical mixing as a modular strategy for interfacial reaction-network catalysis, steering complex transformations through intermediate relay, catalytic shunting and thermodynamic cascading.

articles.title: Unraveling complexity: advances in metal-catalyzed sequential double hydrofunctionalization of alkynes
articles.abstract: This review comprehensively summarizes metal-catalyzed sequential double hydrofunctionalization of alkynes (SDHFA), covering diverse reaction types and selectivity patterns, and highlighting representative mechanisms and synthetic applications.

articles.title: A multiscale assessment of general resilience capacity in China’s coastal social-ecological systems: a national baseline and nested diagnosis in Rongcheng
articles.abstract: IntroductionCoastal social-ecological systems face climate change, resource exploitation, and fragmented governance. Hazard-specific assessments cannot fully represent their capacity to cope with uncertain disturbances, while connections between nationally consistent screening and fine-scale local diagnosis remain limited.MethodsDrawing on general resilience theory, we developed a three-tier, ten-attribute framework linking a national baseline with a nested assessment in Rongcheng. Coastal land and marine subsystems were evaluated using a nominal 2025 temporal window that incorporated the closest reliable products for slowly updated variables. The analysis included indicator standardization, scale-specific weighting, composite assessment, Jenks natural breaks classification, and spatial autocorrelation analysis.ResultsThe mean general resilience capacity indices were 0.359 for national coastal land and 0.470 for national coastal waters. Low and relatively low classes accounted for 39.75% of national coastal land, whereas moderate and relatively high classes accounted for 65.48% of national coastal waters. In Rongcheng, moderate and relatively low classes jointly represented 68.30% of coastal land. Relatively low and relatively high classes accounted for 56.33% of coastal waters, with a coefficient of variation of 0.282, indicating pronounced intra-bay heterogeneity.DiscussionThe national assessment provides a consistent baseline for broad-scale screening, whereas the Rongcheng assessment identifies bay- and shoreline-scale units for future field verification. Because the assessments differ in indicators, weights, and spatial supports, their results should be interpreted within their respective scales rather than compared directly. Scale-matched monitoring and governance feedback can connect national screening with local diagnosis.

articles.title: Contrasting species composition between common and rare woody species in the intake area of the South-to-North Water Diversion Project
articles.abstract: Understanding the species composition and structural dynamics of both common and rare species in forest communities is fundamental to comprehending forest ecosystem functioning. The intake area of the South-to-North Water Diversion Project, recognized as an ecologically sensitive region, harbors forest communities that play a pivotal role in water resource conservation and regional environmental stability. A thorough investigation into the species composition and distributional patterns of common and rare species within this area provides critical scientific insights into biodiversity conservation and community assembly mechanisms. To address these questions, we established 36 permanent plots of 20 × 20 m in the intake area of Nanyang City, Henan Province. Within each plot, we systematically surveyed all woody species and subsequently analyzed their species composition, diameter- and height-class structure, as well as the sexual system composition of both common and rare species. Our results revealed that: (1) A total of 2, 210 woody individuals were recorded in the intake area, belonging to 26 families, 33 genera, and 39 species. Common species exhibited absolute dominance in both individual abundance and importance value. (2) Species accumulation curves showed a sharp increase in species number when plot counts were below 20, followed by a marked deceleration thereafter. (3) Common species dominated across all diameter and height classes, while rare species were largely confined to diameter class II (5 cm ≤ DBH < 10 cm) and height class III (6 m ≤ H < 9 m), indicating a conspicuous growth-stage bottleneck. (4) Common species were predominantly monoecious plant, whereas hermaphroditic species occurred mainly as rare species. Collectively, these findings demonstrate that common and rare species jointly underpin the stand structural integrity, species diversity, and long-term successional potential of the forest community in intake area.

articles.title: Land use intensification results in abrupt transitions between extensively and intensively managed grasslands
articles.abstract: Read the free Plain Language Summary for this article on the Journal blog. Abstract Understanding whether land use intensification causes regime shifts (i.e. persistent, large changes in ecosystem states) is of key importance for management, particularly if these shifts occur abruptly as thresholds in land use intensity are crossed. Further, these threshold responses can show hysteretic dynamics, where the transition between states cannot simply be undone by reducing land use intensity to its initial level, and instead larger changes are required. However, quantitative evidence for threshold responses and their dynamics remain scarce. Here we use a unique, long‐term grassland database in Germany to identify threshold responses to land use intensity. We include data on the response of 16 ecosystem functions (including plant biomass, herbivory, litter decomposition, pathogen infection, water recharge, C and N fluxes and retention and enzymatic activity) and the diversity of 21 taxa (including above‐ground and below‐ground taxa such as vascular plants, lichens, bryophytes, arthropods, vertebrates, fungi, protists and bacteria). Then, we use increased variance as an early warning signal to evaluate if threshold responses are indicative of critical transitions between states. Finally, we use temporal data to identify hysteretic dynamics associated with those transitions. We show that 5 out of 10 above‐ground taxa, fungal diversity, shoot biomass and soil N retention showed threshold responses to land use intensity, that is abrupt changes between extensively and intensively managed grasslands. Some of the thresholds were associated with increased variance in the response variables, suggesting a potential critical transition between ecosystem states. Time‐series analysis indicated that ecosystem functions showed a hysteretic response to land use intensity, but diversity measures did not. Our results suggest threshold responses to land use intensity are relatively common in the grasslands we studied. These thresholds show abrupt changes in the ecosystem when highly diverse extensively managed grasslands are managed slightly more intensively. Further, shifting back to the functioning seen in extensively managed grasslands may be challenging, as it requires larger reductions in land use intensity than those required to shift to the high intensity state. Identifying thresholds along land use gradients is critical to prevent ecosystem degradation and conserve biodiversity and ecosystem functions in semi‐natural grasslands. Read the free Plain Language Summary for this article on the Journal blog. Resumen Identificar cambios de régimen (i.e. grandes cambios persistentes en los estados de los ecosistemas) a lo largo del proceso de intensificación agraria es fundamental para la gestión, especialmente si estos cambios ocurren de forma abrupta al cruzar determinados umbrales de intensificación. Además, estos umbrales pueden mostrar dinámicas de histéresis, donde la transición entre estados no se puede revertir simplemente reduciendo la intensificación a niveles previos al cambio, sino que son necesarias reducciones mayores. Sin embargo, faltan evidencias cuantitativas de la existencia de estos umbrales y su dinámica asociada. En este trabajo utilizamos una base de datos longitudinal en Alemania para identificar respuestas umbrales a lo largo de un gradiente de intensificación agraria. Esta base de datos incluye la respuesta de 16 funciones del ecosistema (incluyendo biomasa vegetal, herbivoría, descomposición de hojarasca, infección por patógenos, recarga hídrica, flujos y retenciones de C y N, y actividades enzimáticas) y la diversidad de 21 taxones (incluyendo taxones superficiales y subterráneos como plantas vasculares, líquenes, briófitos, artrópodos, vertebrados, hongos, protistas y bacterias).…

articles.title: Climate Warming Impaired the CO2 Sink Capacity and Efficiency in a Suaeda salsa‐Dominated Salt Marsh
articles.abstract: Salt marshes are among the most valuable carbon sinks globally but are highly vulnerable to ongoing climate warming, which profoundly affects ecosystem photosynthesis and respiration and may therefore alter their CO2 sink capacity and efficiency. However, whether climate warming will enhance or reduce the function of salt marshes to act as CO2 sinks remains uncertain. Here, we investigated the interannual variations in salt marsh CO2 sink capacity (net ecosystem exchange, NEE) and efficiency (ecosystem carbon use efficiency, CUE) in response to climate warming, using a long‐term eddy covariance dataset (2011–2024) from the Yellow River Delta, supplemented by a manipulative warming experiment (2017–2021) and a multi‐site eddy covariance dataset spanning China and North America (68 site‐years). At the study site, we quantified multiyear mean values for NEE as −107 ± 59 g C m−2 year−1 and for CUE as 0.41 ± 0.16, both of which showed strong interannual variability. Moreover, rising temperatures were primarily and negatively associated with yearly changes in CO2 sink capacity and efficiency, and these relationships were closely linked to lower gross primary production. The warming experiment further showed that the warming‐induced reductions in CO2 sink capacity and efficiency were accompanied by increased soil salinity and reduced plant growth. Similar negative associations between temperature and both CO2 sink capacity and efficiency were also observed at several sites in the multi‐site dataset. Overall, this study improves our understanding of the coupling between climate warming and the CO2 sink function of salt marshes and suggests that continued warming may reduce net atmospheric CO2 uptake across this biome in the future.

articles.title: Correction to “Jaguar Range‐Wide Connectivity: Prioritising Core Areas and Corridors Between and Within Protected Areas and Indigenous Lands”
Co‐Benefits of Intercropping on Crop Productivity, Soil Organic Carbon Sequestration and N2O Mitigation
articles.abstract: Intercropping is a promising sustainable agriculture practice, but its adoption is hindered by the potential reduction in benefits when shifting from monoculture to intercropping, especially if there are trade‐offs between yield, soil organic carbon (SOC) and nitrous oxide (N2O) emissions. In this study, we synthesized 3843 paired observations from 510 field‐based studies that compared the yields, SOC and N2O emissions of intercropping systems (only crop‐crop intercropping for grain yield and including crop‐tree agroforestry in addition to crop‐crop intercropping for SOC and N2O) with monoculture systems. Our meta‐analysis revealed that on average, intercropping increased grain yields by 22.3%, calorie production by 16.1% and protein yields by 14.4%, while reducing N2O emissions by 14.3%. Legume‐based intercropping was found to be more effective than non‐legume intercropping. Intercropping also significantly increased SOC content, with crop‐tree agroforestry outperforming crop‐crop intercropping (average increases of 15.5% and 6.1%, respectively). However, the effectiveness of intercropping systems varies depending on climate, soil properties and management practices. Based on data‐driven machine learning models, our upscaling analyses show that converting monoculture land to cereal‐legume intercropping could increase grain yields by 5.35 × 108 Mg yr.−1, potentially feeding nearly 1013 million people. This conversion could also enhance SOC stocks by 2.84 Pg C yr.−1 and reduce N2O emissions by 625 Gg N yr.−1, resulting in a reduction of 10.6 Pg CO2‐eq yr.−1 for net global warming potential. Overall, converting monoculture systems to intercropping could generate approximately US$595 billion in economic benefits annually. These findings highlight the critical role of intercropping as a scalable nature‐based solution for addressing the dual challenges of global food security and climate change.

articles.title: Seeing Species Where They Are Not: Why eDNA Needs Better Taxonomic Standards
Microglia-mediated extracellular matrix disruption drives neuronal dysfunction, motor impairments, and sedation following alcohol abuse
articles.abstract: Alcohol’s brain effects are attributed to neurons, leaving microglial functional involvement untested. Paouri, Stanko, et al. show that microglia drive alcohol-induced sedation, motor impairment, and synaptic and neuronal loss through MyD88-dependent perisynaptic extracellular matrix (ECM) disruption. Equivalent neuron-targeted sedation bypassing microglia spares the ECM. Brain ECM loss also marks human alcohol use disorder, identifying a therapeutic target distinct from neuronal interventions.

articles.title: No effect of short‐term exposure to ocean acidification on individual‐level variation in behaviour and susceptibility to predation in a Great Barrier Reef damselfish
articles.abstract: This study shows that projected ocean acidification does not alter behaviour or predation risk in coral reef fish, challenging earlier assumptions. By quantifying consistent individual‐level behavioural differences and relating individual traits to survival during a live‐predation trial, it also provides evidence for a boldness–predation trade‐off in a small‐bodied demersal fish. Abstract Ocean acidification, caused by rising carbon dioxide (CO2) in the atmosphere, has been reported to negatively impact a wide variety of behaviours in fishes, including activity, exploration, and predator avoidance. These effects have been documented at the population level, but many animal species naturally show large and repeatable individual‐level differences in behaviour. How environmental stressors, such as ocean acidification, affect behavioural variation at the individual level remains largely unknown but is vital in understanding adaptation given natural selection operates on variation at the individual rather than population level. Using a statistical approach allowing variation in means and variation in variance to be modelled within a single framework, we quantified individual‐level differences across five behaviours in the coral reef Ambon damselfish Pomacentrus amboinensis (emergence time, activity level, time spent sheltering, thigmotaxis and novel object inspection). We measured behaviour in a novel environment assay, twice before (CO2 ~450 μatm) and twice following 4–6 days of exposure to predicted end‐of‐century ocean acidification conditions (~1100 μatm). Following behavioural assays, we tested individual survival in a live predation experiment. We used predatory rock cod, Cephalopholis microprion, acclimated to the same CO2 treatments as Ambon damsels and examined predictors of survival probability. All behaviours in damselfish were moderately and significantly repeatable, with no marked differences in repeatability estimates between the ambient CO2 and elevated CO2 treatment groups. Exposure to end‐of‐century ocean acidification conditions had no effect on any of the five behaviours measured, both in terms of group means and residual (within‐individual) variance. The probability of survival in the predation trials was similar for damselfish in the ambient and elevated CO2 treatment groups. Smaller damselfish as well as those that spent a greater amount of time inspecting a novel object (i.e. bolder individuals) had a lower probability of survival regardless of their CO2 treatment. Our results challenge assumptions about the impacts of ocean acidification on coral reef fish behaviour and susceptibility to predation, both at the population and individual level. They also provide support for a trade‐off between boldness and predation risk in fish. Résumé L'acidification des océans, causée par l'augmentation du dioxyde de carbone (CO2) atmosphérique, a été associée à des effets négatifs sur le comportement des poissons, notamment l'activité, l'exploration et l'évitement des prédateurs. Ces effets ont principalement été étudiés à l'échelle des populations, alors que de nombreuses espèces présentent d'importantes différences interindividuelles répétables dans leur comportement. Comment les facteurs de stress environnementaux influencent cette variation individuelle demeure largement inconnue, bien qu'elle soit essentielle à notre compréhension de l'adaptation. À l'aide d'une approche statistique permettant de modéliser simultanément les changements de moyenne et de variance, nous avons quantifié les différences interindividuelles dans cinq comportements chez le poisson‐demoiselle (Pomacentrus amboinensis): le temps d'émergence, le niveau d'activité, le temps passé à l'abri, la thigmotaxie et l'inspection d'un nouvel objet. Le comportement a été mesuré deux fois avant (CO2 ~ 450 μatm) et deux fois après une exposition à court terme aux conditions d'acidification prévues pour la fin du siècle (~1100 μatm).…

articles.title: Silver-driven valence modulation of NiFe active sites via self-stabilization enables robust high-current OER durability of Ag/NiFe layered double hydroxides
Coordination effect modulates surface metal coverage for boosting nitrate electroreduction to ammonia
Mitigating the toughness-efficiency trade-off in perovskite solar cells through electrospun nanofiber reinforcement
articles.abstract: Metal halide perovskites are promising photovoltaic materials but are mechanically fragile. Incorporating electrospun nylon nanofibers into the perovskite produces a mechanically reinforced photoactive composite with nearly 6-fold higher fracture energy while preserving photovoltaic performance.
